text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 1. PATIENT ARRIVAL]
Step 1 — Reception

Immediately establish:

Name/identity
Age
Gestational age
Gravida/para
Reason for attendance
Whether she is booked at the hospital
Any obvious emergency
Receptionist must immediately identify obvious danger signs

Do not leave a visibly unstable patient waiting.

Examples:

Heavy vaginal bleeding
Convulsion
Collapse/unconsciousness
Severe respiratory distress
Severe abdominal pain
Cord prolapse
Imminent delivery
Severe hypertension symptoms
Major trauma
Severe maternal deterioration

➡️ Call triage/labour ward team immediately.
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 2. INITIAL TRIAGE — TARGET WITHIN 15 MINUTES]
RCOG recommends that women attending maternity triage receive an initial midwife assessment within 15 minutes and then be prioritised using symptom-specific algorithms.

The initial triage is not the complete medical assessment.

Its purpose is:

Identify who cannot safely wait.
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 3. FIRST 60-SECOND SAFETY SCREEN]
Think:

A — Airway
Patent?
Speaking normally?
Stridor?
Facial/tongue swelling?
B — Breathing
Respiratory rate
SpO₂
Work of breathing
Chest pain
Cyanosis
C — Circulation
Pulse
BP
Capillary refill
Skin colour
Vaginal blood loss
IV access if unstable
D — Disability
Conscious level
GCS
Seizure
Severe headache
Visual disturbance
Confusion
E — Exposure/obstetric assessment
Vaginal bleeding
Liquor loss
Contractions
Abdominal pain
Fetal movements
Trauma
Temperature
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 4. INITIAL MATERNAL OBSERVATIONS]
Record:

| Parameter | Assess |
|---|---|
| BP | Hypertension/hypotension |
| Pulse | Tachycardia/bradycardia |
| RR | Respiratory compromise |
| SpO₂ | Hypoxaemia |
| Temperature | Infection/sepsis |
| Consciousness | GCS/mental state |
| Pain | Site, severity, onset |
| MEOWS/MEWS | Overall deterioration |
| Urine | Dipstick where appropriate |

Also determine:

Gestational age
Singleton/multiple pregnancy
Previous CS/uterine surgery
High-risk pregnancy
Placenta location if known
Blood group/Rh status if relevant
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 5. INITIAL OBSTETRIC QUESTIONS]
Use a rapid 5-domain history.

A. Labour

Ask:

Are there contractions?
When did they start?
Frequency?
Duration?
Increasing intensity?
Any urge to push?
Previous deliveries?
Previous rapid labour?
B. Membranes

Ask:

Has fluid leaked?
Gush or trickle?
Time of onset?
Colour?
Odour?
Continuous/intermittent?

Particularly:

Clear
Green/meconium
Blood-stained
Foul-smelling
C. Bleeding

Ask:

When?
How much?
Bright red/dark?
Clots?
Pain associated?
Previous placenta praevia?
Trauma/intercourse?
D. Fetal wellbeing

Ask:

Normal movements?
Reduced?
Absent?
Last definite movement?

For reduced fetal movement, current NHS guidance emphasises confirming the history, fetal viability, growth assessment and CTG, with ultrasound when indicated.

E. Maternal symptoms

Specifically ask about:

Headache
Visual disturbance
RUQ/epigastric pain
Breathlessness
Chest pain
Palpitations
Fever/rigors
Vomiting/diarrhoea
Dysuria
Flank pain
Calf pain/swelling
Severe itching
Trauma
Feeling generally unwell
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 6. ASSIGN TRIAGE CATEGORY]
🔴 LEVEL 1 — RED / IMMEDIATE
Principle

The patient cannot safely wait in triage.

Move directly to Labour Ward/Labour Room Operating Room/resuscitation area according to the emergency.

Senior obstetric review immediately.

RCOG similarly recommends that women classified as the highest urgency be transferred to the labour ward for assessment and that urgent cases receive senior obstetric review.

RED CONDITIONS
1. Imminent delivery

Examples:

Crowning
Fully dilated with pushing
Head on perineum
Delivery occurring
Severe urge to push with advanced labour
Immediate actions
Labour ward
Prepare delivery equipment
Senior obstetrician
Midwife
Neonatal team if indicated
IV access
Maternal observations
Fetal assessment
Prepare for neonatal resuscitation
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 2. ACTIVE SIGNIFICANT VAGINAL BLEEDING]
Especially:

Suspected placental abruption
Placenta praevia with significant bleeding
Massive APH
Bleeding + maternal instability
Bleeding + fetal compromise
Examine
Maternal haemodynamic status
Abdomen
Uterine tone/tenderness
Fetal status
DO NOT

Perform a digital vaginal examination until placenta praevia has been excluded when relevant.

Investigations
CBC
Group and save/crossmatch
Coagulation
Fibrinogen
Renal/liver function as clinically indicated
CTG if fetus viable and appropriate
Ultrasound for placental location when appropriate
Treatment

Depends on severity:

ABC
Oxygen if clinically indicated
Large-bore IV access
Blood products
Activate major haemorrhage protocol when indicated
Correct coagulopathy
Expedite birth if maternal/fetal compromise
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 3. ECLAMPSIA / SEVERE HYPERTENSIVE EMERGENCY]
Examples:

Seizure
Severe hypertension
Severe headache
Visual symptoms
RUQ/epigastric pain
Altered consciousness
Pulmonary oedema
Immediate management

ABCDE

Then:

Left lateral positioning
Protect airway
Oxygen if hypoxaemic
IV access
BP monitoring
Blood tests
Urine protein assessment
Fetal CTG
Magnesium sulfate for eclampsia/seizure prophylaxis according to protocol
Urgent antihypertensive treatment for severe hypertension
Senior obstetric/anaesthetic review
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 4. PATHOLOGICAL CTG]
If CTG shows severe fetal compromise:

➡️ Do not wait for routine triage assessment.

Immediate steps
Call senior obstetrician
Review CTG
Identify reversible causes
Maternal observations
Left lateral positioning where appropriate
Stop oxytocin if running
Treat hypotension
Assess contractions
Consider expedited birth
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 5. CORD PROLAPSE]
Immediate actions
Call emergency team
Relieve cord compression
Knee-chest/left lateral with elevation of presenting part
Avoid unnecessary handling of cord
Prepare immediate birth
Usually emergency CS unless vaginal birth is immediately achievable
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 6. MATERNAL COLLAPSE]
Potential causes include:

Haemorrhage
PE
Eclampsia
Sepsis
Arrhythmia
Hypoglycaemia
Anaesthetic complication
Amniotic fluid embolism
Cardiac disease

Management follows maternal resuscitation principles with simultaneous fetal considerations. RCOG emphasises that outcome depends on prompt and effective resuscitation.
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 7. SEVERE RESPIRATORY DISTRESS]
Examples:

Cannot speak full sentences
Severe hypoxaemia
Severe asthma
Suspected PE
Pulmonary oedema
Pneumonia/sepsis

➡️ Immediate ABC assessment and senior/anaesthetic/medical involvement.

🔶 LEVEL 2 — AMBER / EMERGENT
Principle

Potentially serious condition requiring assessment within 15 minutes.

Move to triage assessment area, but do not allow prolonged waiting.

Reassess approximately every 15 minutes or sooner if deteriorating.

AMBER CONDITIONS
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 1. PRETERM LABOUR]
Usually:

<37+0 weeks + regular contractions with cervical change.

Ask:

Contractions
Bleeding
Liquor
Pelvic pressure
Backache
Previous preterm birth

Examine:

Maternal observations
Abdomen
Uterine contractions
Fetal presentation
FHR/CTG

Depending on gestation/local protocol:

Steroids
Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection where indicated
GBS prophylaxis where indicated
Tocolysis in selected women
Transfer to appropriate neonatal facility

Preterm labour/PPROM requires assessment for labour, membrane rupture and infection.
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 2. PPROM]
Suspect if:
Gush/trickle of fluid
No established labour
<37 weeks
Assessment

Maternal:

Temperature
Pulse
BP
RR
MEOWS
Uterine tenderness
Foul discharge

Fetal:

FHR
CTG
Presentation
Diagnosis

Usually:

Sterile speculum examination

Look for:

Pooling
Fluid from cervical os

RCOG recommends history followed by sterile speculum examination; if fluid is not seen, biochemical testing such as IGFBP-1/PAMG-1 may assist diagnosis.

Investigations
FBC
CRP according to local protocol
Fetal assessment
Ultrasound when clinically indicated
Treatment

Depending on gestation and clinical condition:

Antibiotics
Corticosteroids
Magnesium sulfate when indicated
Expectant management where appropriate
Delivery if infection, fetal compromise or another indication

RCOG notes that PPROM increases risks including infection, cord prolapse and placental abruption and recommends antibiotic therapy following diagnosis.
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 3. CHORIOAMNIONITIS / INTRA-AMNIOTIC INFECTION]
Suspect with:

Maternal fever
Maternal tachycardia
Fetal tachycardia
Uterine tenderness
Offensive liquor
Maternal systemic illness
Management
Sepsis assessment
Blood cultures where indicated
FBC/CRP/lactate according to local protocol
IV antibiotics
IV fluids if indicated
CTG
Senior obstetric review
Plan birth according to obstetric circumstances

Do not wait for laboratory confirmation if clinically septic.

4. MECO﻿NIUM-STAINED LIQUOR

Assess:

Gestational age
Colour/thickness of meconium
Fetal movements
CTG
Labour progress

If CTG abnormal:

➡️ Escalate to RED/urgent pathway.

5. BLEEDING <37 WEEKS + CRAMPING

Potential causes:

Preterm labour
Cervical change
Placental abruption
Infection
Cervical lesion

Assessment includes:

Maternal stability
Abdominal examination
CTG
Speculum examination when appropriate
Ultrasound if indicated
Avoid digital VE if placenta praevia has not been excluded
6. SEVERE HYPERTENSION + SYMPTOMS

For example:

≥160 systolic and/or ≥110 diastolic with headache, visual disturbance or RUQ/epigastric pain.

Assess for:

Severe pre-eclampsia
Eclampsia risk
Pulmonary oedema
HELLP

Investigations:

FBC/platelets
AST/ALT
Creatinine
Urine protein assessment
CTG
Ultrasound fetal growth/liquor/Dopplers when indicated

Treat severe hypertension urgently according to local protocol.
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 7. CHEST PAIN / PALPITATIONS / SIGNIFICANT SOB]
Consider:

PE
ACS
Arrhythmia
Anaemia
Pneumonia
Asthma
Pulmonary oedema
Assessment
ABC
ECG
SpO₂
BP
Pulse
Respiratory examination
Appropriate blood tests
PE pathway if clinically suspected

Do not automatically attribute dyspnoea to pregnancy.

8. LABOUR PAIN + PREVIOUS UTERINE SCAR

Particularly:

Previous CS
Myomectomy
Previous uterine surgery

Assess for uterine rupture:

Sudden severe abdominal pain
Abnormal CTG
Maternal instability
Loss of station
Vaginal bleeding
Change in contractions

➡️ Immediate senior obstetric review if rupture suspected.

🟢 LEVEL 3 — GREEN / URGENT
Principle

Stable patient but requires clinical assessment within approximately 60 minutes.

Reassess according to clinical condition, usually 30–60 min if waiting.
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 1. LATENT PHASE OF LABOUR]
Ask:

Contraction frequency
Duration
Pain
Membrane status
Bleeding
Fetal movements

Examine:

Maternal observations
Abdominal examination
Fetal presentation
FHR
Cervical examination when indicated
Management

If reassuring:

Hydration
Analgesia
Mobility
Birth/labour advice
Discharge if appropriate

OR

➡️ Admit if active labour develops, risk factors exist or symptoms cannot safely be managed at home.
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 2. TERM SROM]
Assess
Time of rupture
Fluid colour
Odour
Fetal movements
Contractions
Temperature
Examination
Maternal observations
Abdominal examination
Fetal presentation
FHR

Sterile speculum examination may be appropriate when diagnosis is uncertain.

Management

Depends on:

Gestation
GBS status
Maternal/fetal condition
Labour status
Meconium
Infection
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 3. REDUCED FETAL MOVEMENTS]
Ask
When did movements reduce?
First episode?
Recurrent?
Last movement?
Change from usual pattern?
Any bleeding/liquor/contractions?
Immediate assessment
Maternal observations
Confirm fetal viability
CTG
SFH/growth review
Ultrasound when indicated

For recurrent RFM after 28 weeks, current NHS guidance recommends ultrasound assessment of growth, liquor and umbilical artery Doppler; recurrent RFM after 38+6 weeks should prompt discussion of birth/induction.

Disposition

Normal assessment:

➡️ Reassurance + safety-netting.

Abnormal:

➡️ Senior review/admission/delivery depending on findings.
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 4. MILD BLEEDING AT TERM]
Examples:

Blood-stained show
Mild spotting
Bleeding with contractions

Still exclude significant causes.

Assess:

Maternal stability
Bleeding amount
Pain
Placenta location
CTG
Cervix when safe
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 5. MILD/MODERATE HYPERTENSION]
Example:

BP ≥140/90 but below severe range.

Repeat BP correctly.

Assess:

Symptoms
Proteinuria
FBC
LFT
Renal function
Fetal wellbeing
Growth where indicated

Do not label as "simple hypertension" without assessing for pre-eclampsia.
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 6. ABDOMINAL/BACK/FLANK PAIN]
Differentials:

Labour
UTI/pyelonephritis
Renal stone
Appendicitis
Placental abruption
Uterine rupture
Musculoskeletal pain
Gastrointestinal disease

Examine systematically.

Investigate according to differential.
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 7. CALF PAIN]
Consider DVT.

Ask:

Unilateral swelling
Pain
Redness
Risk factors

Examine legs.

If DVT suspected:

➡️ Follow pregnancy VTE pathway and arrange urgent investigation.

If chest symptoms accompany it:

➡️ PE pathway / higher urgency.
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 8. FALL / MINOR TRAUMA]
Assess:

Mechanism
Abdominal impact
Bleeding
Liquor
Pain
Contractions
Fetal movements

Check:

Maternal observations
Abdominal examination
FHR/CTG
Kleihauer testing/Rh prophylaxis where indicated by gestation/risk/local protocol

Major trauma:

➡️ Emergency trauma pathway.

⚪ LEVEL 4 — WHITE / NON-URGENT
Principle

Stable woman, no immediate maternal or fetal concern.

Examples:

General pregnancy discomfort
Mild cold/flu symptoms without systemic compromise
Routine CTG
Scan review
Blood-result review
Presentation scan
Minor non-acute complaint
Still perform
Maternal observations
Focused history
Fetal assessment appropriate to gestation
Relevant examination
Review antenatal record

White does not mean "no assessment."

It means:

No evidence of an emergency at initial triage.
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 7. COMPLETE PHYSICIAN ASSESSMENT]
Once triaged, the doctor should perform a structured assessment.

HISTORY
Obstetric
G/P
Gestational age
EDD
Previous births
Previous CS
Previous PPH
Previous preterm birth
Previous stillbirth/neonatal death
Previous complications
Current pregnancy
Antenatal complications
Hypertension
Diabetes
FGR
Placental abnormalities
Multiple pregnancy
Anaemia
Infection
Medications
Presenting complaint

Use:

Onset → progression → severity → associated symptoms → fetal symptoms → previous episodes.
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 8. EXAMINATION]
General
Appearance
Pallor
Hydration
Respiratory distress
Consciousness
Vitals
BP
Pulse
RR
SpO₂
Temperature
MEOWS
Abdominal

Assess:

Tenderness
Guarding
Uterine tone
Contractions
Fundal height
Lie
Presentation
Engagement
Fetal heart
Pelvic

Only when indicated.

Possible:

Sterile speculum
Digital vaginal examination
Before digital VE consider:
Placenta praevia
Significant APH
PPROM
Cord presentation/prolapse
Other contraindications
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 9. FETAL ASSESSMENT]
Depending on gestation and presentation:

Fetal heart
Doppler
CTG
CTG assess:

DR C BRAVADO

Define risk
Contractions
Baseline
Variability
Accelerations
Decelerations
Overall assessment
Does it require action?

If pathological:

➡️ Escalate immediately.
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 10. INVESTIGATION MENU]
Not every patient needs everything.

Blood
FBC
Group & save
Crossmatch
CRP
U&E
LFT
Coagulation
Fibrinogen
Blood cultures
Lactate
Glucose

according to presentation.

Urine
Dipstick
Protein/creatinine ratio or ACR according to local hypertension pathway
Culture
Imaging
Ultrasound
Growth scan
Liquor assessment
Dopplers
Placental localisation
Other
ECG
CXR when indicated
VTE imaging
CT/MRI when clinically indicated
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 11. MANAGEMENT WHILE WAITING]
Never leave an unstable patient simply because investigations are pending.

General
Appropriate bed/position
IV access when indicated
Analgesia
Antiemetic
Fluids when indicated
Fetal monitoring
Repeat observations
Senior review
If deterioration occurs:

Immediately upgrade triage category.

For example:

GREEN → AMBER → RED

depending on deterioration.
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 12. REASSESSMENT]
This is a crucial part of triage.

RED

Continuous/high-frequency observation.

Your local protocol specifies approximately:

5-minute observations

for severe emergencies.

AMBER

Approximately:

15-minute reassessment

or sooner if clinically indicated.

GREEN

Approximately:

30–60 minutes

depending on symptoms.

WHITE

No routine continuous reassessment if completely stable, but reassess immediately if:

Pain increases
Bleeding occurs
Liquor changes
Fetal movements reduce
CTG changes
Vitals deteriorate
New symptoms appear
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 13. SENIOR REVIEW]
Escalate to senior obstetrician/consultant when:

RED
Persistent AMBER
Abnormal CTG
Significant bleeding
Severe hypertension
Sepsis
PPROM with complications
Previous uterine scar + concerning symptoms
Suspected fetal compromise
Maternal deterioration
Diagnostic uncertainty
Need for operative delivery
Need for admission with significant risk

RCOG specifically recommends senior obstetric expertise for the most urgent triage categories.
source_file: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION.md
section_path: COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION

text:
[COMPLETE L&D TRIAGE ARRIVAL  ASSESSMENT  MANAGEMENT  DISPOSITION > 14. FINAL DISPOSITION]
Every triage patient should finish with a clear documented disposition.

There are essentially four possibilities:

A. ADMIT LABOUR WARD

Examples:

Active labour
Preterm labour
Significant PPROM
Chorioamnionitis
Abnormal CTG
Significant APH
Severe hypertension
High-risk labour
Previous uterine scar with labour
Need for induction/augmentation
B. ADMIT ANTENATAL/WARD

Examples:

Stable PPROM
Pre-eclampsia requiring monitoring
Hyperemesis/dehydration
Pyelonephritis
DVT requiring treatment
Reduced fetal movements requiring further surveillance
Other maternal conditions
C. OBSERVATION → REASSESS

Useful when:

Early labour
Borderline BP
Uncertain membrane rupture
Mild symptoms
Awaiting CTG
Awaiting blood tests
Awaiting ultrasound
Awaiting senior review
D. DISCHARGE HOME

Only when:

Maternal condition stable + fetal assessment reassuring + diagnosis reasonably established + no indication for admission.

Return immediately for:

🔴 Reduced/absent fetal movements
🔴 Waters breaking
🔴 Green/foul-smelling liquor
🔴 Regular painful contractions
🔴 Severe abdominal pain
🔴 Severe headache
🔴 Visual disturbance
🔴 RUQ/epigastric pain
🔴 Chest pain
🔴 Severe breathlessness
🔴 Fever/rigors
🔴 Collapse
🔴 Seizure
🔴 Any significant deterioration or feeling seriously unwell

For PPROM specifically, NHS advice includes urgent return for fever, offensive/green fluid, bleeding, abdominal/back pain, contractions or reduced fetal movements.

suspected pregnancy.
58. Practical OSCE station: IUD insertion
Examiner may ask:

Q: What are the prerequisites?

Answer:

informed consent.
pregnancy excluded.
assess STI/PID risk.
bimanual examination.
appropriate equipment.
trained clinician.
emergency equipment available.
appropriate analgesia.
documentation.
Q: What complications?

Immediate:

pain.
vasovagal episode.
bleeding.
perforation.

Early:

infection.
expulsion.

Later:

pregnancy.
contraceptive failure.
59. Practical OSCE station: Implant insertion
Examiner asks:

“What is the most important thing after insertion?”

Answer:

Palpate the implant and confirm it is correctly positioned.

Then:

dressing.
documentation.
patient information.
advice about bruising.
return if unable to feel it or develops neurological/vascular symptoms.
60. Practical OSCE station: emergency contraception
Examiner: "What would you recommend?"

Don't immediately prescribe.

First establish:

UPSI timing → cycle → pregnancy risk → medications → breastfeeding → STI risk → preferences.

Then explain:

Copper IUD
most effective.
provides ongoing contraception.
Ulipristal
up to 120 h.
Levonorgestrel
ideally within 72 h.

Then:

explain effectiveness limitations.
discuss ongoing contraception.
pregnancy test if period is delayed/appropriate.
STI advice.
61. Numerical values worth memorising for MRCOG
Blood pressure

≥160/100 mmHg
→ severe hypertension; CHC generally contraindicated.

CHC age/smoking

≥35 years + smoking
→ major risk consideration/possible contraindication depending smoking intensity and other factors.

Copper IUD EC

120 hours / 5 days

Ulipristal EC

120 hours / 5 days

Levonorgestrel EC

72 hours / 3 days

Traditional POP missed-pill window

3 hours

Desogestrel POP

12 hours

DMPA

Approximately 13 weeks between injections.

Implant

Usually 3 years for the etonogestrel implant according to standard licensed duration.

IUD uterine sounding

Often approximately 6–9 cm, but interpret according to device/manufacturer and clinical context.

62. Common MRCOG Part 3 contraception traps
Trap 1

“Does contraception protect against STI?”

❌ No.

Condoms do.

Trap 2

Migraine + aura

❌ Don't prescribe CHC.

Trap 3

Pregnancy + IUD

Think:
ectopic pregnancy.

Trap 4

Missing implant

Don't blindly explore.

Localise it.

Trap 5

IUD perforation

Stop the procedure and assess.

Trap 6

Postpartum CHC

Don't prescribe automatically.

Assess postpartum VTE risk and breastfeeding.

Trap 7

Vasectomy

Not immediately effective.

Trap 8

Emergency contraception

Always ask about all episodes of UPSI, not just the most recent episode.

Trap 9

Ulipristal

Remember the interaction with progestogen-containing contraception.

Trap 10

Teenager requesting contraception

Don't automatically tell parents.

Assess:

confidentiality.
capacity.
safeguarding.
coercion.
63. MRCOG communication phrases to score marks
Shared decision-making

“I can explain the options, but ultimately the choice should be based on your medical eligibility and what fits your priorities.”

Risk communication

“I want to put this risk into perspective. The relative risk may increase, but the absolute risk in a healthy woman is still low.”

If patient refuses

“That's completely your choice. Can I check what concerns you most so I can address them?”

If patient is undecided

“You don't have to decide immediately. I can give you information about the options and we can make a plan that you're comfortable with.”

Safeguarding

“I ask all patients about whether their sexual relationships are consensual and whether anyone is pressuring them, because this is an important part of safe care.”

Safety-netting

“If you develop severe abdominal pain, heavy bleeding, fever, collapse or suspect pregnancy, you should seek urgent medical assessment.”

text:
[EMERGENCY OBSTETRICS — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE MASTER ATLAS > 3. PLACENTA PRAEVIA]
Definition

Placenta located in the lower uterine segment such that it approaches or covers the internal cervical os.

Classic OSCE presentation

Painless, bright-red vaginal bleeding in the second half of pregnancy.

Typical examination
uterus:
soft
non-tender
fetus may be:
malpresenting
high/mobile
fetal heart may initially be normal.
Important distinction
| Feature | Praevia | Abruption |
|---|---|---|
| Bleeding | Bright red | Darker may occur |
| Pain | Usually painless | Painful |
| Uterus | Soft | Tender/tense |
| Contractions | Usually absent | Often present |
| FHR | Often initially normal | Often abnormal |
| Shock | Can be severe | May be disproportionate |
| Visible bleeding | Usually corresponds better to loss | Concealed bleeding possible |
Diagnosis
Ultrasound
transvaginal ultrasound is safe and more accurate for placental localisation.
Assess:
placental edge
relationship to internal os
previous CS scar
signs of PAS.

The current RCOG guideline emphasises early identification of placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum because the combination carries major haemorrhage risk.

MRCOG management
Acute bleed

ABCDE
→ senior help
→ IV access
→ bloods/crossmatch
→ CTG
→ ultrasound
→ assess haemodynamic status.

If unstable:

resuscitate
activate major obstetric haemorrhage pathway
prepare urgent birth.

If stable:

assess gestation
bleeding severity
fetal condition
recurrence
placental location
PAS risk.
Delivery

If placenta praevia persists and covers the os:

vaginal birth is generally contraindicated.
caesarean birth planned according to clinical circumstances and guideline recommendations.

Never say “all placenta praevia = elective CS at exactly X weeks” without considering current RCOG guidance, bleeding history, PAS and local protocol.

text:
[EMERGENCY OBSTETRICS — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE MASTER ATLAS > 4. PLACENTAL ABRUPTION]
Definition

Premature separation of a normally situated placenta before delivery.

Classic presentation

Painful vaginal bleeding + abdominal pain + tender/tense uterus + fetal compromise.

But remember

Bleeding may be concealed.

Therefore:

Do not underestimate abruption because visible vaginal blood loss is small.

Clinical types
Revealed

Blood escapes through vagina.

Concealed

Blood accumulates behind placenta.

Mixed

Both.

Typical findings
abdominal pain
back pain
uterine tenderness
hypertonus
frequent contractions
fetal distress
absent FHR if severe
maternal shock
DIC
Severe abruption

May cause:

Abruption → tissue factor release → coagulation activation → consumption of fibrinogen/platelets → DIC.

Laboratory clue

Low fibrinogen is particularly concerning.

Management
Stable mother + reassuring fetus

Depends on:

gestational age
amount of bleeding
ongoing bleeding
fetal status
maternal condition.
Unstable mother

Maternal resuscitation takes priority.

Fetal compromise + vaginal birth not imminent

→ urgent birth, usually caesarean unless vaginal birth is safer/imminent.

IUFD

If mother stable:

vaginal birth generally preferred.

If maternal instability/coagulopathy:

expedite delivery and correct coagulopathy.

[EMERGENCY OBSTETRICS — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE MASTER ATLAS > 12. PRE-ECLAMPSIA]
Diagnostic framework

After 20 weeks:

BP ≥140/90 mmHg

PLUS:

proteinuria or
maternal organ dysfunction or
uteroplacental dysfunction.

NICE defines hypertension as ≥140 systolic or ≥90 diastolic and severe hypertension as >160 systolic or >110 diastolic.

Proteinuria

Significant proteinuria:

PCR ≥30 mg/mmol
or ACR ≥8 mg/mmol
or ≥2+ dipstick if quantitative testing unavailable.
Severe features
Neurological
severe headache
visual disturbance
clonus
altered mental state
eclampsia
Hepatic
epigastric/RUQ pain
raised transaminases
Renal
creatinine ≥90 µmol/L
Haematological
platelets <150 ×10⁹/L
haemolysis
DIC
Fetal/placental
FGR
abnormal Dopplers
stillbirth.

NICE specifically identifies creatinine ≥90 µmol/L, ALT >70 IU/L or >2× ULN and platelets <150 ×10⁹/L as concerning laboratory deterioration.

text:
[EMERGENCY OBSTETRICS — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE MASTER ATLAS > 24. MATERNAL CARDIAC ARREST — PREGNANCY]
Key modifications
Call cardiac arrest team.
CPR immediately.
Manual left uterine displacement if uterus is sufficiently large to cause aortocaval compression.
Defibrillation uses standard adult energy.
Do not withhold defibrillation because of pregnancy.
Identify reversible causes.
Prepare for resuscitative hysterotomy if indicated and ROSC is not achieved.
Timing principle

If cardiac arrest occurs at/above approximately 20 weeks, prepare for resuscitative hysterotomy immediately; aim to commence by 4 minutes and deliver by 5 minutes where indicated.

text:
[EMERGENCY OBSTETRICS — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE MASTER ATLAS > 40. UNIVERSAL MRCOG EMERGENCY CLOSING STATEMENT]
For almost any emergency station, finish with:

“I would continue ABCDE reassessment, continuously monitor maternal observations and fetal condition where applicable, quantify ongoing blood loss, repeat investigations including lactate and coagulation as clinically indicated, involve the appropriate multidisciplinary team, escalate to critical care if necessary, communicate clearly with the woman and her birth partner, obtain consent where the situation permits, document the sequence of events and management, and arrange appropriate post-event debriefing and follow-up.”

The MRCOG mindset

Do not get trapped trying to make the diagnosis before treating the patient.

The safest sequence is:

RECOGNISE → CALL → RESUSCITATE → INVESTIGATE → DIAGNOSE → DEFINITIVE TREATMENT → REASSESS → ESCALATE → COMMUNICATE → DOCUMENT.

Age 35–39

source_file: gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table.md

text:
[gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table > 27. IVF PREGNANCY]
ACOG recommends considering antenatal surveillance from approximately:

36+0 weeks

for pregnancies conceived by IVF.

This is primarily a surveillance threshold, not automatically a delivery threshold.
source_file: gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table.md

text:
[gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table > 28. OBESITY]
ACOG considers antenatal surveillance according to BMI:

| BMI | Possible surveillance |
|---|---|
| 35–39.9 | From ~37 weeks |
| ≥40 | From ~34 weeks |

Again:

Surveillance ≠ automatic delivery.

ACOG specifically recommends individualized surveillance in obesity because stillbirth risk rises with increasing BMI and advancing gestation.
source_file: gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table.md

text:
[gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table > 29. PREVIOUS STILLBIRTH]
No universal single delivery week.

Management is individualized according to:

cause of previous stillbirth
recurrence risk
maternal anxiety
fetal growth
surveillance.

Usually increased surveillance and consideration of delivery around:

39 weeks

unless a specific recurrent cause indicates earlier birth.
source_file: gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table.md

text:
[gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table > 30. ABRUPTION]
Acute significant abruption

Immediate delivery if:

maternal instability
fetal compromise
major bleeding
coagulopathy.
Chronic/recurrent abruption

No universal fixed week.

ACOG recommends individualized management and increased surveillance.
source_file: gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table.md

text:
[gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table > 31. FETAL ANOMALY]
There is no universal gestational cut-off.

Depends on:

lethal vs non-lethal anomaly
fetal compromise
hydrops
cardiac failure
airway obstruction
chromosomal diagnosis
parental wishes
neonatal/pediatric surgical capability.
source_file: gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table.md

text:
[gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table > 32. HYDROPS]
No single gestational cut-off.

If:

fetal compromise
severe anemia
cardiac failure
infection
maternal mirror syndrome

→ delivery/intervention may be required regardless of gestation.
source_file: gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table.md

text:
[gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table > 33. ALLOIMMUNISATION]
No single week.

Delivery depends on:

MCA-PSV
fetal anaemia
IUT history
hydrops
fetal testing.

ACOG specifically lists alloimmunization with known/suspected fetal effects among conditions that can warrant medically indicated early delivery.
source_file: gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table.md

text:
[gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table > 34. VELAMENTOUS CORD INSERTION / SINGLE UMBILICAL ARTERY]
Not automatically an indication for early delivery.

ACOG suggests:

Weekly surveillance from ~36 weeks

for velamentous cord insertion or SUA in appropriate circumstances.
source_file: gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table.md
section_path: 34. VELAMENTOUS CORD INSERTION / SINGLE UMBILICAL ARTERY

text:
[gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table > 35. LOW PAPP-A / ABNORMAL SERUM MARKERS]
These generally lead to:

serial growth scans
fetal surveillance

rather than automatic early delivery.

For example, ACOG suggests surveillance from approximately 36 weeks for low PAPP-A or elevated inhibin A in specified circumstances.
source_file: gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table.md

text:
[gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table > 36. OVERT DIABETIC VASCULAR DISEASE]
Pregestational diabetes with:

nephropathy
retinopathy
vascular disease
poor glycaemic control

→ individualized early delivery.

Do not automatically wait for 39 weeks.
source_file: gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table.md

text:
[gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table > 37. RENAL DISEASE]
No single week.

Earlier delivery if:

severe hypertension
renal deterioration
pre-eclampsia
FGR
fetal compromise.
source_file: gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table.md

text:
[gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table > 38. THYROID DISEASE]
Well-controlled thyroid disease:

No routine early delivery.

Poorly controlled severe disease:

→ individualized.
source_file: gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table.md

text:
[gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table > 39. SYSTEMIC LUPUS / AUTOIMMUNE DISEASE]
No fixed week.

Deliver according to:

pre-eclampsia
FGR
placental insufficiency
maternal organ involvement
fetal compromise.
source_file: gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table.md

text:
[gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table > 40. INTRAUTERINE INFECTION / CHORIOAMNIONITIS]
This is NOT a “wait until X weeks” condition.

Once clinical chorioamnionitis is diagnosed:

Start antibiotics + expedite delivery

regardless of gestational age.
source_file: gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table.md

text:
[gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table > 41. UTERINE RUPTURE]
Immediate laparotomy/delivery.

No gestational-age cut-off.
source_file: gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table.md

text:
[gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table > 42. CORD PROLAPSE]
Immediate delivery if fetus viable and delivery is indicated.

Usually emergency CS unless vaginal delivery is imminent.
source_file: gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table.md

text:
[gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table > 43. NON-REASSURING FETAL STATUS]
No fixed gestational age.

If persistent severe fetal compromise:

Deliver regardless of gestation when fetal benefit outweighs prematurity risk.
source_file: gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table.md

text:
[gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table > 44. ECLAMPSIA]
No gestational cut-off.

After maternal stabilization:

Delivery is definitive treatment.
source_file: gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table.md

text:
[gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table > 45. HELLP]
No simple “37-week rule.”

If:

maternal deterioration
uncontrolled hypertension
DIC
liver complications
renal dysfunction
neurological symptoms
fetal compromise

→ delivery regardless of gestation after appropriate stabilization.

At viable gestations, expectant management is generally not appropriate when severe maternal disease is present.

46. PLACENTAL ABRUPTION + DIC

Immediate delivery and correction of coagulopathy.

Gestational age does not override maternal emergency.
source_file: gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table.md

text:
[gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table > 47. FETAL DEATH]
Once IUFD is confirmed:

Usually no need for immediate delivery solely because of gestational age unless:

maternal sepsis
haemorrhage
abruption
DIC
severe maternal illness
other indication.
source_file: gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table.md

[gestational-age cut-off  timing-of-delivery table > 48. POST-TERM]
41+0Start/offer induction depending on guideline.42+0Post-term.Delivery should not routinely be delayed beyond this.ACOG's classification defines ≥42 weeks as post-term and supports delivery by 42 weeks in otherwise uncomplicated pregnancy.⭐ THE MRCOG/FCPS “NUMBERS TO MEMORIZE” TABLEIf you only have 2 minutes before an exam, memorize this:

| Condition | Gestational-age number |

| DCDA twins | 37+0 |

| MCMA twins | 32–34 |
| Triplets | 35+0 |
| Placenta previa | 36–37+6 |
| Placenta accreta spectrum | 34–35+6 |
| Vasa previa | 34–37 |

| Elective repeat LSCS | ≥39+0 |

Pre-operative assessment, prerequisites & preparation
Master list of procedures

For examination purposes, divide gynaecological procedures into:

1. Outpatient/minor procedures
Vulval biopsy
Vaginal biopsy
Cervical biopsy
Endometrial biopsy
Pap smear/HPV sampling
Colposcopy-directed biopsy
LLETZ/LEEP
Bartholin cyst/abscess procedures
IUD insertion/removal
Implant insertion/removal
Outpatient hysteroscopy
Outpatient polypectomy
Outpatient endometrial biopsy
2. Hysteroscopic procedures
Diagnostic hysteroscopy
Operative hysteroscopy
Polypectomy
Submucous fibroid resection
Septal resection
Adhesiolysis
Endometrial ablation
Removal of retained intrauterine pathology
3. Laparoscopic procedures
Diagnostic laparoscopy
Chromopertubation
Ovarian cystectomy
Oophorectomy
Salpingectomy
Salpingostomy
Adhesiolysis
Endometriosis surgery
Myomectomy
Laparoscopic sterilisation
Ectopic pregnancy surgery — early pregnancy/obstetric-related and therefore excluded from your requested scope

RCOG's reproductive medicine OSATS specifically includes laparoscopic adhesiolysis, endometriosis surgery, ovarian cystectomy, salpingectomy, salpingostomy and myomectomy, emphasising patient selection, contraindications, consent, positioning, entry and assessment of anatomy.

4. Open abdominal surgery
Laparotomy
Ovarian cyst surgery
Oophorectomy
Salpingo-oophorectomy
Myomectomy
Adhesiolysis
Complex benign pelvic surgery
Gynaecological oncology procedures
5. Hysterectomy
Total abdominal hysterectomy
Total laparoscopic hysterectomy
Laparoscopic-assisted vaginal hysterectomy
Vaginal hysterectomy
Subtotal/supracervical hysterectomy
Radical hysterectomy — oncology
6. Urogynaecology
Anterior repair
Posterior repair
Vaginal vault suspension
Sacrospinous fixation
Sacrocolpopexy
Mid-urethral sling
Burch colposuspension
Periurethral procedures
Fistula repair
7. Oncology
Vulval cancer surgery
Cervical cancer surgery
Endometrial cancer surgery
Ovarian cancer cytoreduction
Lymph-node assessment/dissection
Radical hysterectomy
Pelvic/para-aortic lymphadenectomy
A. UNIVERSAL PRE-OPERATIVE ASSESSMENT

This is the answer you should give first in almost every MRCOG/OSCE surgical station.

1. Confirm patient identity
Full name
Hospital/medical record number
DOB
Procedure
Side/site
Indication
Surgeon
Consent
Planned anaesthetic
Allergies

Use the WHO surgical safety principles/time-out in conjunction with local policy.

2. Confirm the diagnosis and indication

Lifestyle measures
Medical
NSAIDs
Tranexamic acid
Hormonal therapy

Other disease-specific medication
Interventional
UAE for selected fibroids
Endometrial ablation
Hysteroscopic treatment
Image-guided procedures
Surgical
Minimally invasive vs open
Uterus-preserving vs definitive surgery

RCOG's consent principles require discussion of recommended options, alternatives and consequences of no treatment, with adequate time for decision-making and documentation.

Regularity
Duration
Amount
Dysmenorrhoea

Postcoital bleeding
Postmenopausal bleeding

Especially important before:

Bilateral salpingectomy

Ovarian cystectomy
Oncology surgery

Pharmacological prophylaxis where indicated
Timing relative to neuraxial anaesthesia

Important: RCOG Green-top 37a is primarily an obstetric guideline, so its pregnancy/postpartum scoring system should not simply be transplanted onto non-pregnant gynaecological patients. For gynaecological surgery, follow the current local/NICE/anaesthetic VTE assessment pathway.

12. Infection assessment

Look for:

Fever
UTI
PID
Vaginitis
Cervicitis
Skin infection
Respiratory infection
Pelvic abscess
If elective surgery:

Treat active infection where appropriate and reassess fitness for surgery.

13. Nutritional assessment

Particularly for:

Cancer
Major laparotomy
Frail patients
Elderly patients
Chronic illness

Assess:

BMI
Weight loss
Malnutrition
Albumin where clinically appropriate
Nutritional intake
14. Psychological assessment

Ask about:

Anxiety
Previous traumatic examinations
Sexual trauma
Fear of anaesthesia
Concerns regarding fertility
Body image
Sexual function
Cancer concerns

Offer appropriate support.

B. EXAMINATION
1. General examination

Assess:

General condition
Pallor
Jaundice
Hydration
BMI
Nutritional state
Oedema
2. Vital signs

Record:

BP
Pulse
Respiratory rate
SpO₂
Temperature
3. Cardiovascular examination

Especially if:

Cardiac disease
Major surgery
Older patient
Abnormal history
4. Respiratory examination

Particularly:

Obesity
OSA
Smoking
Respiratory disease
Major surgery
5. Abdominal examination

Assess:

Mass
Tenderness
Previous scars
Hernias
Hepatomegaly
Ascites
Abdominal distension
Previous scars are especially important before laparoscopy.
6. Pelvic examination

Depending on indication:

Vulva
Lesions
Ulcers
Masses
Scarring
Speculum
Cervical lesion
Bleeding
Discharge
Prolapse
Vaginal lesions
Bimanual

Assess:

Uterine size
Mobility
Position
Adnexal mass
Tenderness
Pelvic fixation
Rectovaginal

Consider for:

Deep endometriosis
Suspected malignancy
Posterior compartment disease
Rectovaginal involvement

RCOG specifically notes that intimate examination may be required during gynaecological procedures under anaesthesia and that this should be incorporated into consent.

C. INVESTIGATIONS
Basic preoperative investigations

Do not order every test for every patient. Investigations should be guided by:

Age
Comorbidity
ASA grade
Procedure
Expected blood loss
Anaesthesia
Local policy.
Common investigations
FBC
Group and save
Crossmatch when significant blood loss is anticipated
U&E/creatinine
LFT when indicated
Glucose/HbA1c where indicated
Coagulation profile when indicated
ECG when indicated
CXR only when clinically indicated
Pregnancy test where applicable
Urinalysis/urine culture when indicated
D. PROCEDURE-SPECIFIC INVESTIGATIONS
1. Fibroid surgery

Before:

Pelvic ultrasound
MRI if complex mapping is required
FBC
Ferritin/iron studies if anaemic
Pregnancy exclusion where relevant

Assess:

Number
Size
Location
FIGO classification where appropriate
Cavity distortion
Desire for fertility
2. Endometrial pathology

Depending on presentation:

TVUS
Endometrial biopsy
Hysteroscopy
Histology

For postmenopausal bleeding, ensure appropriate assessment has been completed before definitive surgery.

3. Ovarian mass

Assess:

TVUS
CA-125 where indicated
Other tumour markers depending on age/presentation
RMI or other appropriate risk stratification
CT/MRI when indicated

RCOG's ovarian-mass guidance specifically addresses distinguishing women suitable for benign gynaecological management from those requiring gynaecological oncology referral.

Red flags for oncology referral
Solid components
Papillary projections
Ascites
Bilateral complex masses
Elevated tumour markers
Postmenopausal complex mass
Suspicious imaging
Metastatic disease
4. Endometriosis

Assess:

TVUS
MRI for deep disease where indicated
Bowel symptoms
Bladder symptoms
Fertility goals
Previous surgery
Endometriosis severity/location

Plan possible involvement of:

Urology
Colorectal surgery
Fertility team
5. Prolapse

Perform:

POP-Q examination
Vaginal examination
Cervical assessment
Urinalysis
Postvoid residual where indicated

For stress incontinence:

Cough stress test
Urodynamics in selected patients
6. Incontinence surgery

Assess:

Type of incontinence
Bladder diary
Urinalysis
Postvoid residual
Pelvic examination
Prolapse
Urodynamics when indicated

Discuss:

Conservative treatment
Pelvic-floor physiotherapy
Medical treatment
Surgical options
7. Cervical excisional procedures

Before LLETZ/LEEP:

Cytology/HPV results
Colposcopy findings
Transformation zone
Histology where available
Pregnancy status
Previous excisional procedures

Assess risk of:

Incomplete excision
Cervical stenosis
Bleeding
Infection
Future reproductive implications
E. CONSENT — VERY HIGH-YIELD MRCOG AREA

RCOG emphasises that consent should be a process rather than merely a signature. The patient should understand recommended treatment, alternatives, consequences of no treatment and relevant risks.

Consent framework
1. Diagnosis

"Your diagnosis is..."

2. Proposed procedure

Explain:

What
Why
How
Route
Anaesthetic
3. Benefits

What outcome is expected?

4. Alternatives
No treatment
Medical treatment
Conservative management
Alternative procedure
Different surgical route
5. Risks

Universal:

Pain
Bleeding
Infection
Scarring
Adhesions
VTE
Anaesthetic complications
Need for further surgery
Return to theatre
Death in appropriate major-risk contexts

RCOG's consent guidance specifically identifies VTE/PE, return to theatre, bowel, bladder, ureteric and major vascular injury among serious risks that may need discussion, together with procedure-specific risks.

F. CONSENT FOR LAPAROSCOPY

Always discuss possibility of:

Conversion

"There is a possibility that the operation may need to be converted to an open operation if it is not safe to continue laparoscopically."

Organ injury
Bowel
Bladder
Ureter
Major vessels
Nerve injury
Other
Haemorrhage
Infection
Port-site hernia
Port-site bleeding
Adhesions
VTE
Anaesthetic complications
Shoulder-tip pain
Failed procedure

RCOG's surgical training specifically requires understanding diagnostic laparoscopy, laparotomy, hysterectomy and vaginal surgery, as well as complications and risk reduction.

G. CONSENT FOR HYSTERECTOMY

Discuss:

Route
Abdominal
Vaginal
Laparoscopic
Consequences
Permanent loss of fertility
No future menstruation
Cervix retained vs removed
Ovaries retained vs removed
Ovaries

Discuss:

Conservation
Unilateral oophorectomy
Bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy

If ovaries removed:

Immediate surgical menopause if premenopausal
HRT implications
Specific injuries
Bladder
Ureter
Bowel
Major vessels
Additional possibilities
Adhesiolysis
Cystoscopy where indicated
Conversion from laparoscopy to laparotomy
Blood transfusion
H. CONSENT FOR MYOMECTOMY

Discuss:

Bleeding
Transfusion
Hysterectomy if uncontrollable haemorrhage
Adhesions
Recurrence
Future fibroids
Fertility implications
Possible need for future Caesarean delivery depending on uterine incision — relevant to future pregnancy counselling, although this is not an obstetric procedure
Conversion to laparotomy

For fertility-preserving surgery, document the patient's reproductive goals.

I. CONSENT FOR OVARIAN SURGERY

For ovarian cystectomy:

Cyst rupture
Bleeding
Loss of ovarian tissue
Reduced ovarian reserve
Oophorectomy if unavoidable
Unexpected malignancy
Conversion to laparotomy

If malignancy is suspected:

Consent must reflect the possibility that the procedure may need to be modified according to intraoperative findings and oncological principles.

J. CONSENT FOR HYSTEROSCOPY

Discuss:

Pain
Bleeding
Infection
Vasovagal episode
Cervical trauma
Uterine perforation
Fluid overload
Incomplete procedure
Need for repeat procedure

For operative hysteroscopy:

Bleeding
Infection
Perforation
Fluid overload/electrolyte disturbance
Thermal injury
Need for further surgery

RCOG's current outpatient hysteroscopy guidance emphasises explaining the procedure, benefits, risks, alternatives and pain-relief options before the appointment, and allowing the patient to reschedule if she needs more time for decision-making.

K. OUTPATIENT HYSTEROSCOPY — SPECIAL PREPARATION

Unlike GA hysteroscopy:

Usually:
No fasting required
Eat and drink normally
Written information beforehand
Discuss analgesia
Medication list
Consent
Explain alternatives
Explain possibility of biopsy/polypectomy
Explain stopping procedure if patient requests

RCOG explicitly states that routine fasting is not required for outpatient hysteroscopy and recommends analgesia before attendance.

L. ANAESTHETIC ASSESSMENT

For GA/regional anaesthesia:

Assess
ASA grade
Airway
BMI
OSA
Cardiovascular status
Respiratory status
Previous anaesthetic problems
Medication
Allergies
Fasting status
VTE risk
Discuss with anaesthetist
General anaesthesia
Regional anaesthesia
Sedation
Local anaesthesia

depending on procedure.

M. BLOOD MANAGEMENT

Preoperative haemoglobin

Expected contamination

Routine bowel preparation is NOT required for most gynaecological operations.

text:
[GYNAECOLOGY DISCHARGE & FOLLOW-UP MASTER LIST > 53. DISCHARGE FOLLOW-UP BY TIME]
A useful MRCOG/clinical exam framework:

| Time | What to review |
|---|---|
| Same day | Stability, diagnosis, treatment, safety-net |
| 24–72 h | Infection, pain, acute complications, PID/ectopic protocols where applicable |
| 1 week | Wound, symptoms, histology if available, treatment response |
| 2 weeks | Surgical recovery, miscarriage/expectant pathways, persistent symptoms |
| 4–6 weeks | Major postoperative recovery, hysterectomy, prolapse/incontinence, pathology |
| 6–12 weeks | Functional recovery, pelvic floor, sexual function, long-term plan |
| 3–6 months | Chronic disease, endometriosis, fibroids, prolapse, recurrent symptoms |
| Long-term | Cancer surveillance, recurrent disease, menopause, chronic pelvic pain |

Important: these are practical intervals, not universal RCOG-mandated timings. The exact timing should be determined by the condition, procedure, pathology and local pathway.

[Important Biochemistry, Immunopathology & Anatomical Landmarks in Gynaecology > 1. REPRODUCTIVE ENDOCRINE BIOCHEMISTRY]
A. Hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis

GnRH → LH/FSH → ovary → oestradiol/progesterone/inhibin → feedback

GnRH
Produced by hypothalamus.
Pulsatile secretion is essential.
Rapid/high-frequency pulses → relatively more LH.
Slow-frequency pulses → relatively more FSH.
Continuous GnRH → pituitary GnRH-receptor downregulation → ↓LH/FSH.
Clinical applications

Continuous GnRH agonists:

Leuprorelin
Goserelin
Triptorelin

Initially:

↑LH/FSH → flare

Then:

receptor downregulation → ↓LH/FSH → hypo-oestrogenic state.

Used in:

Endometriosis
Fibroids
Some fertility protocols
Precocious puberty

text:
[Important Biochemistry, Immunopathology & Anatomical Landmarks in Gynaecology > 2. FSH]
Main actions

FSH acts primarily on granulosa cells.

Stimulates:

Follicular growth
Aromatase activity
Conversion of androgens → oestradiol
Inhibin B production
FSH and ovarian reserve

Early follicular-phase FSH:

Usually measured day 2–5.
Higher FSH can indicate reduced ovarian reserve.

But:

FSH has substantial cycle-to-cycle variation.
AMH and AFC are generally more useful markers of ovarian reserve.

text:
[Important Biochemistry, Immunopathology & Anatomical Landmarks in Gynaecology > 3. LH]
LH acts primarily on theca cells.

LH → theca cells → androgen production.

Androgens diffuse to granulosa cells:

Androgen → aromatase → oestradiol

LH surge

Sustained high oestradiol causes positive feedback.

→ LH surge
→ ovulation
→ luteinisation
→ corpus luteum formation.

7. ANTI-MÜLLERIAN HORMONE — AMH

Produced by:

Granulosa cells of pre-antral and small antral follicles.
Main clinical use

Marker of:

Ovarian reserve
Expected ovarian response during IVF.
Important OSCE point

Does not directly measure egg quality.
Does not reliably predict spontaneous conception.
Falls with increasing age.
Can be relatively elevated in PCOS.

[L&D TRIAGe clinical pathway]
🔴 L&D TRIAGE — RED CASES
Immediate / life-threatening / cannot safely wait
The universal RED algorithm

For any red presentation, say:

“I would immediately move the woman out of routine triage to an appropriate resuscitation/labour ward area, call for senior help, assess ABCDE, obtain maternal observations and fetal assessment where appropriate, establish IV access, investigate and treat simultaneously, identify the cause, and reassess continuously.”

Remember:

CALL → ABCDE → MONITOR → IV ACCESS → BLOOD → FETUS → CAUSE → TREAT → DELIVERY DECISION → REASSESS → DOCUMENT

RCOG specifically describes maternity triage as an emergency portal and emphasises prompt standardised assessment, symptom-specific algorithms and access to senior decision-makers.

1. 🔴 IMMINENT DELIVERY / ADVANCED LABOUR
Recognise
Red flags:

Crowning
Head visible
Fully dilated and actively pushing
Presenting part on perineum
Urge to push with advanced labour
Previous very rapid labour
Bulging perineum
Involuntary pushing
Step 1 — Call for help
Immediately call:

Senior midwife
Obstetric registrar
Consultant obstetrician if high-risk/emergency
Neonatal team if indicated
Anaesthetic team if complications anticipated

Do not send the woman back to routine triage.
Step 2 — Rapid maternal assessment

ABCDE:

Airway
Breathing
Circulation
Disability
Exposure

Record:

BP
Pulse
RR
SpO₂
Temperature
Pain
Consciousness
Step 3 — Obstetric assessment

Rapidly establish:

Gestational age
Gravida/para
Presentation
Membrane status
Bleeding
Fetal movements
Fetal heart rate
Previous CS/uterine surgery
Known placenta praevia/accreta
Multiple pregnancy

If delivery is imminent, do not delay birth for a prolonged history.
Step 4 — Prepare for birth

Prepare:

Delivery equipment
Neonatal resuscitation equipment
IV access
Blood if haemorrhage risk
Appropriate analgesia/anaesthesia
Newborn team
Step 5 — Look for complications

2. 🔴 MAJOR ANTEPARTUM HAEMORRHAGE

RCOG defines APH as bleeding from/in the genital tract from 24+0 weeks until birth. Major causes include placenta praevia and placental abruption.

This is one of the most important RED presentations.
Step 1 — Call it an obstetric haemorrhage

Do not underestimate blood loss.

Call:

Senior obstetrician
Consultant
Anaesthetist
Senior midwife
Blood bank/transfusion laboratory
Theatre team if significant
Neonatal team if fetal compromise/preterm birth possible

If major haemorrhage, activate the local major obstetric haemorrhage protocol.
Step 2 — ABCDE
A — Airway

Ensure patent airway.
B — Breathing
RR
SpO₂
Respiratory effort

Give oxygen if clinically indicated by hypoxaemia/critical illness.
C — Circulation
Immediately:

BP
Pulse
Capillary refill
Mental status
Estimate ongoing blood loss
Two large-bore IV cannulas if significant haemorrhage
Step 3 — Blood investigations

Send urgently:

FBC
Group and save
Crossmatch according to severity
Coagulation screen
Fibrinogen
U&E
LFT when clinically appropriate

Repeat blood tests according to ongoing blood loss and clinical condition.

3. 🔴 ECLAMPSIA
Definition

Eclampsia = seizure in pregnancy/postpartum associated with pre-eclampsia, after excluding other causes.

It is an immediate maternal neurological emergency.
Step 1 — Call emergency team
Immediately:

Obstetrician
Anaesthetist
Midwife
Neonatal team if appropriate
Medical/neurology support if diagnostic uncertainty
Step 2 — During seizure
Protect the woman
Do not restrain
Prevent injury
Protect airway
Position appropriately, usually lateral
Suction available
Oxygen if clinically indicated/hypoxaemic

Do not put anything in her mouth.
Step 3 — ABC

After seizure:

Airway

Ensure airway.

Breathing

Assess:

RR
SpO₂
Aspiration
Pulmonary oedema
Circulation
BP
Pulse
IV access
Disability
GCS
Pupils
Glucose
Neurological status

Check glucose because hypoglycaemia can cause seizure.
Step 4 — Magnesium sulfate

Magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice for eclamptic seizures, according to the established RCOG/NICE obstetric emergency pathway.

Use the local IV/IM regimen and monitoring protocol.

Monitor:

Respiratory rate
Oxygen saturation
Reflexes
Urine output
Conscious level
Magnesium toxicity

Watch for:

Loss of patellar reflexes
Respiratory depression
Reduced consciousness
Oliguria
Antidote

Calcium gluconate

text:
[MASTER ATLAS — GYNAECOLOGICAL PROBLEMS IN PREGNANCY]
MASTER ATLAS — GYNAECOLOGICAL PROBLEMS IN PREGNANCY
PART I — UTERINE CONDITIONS
1. Fibroids in pregnancy ⭐⭐⭐

Problems

Pain/red degeneration
Rapid apparent growth
Pressure symptoms
Malpresentation
Obstructed labour
Placental abnormalities
Fetal growth restriction in selected cases
Preterm birth
Caesarean delivery
Postpartum haemorrhage
Retained placenta
Difficult caesarean if fibroid obstructs lower segment

Assessment

History: pain, bleeding, pressure symptoms
Abdominal examination
Ultrasound:
number
size
site
relation to placenta
relation to cervix/lower segment
fetal growth
MRI only when ultrasound is inadequate or anatomy needs clarification.

Management

Asymptomatic/small: expectant management.
Pain/red degeneration: rest, hydration and appropriate analgesia; exclude important differentials such as abruption, torsion and labour.
Large/multiple fibroids: consultant-led antenatal surveillance.
Consider serial fetal growth assessment where clinically indicated.
Document whether a lower-segment fibroid could obstruct labour.
Mode of birth is individualized.
Caesarean may be required if the fibroid obstructs the birth canal or creates another obstetric indication.
Myomectomy during pregnancy is generally avoided; surgery is reserved for exceptional situations such as an acute surgical abdomen or severe refractory complications.

Exam pearl:
Fibroid ≠ automatic Caesarean.

RCOG identifies fibroids as a major benign gynaecological condition and has recently highlighted the importance of improved pathways for fibroid care.

2. Adenomyosis in pregnancy

Potential issues

Pain
Miscarriage
Preterm birth
Placental complications
Abnormal placentation
Fetal growth problems in some patients
Increased obstetric intervention

Management

Usually expectant.
Specialist obstetric assessment if extensive adenomyosis.
Antenatal surveillance according to associated obstetric risk factors.
No routine surgical treatment during pregnancy.
3. Congenital uterine anomalies

Includes:

Septate uterus
Bicornuate uterus
Unicornuate uterus
Didelphys
Arcuate uterus
Cervical anomalies

Pregnancy risks

Miscarriage
Preterm birth
Malpresentation
Fetal growth restriction
Cervical insufficiency
Placental abnormalities
Caesarean delivery

Management

Confirm anatomy with ultrasound ± MRI if required.
Assess cervical length where clinically appropriate.
Monitor fetal growth.
Presentation determines delivery planning.
Previous reconstructive surgery must be considered.

Important: Do not confuse a uterine anomaly with fibroids or adenomyosis.

4. Previous myomectomy

This deserves its own category.

Assess:

Number of fibroids removed
Depth of uterine incision
Whether endometrial cavity was entered
Surgical approach
Operative report if available

Why it matters

Uterine rupture risk
Placenta praevia/accreta spectrum
Delivery planning

Management

Obtain operative notes where possible.
Individualized mode and timing of birth.
If significant full-thickness uterine surgery/cavity entry has occurred, planned Caesarean may be recommended rather than labour.
5. Endometrial polyps discovered during pregnancy

Usually incidental.

Management

Usually observation.
Avoid hysteroscopic polypectomy during pregnancy unless an exceptional indication exists.
Reassess postpartum if persistent/symptomatic.
6. Endometrial hyperplasia diagnosed before pregnancy

Pregnancy generally interrupts the usual hormonal environment.

Management

Review previous histology.
Establish whether atypia/EIN or malignancy was present.
Involve gynaecological oncology if there is atypia or suspected malignancy.
Definitive treatment is generally deferred until after pregnancy unless cancer is suspected.
PART II — CERVICAL CONDITIONS
7. Cervical polyp in pregnancy ⭐⭐⭐

Presentation:

Postcoital bleeding
Vaginal bleeding
Discharge
Incidental finding

Assessment

Speculum examination
Characterize lesion
Determine whether it appears benign
Consider cervical screening history.

Management

Small, asymptomatic, apparently benign polyp → usually observe.
Significant bleeding, large lesion, atypical appearance → senior gynaecological review.
Histology may be necessary if malignancy cannot be excluded.
Avoid unnecessary removal because cervical polypectomy can cause bleeding and may be associated with pregnancy complications.
8. Cervical ectropion

Common in pregnancy because of hormonal changes.

Presentation

Contact bleeding
Increased discharge

Management

Usually reassurance.
Exclude infection/cervical pathology when indicated.
Treatment is generally unnecessary during pregnancy.
9. Cervical insufficiency

This is a gynaecological/cervical structural problem with major obstetric consequences.

Think when

Previous painless second-trimester loss
Previous spontaneous very preterm birth
Short cervix
Cervical dilatation without labour

Management

Cervical-length surveillance where indicated.
Vaginal progesterone and/or cerclage according to clinical history and cervical findings.
Emergency/rescue cerclage in selected women with cervical dilatation, after excluding labour, infection and membrane rupture.
10. Cervical stenosis

Usually pre-existing.

Potential pregnancy relevance

Usually little effect on pregnancy.
May complicate cervical assessment or procedures.
Labour management depends on obstetric circumstances.
PART III — OVARIAN CONDITIONS
11. Ovarian cyst in pregnancy ⭐⭐⭐

This is one of the most important topics.

Types

Functional

Corpus luteum
Simple cyst

Benign neoplasms

Dermoid/teratoma
Cystadenoma
Endometrioma

Malignant

Epithelial ovarian cancer
Germ-cell tumour
Sex-cord stromal tumour
Metastatic tumour

RCOG's gynaecological curriculum specifically requires knowledge of functional cysts, dermoids, endometriotic cysts and ovarian cyst accidents.

Assessment

Ultrasound:

Size
Simple vs complex
Solid components
Papillary projections
Septations
Bilaterality
Doppler characteristics
Ascites
Other pelvic abnormalities
Management

Simple, benign-appearing, asymptomatic
→ expectant management.

Complex/suspicious
→ specialist assessment.

Acute abdomen
Think:

torsion
rupture
haemorrhage
infection

→ urgent gynaecology review.

12. Ovarian torsion in pregnancy ⭐⭐⭐

Presentation

Sudden unilateral pelvic/abdominal pain
Nausea/vomiting
Adnexal tenderness

Diagnosis

Ultrasound ± Doppler.
Normal Doppler flow does not reliably exclude torsion.

Management

Surgical emergency.
Prompt laparoscopy/laparotomy depending on gestation, anatomy and clinical situation.
Aim for ovarian conservation where feasible.
13. Ruptured ovarian cyst

Presentation

Acute pelvic pain
Possible haemoperitoneum
Haemodynamic instability in severe cases

Management

ABC/resuscitation
FBC, group & save/crossmatch as indicated
Ultrasound
Exclude ectopic pregnancy in early pregnancy
Conservative if stable and bleeding is limited
Surgery if unstable or significant ongoing haemorrhage.
14. Endometrioma in pregnancy

Usually managed conservatively.

Problems

Pain
Torsion
Rupture
Rare malignant transformation

Management

Ultrasound surveillance if appropriate.
Surgery only when clinically indicated, especially acute complications or significant suspicion of malignancy.

RCOG describes ovarian endometriomas as part of endometriosis and notes that management depends partly on whether pregnancy is planned.

15. Mature cystic teratoma / dermoid

Usually benign.

Management

Observe if asymptomatic and benign-appearing.
Surgery if:
torsion
rupture
obstruction
significant growth
suspicious features.
16. Suspected ovarian malignancy in pregnancy ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Expert ultrasound.
MRI without gadolinium when clinically appropriate.
MDT discussion.
Decide:
surveillance
surgery
chemotherapy
delivery timing

Do not delay evaluation simply because the patient is pregnant.

RCOG's curriculum specifically includes ovarian, cervical, endometrial and vulval malignancy.

PART IV — ENDOMETRIOSIS
17. Endometriosis in pregnancy ⭐⭐⭐

Pregnancy does not cure endometriosis.

Possible complications:

Pain
Endometrioma complications
Torsion
Rupture
Rare bowel/bladder complications
Rare spontaneous haemoperitoneum

Management

Usually conservative.
Analgesia appropriate for pregnancy.
Avoid hormonal suppression because pregnancy itself is established.
Surgery only for significant complications or malignancy concern.

RCOG notes that endometriosis can involve the ovaries, bowel, bladder and other pelvic structures and that extensive disease may require multidisciplinary specialist care.

PART V — PELVIC ORGAN PROLAPSE
18. Uterovaginal prolapse in pregnancy ⭐⭐⭐

Rare but important.

Types:

Uterine prolapse
Cervical prolapse
Vaginal wall prolapse
Cystocele
Rectocele
Enterocele

Problems

Vaginal ulceration
Bleeding
Infection
Urinary retention
Constipation
Cervical oedema
Preterm labour
Obstructed labour
Difficulty reducing prolapse
Management

Mild/asymptomatic
→ observation.

Symptomatic

Pelvic examination
Treat ulceration/infection if present
Vaginal pessary may be used in selected patients.
Monitor cervical changes and urinary symptoms.
Assess fetal growth and preterm-birth risk according to clinical situation.

Severe prolapse
→ consultant-led management.

Delivery

Vaginal birth may be possible.
Caesarean is not automatically required.
Caesarean may be necessary if prolapse is irreducible and obstructs labour or another obstetric indication exists.

RCOG's core curriculum explicitly includes uterovaginal prolapse and urogynaecological problems.

19. Cystocele in pregnancy

Management

Conservative.
Treat urinary retention/UTI.
Pessary in selected symptomatic patients.
Delivery usually based on obstetric indications.
20. Rectocele/enterocele in pregnancy

Usually conservative.

Treat:

Constipation
Pelvic pressure
Defaecatory dysfunction

Surgery is generally postponed until postpartum.

PART VI — VULVAL & VAGINAL CONDITIONS
21. Bartholin cyst/abscess

Pregnancy-specific approach

Cyst:
→ conservative if asymptomatic.

Abscess:

Antibiotics when indicated.
Drainage if clinically necessary.
Word catheter is commonly used.
Avoid unnecessary extensive surgery during pregnancy.

Important differential:

Vulval malignancy, particularly in an atypical lesion.
22. Vulval varicosities

May occur due to pelvic venous congestion.

Management

Reassurance
Avoid prolonged standing
Support garments
Analgesia if necessary

Usually regress postpartum.

Important: thrombosis can occur and should be assessed if painful, hard or asymmetric.

23. Vulval/vaginal haematoma

Consider:

Trauma
Delivery-related injury
Spontaneous haematoma

Management

Assess haemodynamic status.
Examine extent.
Analgesia.
Drainage/surgery if expanding, infected or causing significant symptoms/haemodynamic compromise.
24. Lichen sclerosus in pregnancy

Usually does not require major alteration of pregnancy care.

Management

Continue appropriate topical corticosteroid therapy.
Monitor for fissuring/trauma.
Ensure malignancy surveillance.
Vaginal delivery is usually possible.
25. Vulval intraepithelial neoplasia

Management

Specialist vulval disease assessment.
Biopsy suspicious lesions.
Conservative surveillance can be appropriate.
Definitive excision is generally individualized and often deferred when safe.
PART VII — GYNAECOLOGICAL CANCER IN PREGNANCY

This is a major MRCOG topic.

26. Cervical cancer in pregnancy ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Possible presentation:

Postcoital bleeding
Abnormal bleeding
Abnormal cervical appearance
Abnormal screening result
Incidental diagnosis
Initial assessment
Speculum examination
Cervical biopsy when indicated
Histopathology
MRI without gadolinium when staging requires it
MDT referral
Management depends on
Gestational age
Histological type
Stage
Tumour size
Lymph-node status
Patient's wishes
Desire for continuation of pregnancy

Principle:
Do not automatically terminate pregnancy.

Early-stage disease may sometimes be managed while continuing pregnancy, whereas advanced disease may require treatment that cannot safely be delayed.

MDT

Obstetrician
Gynaecological oncologist
Medical oncologist
Radiation oncologist
Neonatologist
Anaesthetist
Specialist midwife
Pathologist/radiologist
27. Endometrial cancer in pregnancy

Extremely uncommon because pregnancy itself is unusual in women with established endometrial carcinoma.

Management

Gynaecological oncology MDT.
Confirm histology.
Determine stage.
Individualize pregnancy continuation versus definitive cancer treatment.
Definitive surgery is generally postpartum if pregnancy can safely continue.
28. Ovarian cancer in pregnancy ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Approach

Suspicious adnexal mass → specialist ultrasound → MDT.

Possible options:

Conservative surveillance

For clearly benign lesions.

Surgery

For:

Suspicious malignancy
Acute complications
Significant growth
Torsion/rupture

Timing is individualized, often aiming for the second trimester when surgery is necessary and pregnancy can safely continue.

Chemotherapy

Some regimens can be used during pregnancy when necessary, generally after the first trimester.

Avoid chemotherapy in the first trimester because of major fetal teratogenic risk.

29. Vulval cancer in pregnancy

Rare.

Management

Biopsy suspicious lesion.
Gynaecological oncology MDT.
Surgical treatment may be necessary during pregnancy depending on stage.
Groin-node assessment and treatment depend on tumour characteristics.
30. Vaginal cancer in pregnancy

Rare.

Management requires:

Biopsy
MRI/staging
MDT
Individualized timing of treatment and delivery.

Radiotherapy is generally incompatible with continuing pregnancy.

PART VIII — INFECTIONS THAT ARE PRIMARILY GYNAECOLOGICAL
31. Bacterial vaginosis

Pregnancy relevance:

Symptomatic infection
Association with preterm birth

Management

Treat symptomatic women according to pregnancy-safe antibiotic guidance.
Routine treatment of asymptomatic BV solely to prevent preterm birth is not generally recommended.
32. Vulvovaginal candidiasis

Very common in pregnancy.

Management

Prefer topical azole therapy.
Avoid oral fluconazole where possible in pregnancy.
33. Trichomoniasis

Management

Test and treat appropriately.
Treat sexual partner(s).
Screen for other STIs.
Use pregnancy-compatible treatment.
34. Chlamydia

Important because of:

Maternal infection
Neonatal conjunctivitis
Neonatal pneumonia

Management

Pregnancy-safe antibiotic treatment.
Partner management.
Test of cure where recommended.
STI screening.
35. Gonorrhoea

Risk of:

Maternal pelvic infection
Neonatal ophthalmia
Disseminated infection

Requires appropriate pregnancy-safe antibiotic treatment and partner notification.

36. Syphilis in pregnancy ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

This becomes an obstetric + infectious disease problem, but is essential in a gynaecological pregnancy atlas.

Management

37. Genital herpes

Primary infection late in pregnancy is particularly important.

Management depends on:
