Delivery planning depends on active lesions/prodrome and clinical circumstances.

PART IX — URINARY/GYNAECOLOGICAL PROBLEMS
38. Stress urinary incontinence in pregnancy

Usually conservative:

Pelvic-floor muscle training
Lifestyle measures
Treat constipation
Avoid unnecessary surgery
39. Overactive bladder
Behavioural modification
Bladder training
Fluid/caffeine advice
Pelvic-floor therapy

Drug treatment is generally avoided unless specialist assessment indicates benefit.

40. Urinary retention due to prolapse

This is an important emergency complication.

Management

Bladder scan
Catheterization if necessary
Reduce prolapse
Treat precipitating factors
Pessary if appropriate
Monitor renal function if prolonged obstruction.
PART X — GYNAECOLOGICAL CONDITIONS RELATED TO PREVIOUS SURGERY
41. Previous cervical surgery

Examples:

LLETZ/LEEP
Cone biopsy
Multiple cervical procedures

Pregnancy implications:

Cervical shortening
Preterm birth
Cervical stenosis
Cervical incompetence in selected patients

Management involves appropriate cervical assessment and preterm-birth prevention strategy based on individual history.

42. Previous endometriosis surgery

Consider:

Adhesions
Distorted pelvic anatomy
Previous bowel/bladder surgery
Caesarean surgical complexity

Important during abdominal surgery.

43. Previous ovarian surgery

Possible:

Reduced ovarian reserve
Adhesions
Altered anatomy
Increased risk of surgical injury

Important when planning Caesarean or other pelvic surgery.

44. Previous extensive pelvic surgery

May result in:

Adhesions
Bowel injury
Bladder injury
Ureteric injury
Difficult Caesarean

Management

Review operative history.
Consider senior surgeon involvement.
Urology/general surgery backup if major adhesions or organ involvement is anticipated.
PART XI — OTHER IMPORTANT GYNAECOLOGICAL CONDITIONS
45. PCOS in pregnancy

Risks include:

GDM
hypertensive disorders
miscarriage
preterm birth
metabolic complications

Management becomes primarily obstetric/metabolic.

46. Endometriosis-associated pregnancy

Consider:

preterm birth
placenta praevia
hypertensive disorders
rare spontaneous haemoperitoneum.
47. Severe pelvic adhesions

Important particularly with:

previous Caesarean
endometriosis
previous PID
previous laparotomy.

Main concern = operative difficulty and visceral injury.

48. Pelvic inflammatory disease discovered in pregnancy

True PID is uncommon once pregnancy is established.

If pelvic pain/fever occurs, consider:

appendicitis
UTI/pyelonephritis
chorioamnionitis
ovarian torsion
ectopic/heterotopic pregnancy in early pregnancy
tubo-ovarian abscess.
49. Tubo-ovarian abscess

Rare but potentially serious.

Management

Antibiotics appropriate for pregnancy.
MDT involvement.
Drainage/surgery if abscess is large, ruptured, refractory or causing sepsis.
50. Genital tract congenital anomalies

Examples:

Vaginal septum
Transverse vaginal septum
Cervical agenesis/abnormality
Uterine anomalies
Mullerian anomalies

Management is individualized according to anatomy and obstruction.

THE HIGH-YIELD MRCOG MASTER CLASSIFICATION

For examination purposes, remember pregnancy-related gynaecological disease under 10 headings:

| Category | Conditions |
|---|---|
| 1. Uterus | Fibroid, adenomyosis, uterine anomaly, previous myomectomy, endometrial polyp/hyperplasia |
| 2. Cervix | Cervical polyp, ectropion, cervical insufficiency, previous LLETZ/cone |
| 3. Ovary | Simple cyst, dermoid, endometrioma, cystadenoma, torsion, rupture, ovarian cancer |
| 4. Endometriosis | Pelvic, ovarian, bowel, bladder disease |
| 5. Prolapse | Uterine prolapse, cystocele, rectocele, enterocele |
| 6. Vulva/vagina | Bartholin disease, vulval varicosities, lichen sclerosus, VIN, vaginal lesions |
| 7. Cancer | Cervical, ovarian, endometrial, vulval, vaginal |
| 8. Infection | BV, candidiasis, trichomoniasis, chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis, herpes |
| 9. Urogynaecology | SUI, OAB, urinary retention, prolapse-related obstruction |
| 10. Previous surgery/adhesions | Myomectomy, LLETZ, cone, ovarian surgery, endometriosis surgery, laparotomy |
UNIVERSAL RCOG APPROACH TO ANY GYNAECOLOGICAL CONDITION IN PREGNANCY

For every case, use this sequence:

STEP 1 — Is mother stable?
ABC
BP
pulse
RR
temperature
oxygen saturation
pain
bleeding
sepsis
STEP 2 — Is fetus well?

Depending on gestation:

fetal heart
CTG
ultrasound
growth
liquor
placenta
Dopplers where indicated.
STEP 3 — Identify the gynaecological pathology

History → examination → ultrasound → appropriate MRI/biopsy/laboratory testing.

STEP 4 — Decide whether it is:

A. Incidental and benign

→ observe.

B. Symptomatic but stable

→ conservative/specialist management.

C. Acute surgical condition

→ urgent surgery.

D. Suspicious for malignancy

→ gynaecological oncology MDT.

E. Infection/sepsis

→ cultures + pregnancy-safe antimicrobial treatment + source control.

STEP 5 — Ask the five pregnancy questions
Does it threaten the mother?
Does it threaten the fetus?
Does it obstruct labour?
Does it require surgery now or can surgery wait?
Does it change timing/mode of delivery?
STEP 6 — MDT when appropriate

Particularly:

Gynaecologist + obstetrician + maternal-fetal medicine + gynaecological oncologist + radiologist + pathologist + anaesthetist + neonatologist, with other specialties according to the organ involved.

text:
[MASTER GYNAECOLOGY SIGNS, EponYMS, TRIADS, SYNDROMES & DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA > 72. THE EXAMINATION FRAMEWORK TO MEMORIZE]
For any gynecological disease, think in this sequence:

SYMPTOMS → PHYSICAL SIGN → Eponym/triad → FIRST-LINE INVESTIGATION → DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA → GOLD-STANDARD/CONFIRMATORY TEST → CLASSIFICATION/STAGING

For example:

Endometriosis

Dysmenorrhoea/deep dyspareunia → uterosacral tenderness/nodule → ground-glass endometrioma → TVUS → clinical/imaging diagnosis → laparoscopy/histology when required → stage/location

PCOS

Oligomenorrhoea + hirsutism → hyperandrogenism → Rotterdam → exclude mimics → metabolic assessment

PID

Pelvic pain → cervical motion/uterine/adnexal tenderness → STI testing + inflammatory markers/imaging as indicated → clinical diagnosis → complications assessment

Ovarian torsion

Acute unilateral pain + vomiting → adnexal tenderness → enlarged ovary/whirlpool → urgent gynaecological assessment → surgery confirms torsion

Endometrial cancer

Postmenopausal bleeding → abnormal endometrium → endometrial sampling → histology → staging

Highest-yield distinction

Physiological sign ≠ pathological sign ≠ diagnostic criterion ≠ gold standard.

For MRCOG/FCPS-style questions, this distinction is particularly important. For example:

Strawberry cervix → strongly suggests trichomoniasis, but microbiological testing is more definitive.
Chandelier sign → supports PID, but is not pathognomonic.
Ground-glass ovary → suggests endometrioma.
Whirlpool sign → strongly suggests torsion, but absence does not exclude it.
CA125 elevation → does not diagnose ovarian cancer.
Normal ultrasound → does not exclude endometriosis.
Polycystic ovarian morphology → does not by itself diagnose PCOS.
Postmenopausal bleeding → is a red flag requiring assessment, not itself a diagnosis.

This is the consolidated physiological + pathological gynecology signs, eponyms, triads, syndromes, imaging signs, histological signs and diagnostic-criteria master reference, with obstetrics excluded.

High leak

PPROM = rupture of membranes before 37+0 weeks and before onset of labour.

RCOG GTG 73 specifically covers suspected PPROM from 24+0 to 36+6 weeks.

First-line assessment

History

When did leaking start?
Continuous/intermittent?
Colour?
Odour?
Amount?
Blood/meconium?
Contractions?
Fever/rigors?
Fetal movements?

Examination

Maternal observations
Fetal assessment
Sterile speculum examination

Avoid unnecessary digital vaginal examination when PPROM is suspected.

Diagnosis

If fluid is seen at speculum → supports diagnosis.

If no fluid is seen, RCOG recommends considering IGFBP-1 or PAMG-1 vaginal-fluid testing to aid diagnosis.

Important complications
Chorioamnionitis
Preterm birth
Cord prolapse
Placental abruption
Pulmonary hypoplasia in very early PPROM
3. 🩸 Antepartum haemorrhage

Very important: RCOG defines APH as bleeding from/in the genital tract from 24+0 weeks until birth.

Differential diagnosis
| Condition | Typical clues |
|---|---|
| Placenta praevia | Usually painless bright-red bleeding |
| Placental abruption | Painful bleeding, uterine tenderness/rigidity |
| Vasa praevia | Bleeding after ROM + acute fetal compromise |
| Bloody show | Small amount with labour |
| Cervical ectropion | Contact bleeding |
| Cervical polyp | Contact bleeding |
| Cervical malignancy | Persistent/irregular bleeding |
| Vaginal trauma | History of intercourse/trauma |
| Uterine rupture | Pain, shock, fetal compromise, previous uterine scar |
APH immediate approach

ABC → maternal resuscitation → fetal assessment → identify source → prepare blood products if significant.

Check:

FBC
Group and save/crossmatch
Coagulation profile if significant bleeding/abruption
RhD status
Kleihauer where indicated
Ultrasound for placental location/fetal assessment
🚨 Never forget

Do NOT perform a digital vaginal examination until placenta praevia has been excluded if placenta location is unknown and significant APH is present.

4. 👶 Reduced fetal movements

One of the highest-yield triage presentations.

24–28 weeks
Confirm fetal heartbeat with Doppler
Maternal assessment
BP
Urinalysis
Fundal-height assessment
Further ultrasound if indicated.
>28 weeks

PART LVIII — HIGH-YIELD "WHY?" QUESTIONS
| Question | Core explanation |
|---|---|
| Why is the ureter vulnerable during hysterectomy? | It lies close to the uterine artery and cervix/cardinal ligament region. |
| Why can cervical cancer spread to pelvic nodes? | Cervical lymphatics drain through parametrial and pelvic nodal pathways. |
| Why can fundal uterine disease involve inguinal nodes? | Lymphatics can accompany the round ligament. |
| Why does ovarian cancer involve para-aortic nodes? | Ovarian embryology and lymphatic drainage relate to its original posterior abdominal location. |
| Why does endometriosis cause pain? | Inflammation, haemorrhage, fibrosis, adhesions and altered nociception contribute. |
| Why does PCOS cause anovulation? | Abnormal follicular development with androgenic, gonadotrophin and metabolic signalling prevents normal dominant follicle maturation. |
| Why does pregnancy cause anaemia? | Plasma volume rises more than RBC mass. |
| Why does creatinine fall in pregnancy? | GFR and renal blood flow increase. |
| Why does PaCO₂ fall? | Progesterone increases maternal ventilation. |
| Why does breastfeeding suppress ovulation? | Prolactin suppresses hypothalamic GnRH/LH pulsatility. |
| Why does brain sparing occur? | Increased placental resistance causes fetal redistribution toward vital organs. |
| Why does shoulder dystocia occur? | The shoulders fail to complete normal rotation/descent, often with anterior shoulder impaction behind the symphysis. |
| Why does PAS cause major haemorrhage? | Abnormal placental adherence/invasion prevents normal separation and effective uterine haemostasis. |

[MASTER OBGYN DIFFERENTIAL & DEFINITIVE DIAGNOSIS ATLAS > 65. MASTER DIAGNOSTIC SEQUENCE FOR ANY OBGYN CASE]
For an MRCOG/FCPS answer, use this sequence:

1. Stabilise
→ ABCDE
→ maternal haemodynamics
→ fetal status if pregnant

2. Establish pregnancy status
→ urine/serum β-hCG when relevant

3. Localise the problem
→ obstetric / gynaecological / surgical / urinary

4. Generate differential diagnoses
→ common first
→ dangerous diagnoses first
→ diagnosis not to miss

5. Initial investigations
→ FBC
→ blood group/Rh where relevant
→ urine
→ β-hCG
→ relevant cultures
→ ultrasound

6. Targeted investigations
→ hormones
→ Doppler
→ CT/MRI
→ hysteroscopy
→ colposcopy
→ laparoscopy

7. Definitive confirmation
→ histopathology / imaging / microbiology / operative findings depending on disease

8. Stage/severity assessment
→ maternal severity
→ fetal severity
→ cancer stage
→ disease extent

9. Management

10. Follow-up and recurrence/risk assessment

The highest-yield distinction to remember

“Initial diagnosis” is what you suspect from the presentation.
“Differential diagnosis” is what else could explain it.
“Definitive diagnosis” is the evidence that establishes the actual condition.

For example:

Pain + amenorrhoea + positive β-hCG
→ Initial: suspected ectopic pregnancy
→ Differentials: miscarriage, corpus luteum, PUL
→ Definitive/confirmatory: TVUS demonstrating an extrauterine gestation; operative confirmation if required.

Postmenopausal bleeding
→ Initial: abnormal postmenopausal bleeding
→ Differentials: atrophy, polyp, hyperplasia, cancer
→ Definitive: endometrial histopathology when endometrial pathology is suspected.

Heavy menstrual bleeding + enlarged irregular uterus
→ Initial: structural uterine pathology, likely fibroid
→ Differentials: adenomyosis, polyp, malignancy
→ Confirmatory: ultrasound
→ Definitive pathological diagnosis: histology if tissue is obtained.

Placental invasion confirmed histologically after delivery/hysterectomy.

text:
[MASTER OBSTETRIC & GYNAECOLOGICAL DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA > 4. DEFINITIVE/GOLD-STANDARD CONFIRMATION]
→ highest level of confirmation, often histology, direct visualisation or specific imaging.

For example:

Ovarian cancer: CA-125 = supportive → ultrasound = imaging assessment → CT = staging → histology = definitive diagnosis.

Whereas:

Pre-eclampsia: there is no histological “gold standard”; the diagnosis is clinical, based on new hypertension after 20 weeks plus proteinuria and/or maternal/uteroplacental dysfunction.

And:

Endometriosis: laparoscopy is capable of direct surgical confirmation, but modern NICE practice does not require diagnostic laparoscopy for every woman; TVUS is recommended during diagnostic assessment and a normal scan does not exclude disease.

This distinction between screening → initial → diagnostic → definitive is the framework I would use for the entire MRCOG/FCPS OBGYN diagnostic atlas.

Don't memorise every laboratory value as a rigid “normal/abnormal” cut-off.For exams and clinical practice, divide values into:A. Physiological pregnancy ranges
→ Hb ↓, WBC ↑, creatinine ↓, ALP ↑, fibrinogen ↑, D-dimer ↑, albumin ↓.B. Formal diagnostic thresholds
→ 140/90, 160/110, PCR 30, ACR 8, creatinine 90, ALT 40, platelets 150.C. Disease-severity thresholds
→ ALT 70, bile acids 100, MCA-PSV 1.5 MoM, Hb 85, fibrinogen 2 g/L.D. Screening thresholds
→ aneuploidy ≥1:150, RMI ≥250.E. Assay-dependent reference values
→ TSH, FT4, ferritin, AMH, testosterone, prolactin, vitamin levels, etc. should be interpreted using the relevant laboratory/assay and clinical context.NICE's current antenatal framework recommends booking FBC, blood group/RhD and infectious-disease/haemoglobinopathy screening, with repeat FBC and antibody testing at 28 weeks. NICE's current fertility guideline was updated in March 2026, so older MRCOG notes containing older AMH/FSH or semen reference values should be checked against the new recommendations.NICE Antenatal Care guideline NG201

| PUL | — | — | Serial β-hCG + repeat TVUS |
Ectopic pregnancy — remember

Investigation of choice:
TVUS + quantitative β-hCG

No β-hCG "discriminatory zone" should be used alone to diagnose ectopic pregnancy.

| <50 | Severe bleeding-risk range |
Liver

Use the laboratory's pregnancy/reference range.

ALT/AST >40 IU/L is used in the NICE definition as biochemical hepatic involvement in the appropriate clinical context.

Neurological

Severe headache, visual symptoms, hyperreflexia/clonus or seizures are clinical severe features and cannot be reduced to one laboratory number.

text:
[MASTER OBSTETRIC INVESTIGATIONS & CUT-OFFS > 12. HELLP]

| Elevated liver enzymes | ↑AST/ALT |
| Low platelets | <100 ×10⁹/L |

HELLP = haemolysis + elevated liver enzymes + low platelets.

13. PLGF / sFlt-1:PlGF

There is no universal numerical threshold that can safely be applied to every assay.

Memorise:

Use the manufacturer's validated assay-specific threshold and local NICE/RCOG pathway.

Do not transfer an sFlt-1:PlGF ratio from one commercial assay to another.

MASTER RCOG/NICE OBSTETRIC INVESTIGATION TABLE
I. EARLY PREGNANCY
| Condition | First-line investigation | Gold standard / IOC | Normal / reassuring | Abnormal / diagnostic cut-off |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pregnancy confirmation | Urine pregnancy test | Quantitative serum β-hCG + TVUS when clinically indicated | Negative | Positive pregnancy test |
| Pregnancy of unknown location | TVUS + quantitative β-hCG | Serial β-hCG + repeat TVUS | Appropriate hCG trend + IUP | Abnormal trend/US → ectopic/PUL pathway |
| Ectopic pregnancy | TVUS + quantitative β-hCG | TVUS demonstrating extrauterine pregnancy | Confirmed IUP | Extrauterine sac/yolk sac/embryo ± cardiac activity |
| Miscarriage | TVUS | TVUS using accepted diagnostic criteria | Viable IUP | CRL ≥7 mm without cardiac activity or MSD ≥25 mm without embryo, when correctly assessed |
| Recurrent miscarriage | Pelvic ultrasound + APS testing | 3D uterine imaging + APS testing ± genetic evaluation | Normal uterus/negative APS | APS persistent positivity ≥12 weeks apart |
| Molar pregnancy | TVUS + quantitative β-hCG | Histopathology of products of conception | Normal pregnancy morphology/hCG | Molar histology + markedly abnormal hCG |
| Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia | Serial quantitative β-hCG | Serial quantitative β-hCG + specialist assessment | Appropriate falling hCG | Plateau/rise/persistent hCG after evacuation |
| Hyperemesis gravidarum | Clinical assessment + U&E/FBC/LFT | Clinical diagnosis supported by laboratory assessment | Normal hydration/electrolytes | Dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, weight loss |
II. FETAL GROWTH & WELLBEING
| Condition | First-line | Gold standard / IOC | Normal | Abnormal / cut-off |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SGA | SFH screening | Ultrasound EFW/AC | ≥10th centile | <10th centile |
| Severe SGA | Ultrasound | Ultrasound EFW/AC | ≥3rd centile | <3rd centile |
| FGR | Ultrasound growth assessment | Serial ultrasound + Doppler assessment | Appropriate growth/placental function | EFW/AC <10th + evidence of placental dysfunction |
| Fetal wellbeing | CTG when indicated | CTG + ultrasound/Doppler according to clinical situation | Baseline 110–160; variability 5–25 bpm | Abnormal CTG features |
| Reduced fetal movements | CTG | CTG + ultrasound for growth/liquor ± Doppler | Reassuring CTG/growth | Abnormal CTG or growth/liquor/Doppler |
| Fetal anaemia | MCA-PSV Doppler | MCA-PSV Doppler; fetal blood sampling if definitive Hb required | <1.5 MoM | ≥1.5 MoM |
| Hydrops fetalis | Ultrasound | Detailed ultrasound + fetal echocardiography ± genetic/infectious work-up | No abnormal fluid collections | ≥2 fetal fluid compartments affected |
| Oligohydramnios | Ultrasound | DVP/AF assessment | DVP 2–8 cm | DVP <2 cm |
| Polyhydramnios | Ultrasound | DVP/AF assessment | DVP 2–8 cm | DVP >8 cm |

| Condition | First-line | Gold standard / IOC | Key diagnostic finding |
|---|---|---|---|
| Placenta praevia | Transabdominal US | TVUS | Placental relationship to internal os |

IV. ANEUPLOIDY & FETAL ANOMALIES
| Condition | First-line | Gold standard / definitive investigation | Important value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Down syndrome screening | Combined screening | CVS/amniocentesis for diagnosis | Screening ≠ diagnosis |
| Aneuploidy screening | Combined test or cfDNA | Invasive diagnostic testing | QF-PCR/karyotype ± microarray |
| Increased NT | First-trimester US | Detailed fetal assessment ± invasive testing | ≥3.5 mm significant increased NT |
| Neural tube defect | Anomaly ultrasound | Detailed targeted ultrasound | AFP interpreted by MoM |
| Fetal cardiac anomaly | Routine anomaly scan | Fetal echocardiography | Structural/functional abnormality |
| Fetal arrhythmia | Ultrasound/CTG | Fetal echocardiography + M-mode/Doppler | Abnormal rhythm/rate |
V. PRETERM LABOUR & MEMBRANES
| Condition | First-line | Gold standard / IOC | Cut-off |
|---|---|---|---|
| Short cervix | TV cervical-length scan | TV cervical-length measurement | ≤25 mm |
| Suspected preterm labour | Clinical assessment + speculum | TVCL and/or fFN according to pathway | CL ≤25 mm; fFN ≥50 ng/mL |
| PPROM | Sterile speculum | Visible pooling / validated biochemical test when needed | Pooling of liquor |
| PPROM with no pooling | PAMG-1/IGFBP-1 where appropriate | Validated biochemical ROM test | Positive test supports ROM |
| Established preterm labour | Clinical assessment | Clinical diagnosis supported by cervical change/regular contractions | No single universal numerical cut-off |
VI. HYPERTENSIVE DISEASE
| Condition | First-line | Gold standard / IOC | Normal | Diagnostic/severe |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hypertension | BP measurement | Repeated/confirmed BP measurement | <140/90 | ≥140/90 |
| Severe hypertension | BP | BP measurement | <160/110 | ≥160 systolic or ≥110 diastolic |
| Pre-eclampsia | BP + urine protein + blood tests | Clinical diagnosis using BP + proteinuria/organ dysfunction + fetal/placental assessment | No hypertension/organ dysfunction | ≥140/90 + qualifying proteinuria/organ dysfunction |
| Proteinuria | ACR/PCR | Quantitative ACR/PCR | PCR <30; ACR <8 | PCR ≥30; ACR ≥8 |
| HELLP | FBC + LFT + haemolysis screen | Clinical + laboratory diagnosis | Normal platelets/LFT/haemolysis | Platelets <100 + elevated enzymes + haemolysis |
VII. GESTATIONAL DIABETES
| Condition | First-line | Gold standard / IOC | Normal | Diagnostic |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GDM | Risk-based glucose testing | 75-g 2-hour OGTT | Fasting <5.6; 2-h <7.8 mmol/L | Fasting ≥5.6 OR 2-h ≥7.8 |
| Overt diabetes | Plasma glucose/HbA1c where appropriate | Diagnostic plasma glucose criteria | Below diabetes range | FPG ≥7.0; 2-h ≥11.1; HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol |
| Glycaemic monitoring in GDM | Capillary glucose | SMBG/CGM where clinically indicated | Individualised targets | Persistent values above treatment targets |
VIII. INTRAHEPATIC CHOLESTASIS
| Condition | First-line | Gold standard / IOC | Normal | Abnormal/severe |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ICP | Bile acids + LFT | Serum total bile acids | <19 µmol/L | ≥19 |
| Mild ICP | Bile acids | Serum bile acids | <19 | 19–39 |
| Moderate ICP | Bile acids | Serum bile acids | <40 | 40–99 |
| Severe ICP | Bile acids | Serum bile acids | <100 | ≥100 µmol/L |
IX. HAEMATOLOGY
| Condition | First-line | Gold standard / IOC | Normal | Abnormal/severe |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Anaemia | FBC | FBC ± iron studies | Hb ≥110 g/L commonly used | <110 g/L |
| Severe anaemia | FBC | FBC | — | Hb <70 g/L |
| Iron deficiency | FBC + ferritin | Ferritin | ≥30 µg/L | <30 µg/L |
| Thrombocytopenia | FBC | FBC ± blood film | ≥150 ×10⁹/L | <150 |
| Severe thrombocytopenia | FBC | FBC | ≥50 | <50 ×10⁹/L |
X. RED-CELL ALLOIMMUNISATION
| Condition | First-line | Gold standard / IOC | Important threshold |
|---|---|---|---|
| Maternal red-cell antibodies | Antibody screen | Antibody identification + quantification/titre | Depends on antibody |
| Anti-D | Antibody level | Quantitative anti-D | >4 IU/mL specialist referral; >15 IU/mL severe risk |
| Anti-c | Antibody level | Quantitative anti-c | >7.5 IU/mL referral; >20 IU/mL high risk |
| Anti-K | Antibody screen | Specialist fetal medicine assessment | Any detectable anti-K |
| Fetal anaemia from antibodies | MCA-PSV | MCA-PSV Doppler | ≥1.5 MoM |
XI. INFECTIONS
| Infection | First-line | Gold standard / definitive | Important result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Syphilis | Treponemal + non-treponemal serology | Serological diagnosis | Fourfold titre change = significant response |
| HIV | 4th-gen Ag/Ab | Confirmatory laboratory testing | Reactive screen → confirm |
| Hepatitis B | HBsAg | HBsAg + HBV DNA when indicated | HBsAg positive |
| Hepatitis C | Anti-HCV | HCV RNA | RNA positive = current infection |
| Rubella immunity | Rubella IgG | Rubella IgG | Positive = immune |
| Varicella immunity | VZV IgG | VZV PCR for active lesions | IgG positive = immune |
| Parvovirus B19 | IgG + IgM | Serology ± PCR | Recent infection → fetal surveillance |
| Toxoplasmosis | IgG + IgM | Reference testing/avidity ± PCR | Interpret by timing/assay |
| CMV | IgG + IgM ± avidity | Amniotic-fluid PCR when indicated | Fetal infection requires appropriate testing |
XII. URINARY/RENAL
| Condition | First-line | Gold standard / IOC | Normal | Abnormal |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| UTI | Urine dipstick + MSU where indicated | MSU culture & sensitivity | No significant bacteriuria | Significant bacteriuria/positive culture |
| Pyelonephritis | MSU + FBC/U&E | Urine culture + clinical diagnosis | No infection | Fever/systemic illness + urinary source |
| Renal colic | Ultrasound | US → MRI if needed | No obstruction | Stone/obstruction |
XIII. THYROID
| Condition | First-line | Gold standard / IOC | Normal | Abnormal |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hypothyroidism | TSH + FT4 | TSH + FT4 using pregnancy-specific ranges | Within trimester-specific range | Elevated TSH ± low FT4 |
| Hyperthyroidism | TSH + FT4/FT3 | TSH + FT4/FT3 | Normal | Suppressed TSH + elevated FT4/FT3 |
| Graves disease | TSH/FT4 + clinical assessment | TRAb | Negative | Positive TRAb |
XIV. CARDIORESPIRATORY
| Condition | First-line | Gold standard / IOC | Important abnormality |
|---|---|---|---|
| Maternal cardiac disease | ECG + echocardiography | Echocardiography | Structural/functional abnormality |
| Arrhythmia | ECG | ECG + Holter/event monitor | Documented abnormal rhythm |
| Peripartum cardiomyopathy | Echo | Echocardiography | LVEF <45% |
| Asthma | Clinical + PEF | Spirometry when appropriate | Reduced airflow |
XV. VTE
| Condition | First-line | Gold standard / IOC | Key result |
|---|---|---|---|
| DVT | Compression ultrasound | Compression duplex ultrasound | Non-compressible vein |
| PE | ECG + CXR ± CUS | V/Q or CTPA when imaging required | Imaging-confirmed PE |
| Pregnancy D-dimer | Not standalone | No universal gold-standard use | Do not use isolated universal cut-off |
XVI. SURGICAL OBSTETRIC CONDITIONS
| Condition | First-line | Gold standard / IOC |
|---|---|---|
| Appendicitis | Ultrasound | MRI if US inconclusive |
| Cholelithiasis/cholecystitis | Abdominal US | Ultrasound |
| Renal colic | Renal US | MRI/appropriate imaging if required |
| Bowel obstruction | Clinical + abdominal imaging | CT/MRI according to circumstances |
XVII. DIABETIC EMERGENCIES
| Condition | First-line | Gold standard / IOC | Important cut-off |
|---|---|---|---|
| DKA | Glucose + ketones + VBG/U&E | Clinical + biochemical diagnosis | β-OHB ≥3 mmol/L strongly supports DKA |
| DKA severity | VBG/ABG | Blood gas | pH <7.30 concerning |
| Anion-gap acidosis | U&E + blood gas | Biochemical assessment | Increased AG |
| Euglycaemic DKA | Ketones + blood gas | Clinical/biochemical diagnosis | Can occur without marked hyperglycaemia |
XVIII. INTRAPARTUM ASSESSMENT
| Condition | First-line | Gold standard / IOC | Normal/abnormal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fetal wellbeing during labour | CTG when indicated | CTG interpreted according to full criteria | Baseline 110–160; variability 5–25 |
| Malposition | Clinical examination | Intrapartum ultrasound | Position/station documented |
| Breech | Abdominal examination | Ultrasound | Presentation documented |
| Shoulder dystocia | Clinical diagnosis | Clinical diagnosis | No investigation should delay manoeuvres |
| Cord prolapse | Vaginal examination | Clinical diagnosis | No imaging should delay emergency delivery |
XIX. INTRA-AMNIOTIC INFECTION & SEPSIS
| Condition | First-line | Gold standard / IOC | Important findings |
|---|---|---|---|
| Intra-amniotic infection | Clinical assessment + maternal/fetal observations | Clinical diagnosis | Maternal fever, fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, purulent liquor |
| Maternal sepsis | Sepsis assessment + cultures/lactate | Clinical diagnosis + source identification | Lactate ≥2 concerning; ≥4 severe physiological derangement |
| Chorioamnionitis | Clinical | Clinical | No single diagnostic blood-test cut-off |
XX. POSTPARTUM HAEMORRHAGE
| Condition | First-line | Gold standard / IOC | Important threshold |
|---|---|---|---|
| PPH | Quantified blood loss + maternal assessment | Clinical + quantified blood loss | ≥500 mL vaginal; ≥1000 mL CS traditional definition |
| PPH coagulopathy | FBC/coagulation/fibrinogen | Fibrinogen + coagulation profile | Fibrinogen <2 g/L major concern |
| Major PPH | FBC, crossmatch, coagulation, fibrinogen | Comprehensive haemorrhage assessment | Treat according to physiology, not volume alone |
XXI. RETAINED PRODUCTS / POSTPARTUM INFECTION
| Condition | First-line | Gold standard / IOC | Key finding |
|---|---|---|---|
| RPOC | TVUS | TVUS + colour Doppler | Intrauterine mass ± vascularity |
| Secondary PPH | FBC + TVUS | TVUS + colour Doppler when RPOC suspected | RPOC/vascular lesion |
| Postpartum endometritis | Clinical assessment | Clinical diagnosis | Fever + uterine tenderness ± offensive lochia |
XXII. STILLBIRTH
| Condition | First-line | Gold standard / definitive assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Suspected fetal death | Ultrasound | Ultrasound demonstrating absent fetal cardiac activity |
| Cause of stillbirth | Placental/fetal/maternal assessment | Multidisciplinary investigation: placental histology + fetal examination/autopsy ± genetics, FMH, APS/infection testing as indicated |
XXIII. MULTIPLE PREGNANCY
| Condition | First-line | Gold standard / IOC | Key finding |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chorionicity | First-trimester US | First-trimester ultrasound | Lambda vs T-sign |
| TTTS | Ultrasound | Serial ultrasound | Donor oligo + recipient polyhydramnios |
| TAPS | MCA Doppler | Bilateral MCA-PSV Doppler | Intertwin anaemia/polycythaemia pattern |
| TRAP | Ultrasound | US + colour Doppler | Reversed arterial perfusion |
XXIV. INVASIVE FETAL TESTING
| Procedure | First-line indication | Definitive investigation | Timing |
|---|---|---|---|
| CVS | Diagnostic genetic testing required | CVS with QF-PCR/karyotype ± microarray | 11+0–13+6 weeks |
| Amniocentesis | Diagnostic genetic/infection testing | Amniotic fluid genetic/molecular testing | ≥15 weeks |
| Cordocentesis | Suspected fetal anaemia/selected indications | Fetal blood sampling | Selected cases |
| IUT | Severe fetal anaemia | Cordocentesis-guided intrauterine transfusion | Specialist fetal medicine |

For your final MRCOG/FCPS notes, I recommend using:FLI = First-line investigation
IOC = Investigation of choice
GS = Gold standard/definitive testand writing “No true gold standard” whenever the diagnosis is fundamentally clinical—for example placental abruption, shoulder dystocia, cord prolapse, chorioamnionitis and postpartum endometritis. This prevents the common exam error of calling an ultrasound or blood test a “gold standard” when it actually is not.Combine all
MASTER RCOG/NICE OBSTETRICS
Conditions → First-Line Investigation → Investigation of Choice → Gold Standard → Normal → Abnormal → Diagnostic Cut-off → Severe/Critical Cut-off → InterpretationExam rule: First-line ≠ gold standard. Where no true gold-standard test exists, it is explicitly stated. Numerical values should be interpreted with gestational age, laboratory reference ranges, MoM/centiles, assay and clinical context.

I. EARLY PREGNANCY
| Condition | First-line investigation | IOC / preferred | Gold standard / definitive | Normal | Abnormal / diagnostic | Severe / important |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pregnancy confirmation | Urine pregnancy test | Quantitative β-hCG if needed | — | Negative | Positive | — |
| Pregnancy of unknown location | TVUS + quantitative β-hCG | Serial β-hCG + repeat TVUS | Definitive location by ultrasound | Appropriate trend + IUP | Abnormal trend/US | No single β-hCG cut-off |
| Ectopic pregnancy | TVUS + β-hCG | TVUS | Extrauterine pregnancy on TVUS | IUP | Tubal/extrauterine sac, yolk sac, embryo ± cardiac activity | Rupture/haemodynamic instability |
| Miscarriage | TVUS | TVUS with accepted criteria | Diagnostic TVUS criteria | Viable IUP | CRL ≥7 mm without heartbeat or MSD ≥25 mm without embryo when correctly assessed | Haemorrhage/instability |
| Recurrent miscarriage | APS tests + pelvic US | 3D uterine imaging + APS/genetic evaluation | Cause-specific | Negative APS/normal uterus | Persistent APS antibodies/anomaly | Previous severe pregnancy outcome |
| Molar pregnancy | TVUS + β-hCG | US + β-hCG | Histopathology | Normal gestation | Molar morphology | Persistent/rising hCG → GTN |
| GTN | Serial β-hCG | Serial quantitative β-hCG | Specialist GTD assessment | Appropriate hCG decline | Plateau/rise/persistent hCG | Metastatic disease |
| Hyperemesis gravidarum | Clinical + U&E/FBC/LFT | Clinical + biochemical assessment | Clinical diagnosis | Hydrated, normal electrolytes | Dehydration/electrolyte disturbance/weight loss | AKI, severe electrolyte abnormality |
Key early-pregnancy numbers
CRL ≥7 mm + absent cardiac activity → diagnostic pregnancy failure when criteria are correctly met.
MSD ≥25 mm + no embryo → diagnostic pregnancy failure when correctly assessed.
APS: positive tests generally require 2 positive results ≥12 weeks apart.
Ketonuria alone does not diagnose hyperemesis.
There is no universal β-hCG value diagnosing ectopic pregnancy.

| Condition | First-line | IOC | Gold standard / definitive | Normal | Abnormal | Severe |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SGA | SFH | Ultrasound EFW/AC | Ultrasound | ≥10th centile | <10th | <3rd centile |
| FGR | Growth US | Serial growth + Doppler | Serial US + Doppler | Appropriate growth/placental function | Growth restriction + placental dysfunction | Severe growth restriction/abnormal Doppler |
| Reduced fetal movements | CTG | CTG + US growth/liquor ± Doppler | — | Reassuring assessment | Abnormal CTG/growth/liquor | Fetal compromise |
| Fetal wellbeing | CTG when indicated | CTG + US/Doppler | Combined clinical assessment | Baseline 110–160, variability 5–25 | Abnormal CTG features | Pathological CTG |
| Fetal anaemia | MCA-PSV | MCA-PSV | FBS for definitive fetal Hb | <1.5 MoM | ≥1.5 MoM | Severe anaemia |
| Hydrops | Ultrasound | Detailed US + fetal echo | Cause-specific assessment | No abnormal fluid | ≥2 abnormal fluid compartments | Severe hydrops |
| Oligohydramnios | US | DVP | DVP/AF assessment | 2–8 cm | <2 cm | Severe according to context |
| Polyhydramnios | US | DVP | DVP/AF assessment | 2–8 cm | >8 cm | Severity depends on AF measurement |

[MASTER OBSTETRIC INVESTIGATIONS & CUT-OFFS2 > 89. PRE-ECLAMPSIA — MODERN DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA]
This is one of the most important corrections to the traditional textbook list.

Diagnosis requires:
A. New hypertension after 20 weeks

≥140 systolic OR ≥90 diastolic

PLUS

B. ≥1 new maternal/uteroplacental complication
Proteinuria
PCR ≥30 mg/mmol, OR
ACR ≥8 mg/mmol, OR
Dipstick ≥2+ if quantitative testing unavailable/appropriate.

NICE does not recommend routine 24-hour urine collection for quantification.

OR renal dysfunction
Creatinine ≥90 µmol/L
OR hepatic dysfunction
ALT/AST >40 IU/L
With or without RUQ/epigastric pain
OR neurological complications
Eclampsia
Altered mental status
Blindness
Stroke
Clonus
Severe headache
Persistent visual scotomata
OR haematological complications
Platelets <150 ×10⁹/L
Haemolysis
DIC
OR uteroplacental dysfunction
Fetal growth restriction
Abnormal umbilical artery Doppler
Stillbirth

These are the current NICE diagnostic concepts.

Therefore:

❌ Oedema is NOT diagnostic.

❌ Proteinuria is NOT mandatory.

90. Severe hypertension

≥160 systolic OR ≥110 diastolic

Clinical emergency requiring prompt assessment/treatment.

NICE recommends antihypertensive treatment for severe hypertension and close monitoring.

91. Clinical signs of severe pre-eclampsia
Severe headache
Visual disturbance
Epigastric/RUQ pain
Hyperreflexia
Clonus
Oliguria
Pulmonary oedema
Altered mental state
Severe hypertension
92. Clonus

Rhythmic involuntary contractions following sudden dorsiflexion of ankle.

Suggests neuromuscular irritability, especially concerning in severe hypertensive disease.

Not diagnostic by itself.

93. Eclampsia

New-onset seizure in pregnancy or postpartum associated with a hypertensive disorder after exclusion of other causes.

Important:

Eclampsia can occur without obvious severe hypertension or significant proteinuria.

text:
[MASTER OBSTETRIC PROCEDURES & MANOEUVRES ATLAS > 74. RESUSCITATIVE DELIVERY]
Indication

Maternal cardiac arrest in advanced pregnancy when uterine decompression can improve maternal resuscitation and potentially fetal outcome.

Principle

Maternal resuscitation is primary.

Sequence

CALL → CPR → LEFT UTERINE DISPLACEMENT → PREPARE DELIVERY → RESUSCITATIVE DELIVERY WITHOUT DANGEROUS DELAY → CONTINUE ALS + NEONATAL RESUSCITATION

Practical principle

Do not delay delivery simply to transport a cardiac-arrest patient to theatre.

Common teaching:

Aim for delivery by approximately 4 minutes if ROSC has not occurred, while CPR continues.

text:
[MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS > 1. NORMAL / LOW-RISK PREGNANCY]
| Condition | Preferred timing | Preferred mode |
|---|---|---|
| Uncomplicated singleton, cephalic | Spontaneous labour at term | Vaginal birth |
| Elective caesarean without another indication | ≥39+0 weeks | Caesarean |
| Previous uncomplicated 1 LSCS – planned VBAC | Await spontaneous labour | VBAC |
| Previous CS – ERCS | ≥39+0 weeks | Planned CS |
| Previous vaginal birth | Usually await spontaneous labour | Vaginal birth |
| Post-term pregnancy | IOL generally offered by 41+0 weeks | Induction → vaginal birth if successful |

RCOG specifically recommends that elective repeat caesarean is generally performed from 39+0 weeks, because earlier planned CS increases neonatal respiratory morbidity.
source_file: MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS.md

text:
[MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS > 2. HYPERTENSIVE DISORDERS]
Gestational hypertension
| Severity | Timing | Mode |
|---|---|---|
| BP <160/110, no complications | Do not routinely plan birth <37 wk | IOL/Vaginal if suitable |
| ≥37 wk | Individualised with senior obstetrician | IOL usually preferred if suitable |
| Severe hypertension ≥160/110 or maternal/fetal deterioration | Any gestation if indicated | IOL or CS depending on urgency |

NICE specifically advises against planned early birth before 37 weeks for gestational hypertension when BP is <160/110 and there are no other indications.

Pre-eclampsia
| Condition | Timing | Mode |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-eclampsia <34 wk, stable | Expectant management if safe | Later IOL/CS |
| 34–36+6 wk, stable | Individualised | IOL if feasible |
| ≥37 wk | Birth within 24–48 h | IOL or CS |
| Severe PE/eclampsia/HELLP with maternal compromise | Immediate/urgent birth regardless of gestation | Often CS if urgent; IOL if safe |

RCOG states that pre-eclampsia is ultimately cured by birth, but timing and route depend on maternal and fetal circumstances. NICE recommends initiating birth within 24–48 hours from 37 weeks.

text:
[MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS > 3. DIABETES IN PREGNANCY]
Pre-existing type 1 / type 2 diabetes
| Situation | Timing | Mode |
|---|---|---|
| Uncomplicated T1DM/T2DM | 37+0–38+6 wk | IOL or CS if indicated |
| Maternal/fetal complications | Before 37 wk may be required | IOL/CS depending on circumstances |
| Suspected macrosomia | Individualised | Discuss vaginal birth vs IOL vs CS |

NICE recommends elective birth between 37+0 and 38+6 weeks for uncomplicated pre-existing diabetes.

Gestational diabetes
| GDM | Timing | Mode |
|---|---|---|
| Diet-controlled, uncomplicated | Await labour, but birth by 40+6 | Vaginal/IOL |
| Medication/insulin-treated | Individualised according to control and complications | IOL usually possible |
| Poor control / pre-eclampsia / FGR / other complications | Earlier | IOL/CS according to indication |
| Macrosomia | Individualised counselling | IOL/vaginal/CS |

NICE recommends birth no later than 40+6 weeks in uncomplicated GDM and earlier birth when maternal/fetal complications exist.
source_file: MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS.md

text:
[MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS > 4. FETAL GROWTH RESTRICTION / SGA]
This is particularly important for MRCOG.

| Fetal condition | Timing | Mode |
|---|---|---|
| SGA but normal surveillance | Usually 39 wk–40 wk latest | Vaginal birth |
| FGR with abnormal surveillance | Earlier | Depends on CTG/Doppler |
| Abnormal umbilical artery Doppler | Earlier delivery | Often CS depending on severity/gestation |
| Absent/reversed end-diastolic flow | Preterm planned birth often required | Frequently CS |
| Severe fetal compromise | Immediate delivery | Usually CS if vaginal delivery not imminent |

RCOG emphasises that timing is based on growth, Doppler, CTG and overall fetal condition rather than fetal size alone. Its July 2026 update also confirms that RCOG no longer specifically endorses a single fetal growth chart.

Exam pearl

SGA ≠ FGR.

A constitutionally small fetus with reassuring surveillance may safely reach term, whereas true placental FGR with abnormal Doppler may require substantially earlier delivery.
source_file: MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS.md

text:
[MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS > 5. PLACENTAL CONDITIONS]
Placenta praevia
| Placental location | Mode | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| Placenta ≥20 mm from internal os | Vaginal birth may be possible | Term if uncomplicated |
| Placenta <20 mm from internal os at 36 wk | CS safest | Usually 36–37 wk |
| Major placenta praevia | CS | Usually 36–37 wk |
| Recurrent/heavy APH | Earlier delivery | CS |
| Maternal/fetal instability | Emergency | Emergency CS |

RCOG's current patient guidance states that if the placental edge is <20 mm from the cervix at 36 weeks, caesarean is safest; uncomplicated praevia generally has CS around 36–37 weeks, earlier if significant bleeding occurs.
source_file: MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS.md

text:
[MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS > 6. PLACENTA ACCRETA SPECTRUM]
| Condition | Timing | Mode |
|---|---|---|
| Suspected PAS | 35–37 wk, individualised | Planned CS in specialist centre |
| Placenta accreta/increta/percreta with previous CS + praevia | Usually planned preterm CS | Often CS + planned hysterectomy |
| Major haemorrhage/instability | Immediate | Emergency CS ± hysterectomy |

RCOG's updated 2026 guidance recommends specialist planning; the timing is generally 35–37 weeks, depending on individual circumstances.
source_file: MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS.md

text:
[MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS > 7. VASA PRAEVIA]
This is a classic CS condition.

| Condition | Timing | Mode |
|---|---|---|
| Diagnosed antenatally, stable | ~34–36 wk | Planned CS |
| Labour/ROM with vasa praevia | Immediate | Emergency CS |
| Fetal compromise after vessel rupture | Immediate | Emergency CS |

RCOG currently advises planned CS around 34–36 weeks for antenatally diagnosed vasa praevia.
source_file: MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS.md

text:
[MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS > 8. PLACENTAL ABRUPTION]
| Situation | Timing | Mode |
|---|---|---|
| Stable mother + live fetus + labour progressing | Immediate/appropriate | Vaginal birth often preferred |
| Stable mother + live fetus + vaginal delivery not imminent | Urgent | CS |
| Maternal instability/major haemorrhage | Immediate | CS if fetus alive and vaginal birth not imminent |
| IUFD | Birth required, but vaginal birth preferred unless maternal indication for CS | Vaginal |
| Severe DIC | Correct coagulopathy while expediting birth | Usually vaginal if fetus dead |
Exam pearl

Abruption + dead fetus → vaginal delivery is generally preferred.
source_file: MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS.md

text:
[MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS > 9. MULTIPLE PREGNANCY]
DCDA twins

~37 weeks

Vaginal birth possible if Twin 1 cephalic and no contraindication.
CS if obstetric indication.
MCDA twins

~36 weeks

Vaginal birth possible in suitable cases.
CS if indication.
MCMA twins

32–34 weeks

Planned CS generally recommended.
Triplets

~35 weeks

Usually planned CS.

RCOG gives approximately 37 weeks for uncomplicated DCDA twins, 36 weeks for MCDA twins, 32–34 weeks for MCMA twins and 35 weeks for triplets.

text:
[MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS > 10. BREECH PRESENTATION]
At 36 weeks, discuss:

ECV
Planned CS
Planned vaginal breech birth in carefully selected circumstances

RCOG notes that ECV is usually performed after 36–37 weeks.

| Situation | Mode |
|---|---|
| Breech → successful ECV | Vaginal birth |
| Persistent breech, suitable for vaginal breech birth | Planned vaginal breech possible |
| Persistent breech, unsuitable for vaginal breech birth | Planned CS |
| Footling breech | CS generally |
| Hyperextended fetal neck | CS generally |
| Placenta praevia + breech | CS |
| Fetal anomaly incompatible with vaginal breech | CS/individualised |
source_file: MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS.md

text:
[MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS > 11. TRANSVERSE / OBLIQUE LIE]
| Situation | Management |
|---|---|
| Before term | Observe |
| Persistent transverse lie near term | ECV may be considered |
| Persistent transverse lie at labour | CS |
| Transverse lie + ROM | Emergency due to cord prolapse risk → usually CS |

Persistent transverse lie = caesarean delivery.
source_file: MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS.md

text:
[MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS > 12. PREVIOUS CAESAREAN]
One previous lower-segment CS

Two major options:

VBAC
Await spontaneous labour if appropriate.
Continuous intrapartum fetal monitoring.
Immediate access to emergency CS.
ERCS
From 39+0 weeks.
Planned CS.

RCOG explicitly identifies 39+0 weeks as the preferred timing for ERCS.
source_file: MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS.md

text:
[MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS > 13. PRETERM PRELABOUR RUPTURE OF MEMBRANES]
There is no single delivery week for all PPROM.

| Situation | Approach |
|---|---|
| PPROM without infection/fetal compromise | Expectant management when appropriate |
| Chorioamnionitis | Deliver |
| Fetal compromise | Deliver |
| Placental abruption | Deliver |
| Established labour | Deliver |
| Severe maternal disease | Deliver |
Mode

PPROM itself is NOT an indication for CS.

If fetus is cephalic and no obstetric contraindication:

Vaginal birth is preferred.
source_file: MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS.md

text:
[MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS > 14. PRETERM LABOUR]
Preterm labour itself does not automatically mean CS.

| Presentation | Mode |
|---|---|
| Cephalic fetus | Vaginal birth generally |
| Breech/other malpresentation | Individualised |
| Fetal compromise | CS if appropriate |
| Very preterm breech | CS may be considered depending on gestation and circumstances |
source_file: MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS.md

text:
[MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS > 15. INTRAHEPATIC CHOLESTASIS OF PREGNANCY]
This is a very high-yield numerical question.

| Bile acids | Timing of planned birth |
|---|---|
| 19–39 µmol/L | By 40 wk may be considered; expectant management also reasonable if no other risk |
| 40–99 µmol/L | 38–39 wk |
| ≥100 µmol/L | 35–36 wk |
Mode

ICP does NOT itself require CS.

IOL → vaginal birth is appropriate.
Planned CS only for obstetric indication.

RCOG explicitly states that planned CS is not required merely because of ICP.
source_file: MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS.md

text:
[MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS > 16. MATERNAL OBESITY]
Obesity alone is NOT an indication for CS.

| Situation | Timing/mode |
|---|---|
| Obesity alone | Await spontaneous labour |
| Obesity + diabetes | Follow diabetes recommendations |
| Obesity + pre-eclampsia | Follow hypertensive indication |
| Obesity + macrosomia | Individualised |
| Previous CS | VBAC/ERCS based on standard criteria |
source_file: MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS.md

text:
[MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS > 17. ANAEMIA]
Mild/moderate anaemia

No indication for early delivery or CS.

Treat the cause and correct iron deficiency.

Severe anaemia

Delivery timing is individualised according to maternal condition.

Anaemia alone ≠ CS.
source_file: MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS.md

text:
[MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS > 18. THROMBOCYTOPENIA]
| Condition | Delivery |
|---|---|
| Gestational thrombocytopenia | Usually normal timing/mode |
| ITP | Usually vaginal birth |
| Severe thrombocytopenia | Individualised |
| HELLP | Deliver according to maternal/fetal condition |

Thrombocytopenia alone is not an indication for CS.

The major issue is often anaesthetic planning, particularly neuraxial anaesthesia.
source_file: MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS.md

text:
[MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS > 19. THYROID DISEASE]
Well-controlled hypothyroidism/hyperthyroidism
No special early delivery solely because of thyroid disease.
Vaginal birth normally appropriate.
Uncontrolled severe thyrotoxicosis

Maternal stabilisation is essential; timing/mode depends on maternal/fetal condition.
source_file: MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS.md

text:
[MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS > 20. RENAL DISEASE]
Stable chronic kidney disease:

No automatic CS.
Timing individualised according to renal function, BP, fetal growth and maternal condition.

If severe maternal deterioration or superimposed pre-eclampsia:

Deliver according to maternal/fetal indication.

text:
[MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS > 21. SYSTEMIC LUPUS / AUTOIMMUNE DISEASE]
Stable disease:

No automatic early birth or CS.

Delivery depends on:

disease activity
hypertension/pre-eclampsia
FGR
fetal surveillance
maternal organ involvement.

RhD alloimmunisation

text:
[MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DELIVERY ATLAS > 39. SUMMARY — THE NUMBERS YOU SHOULD MEMORISE]
⭐ MRCOG HIGH-YIELD DELIVERY TIMINGS
| Condition | Timing |
|---|---|
| Elective CS | ≥39+0 wk |
| ERCS after previous CS | ≥39+0 wk |
| Pre-eclampsia | ≥37 wk → birth within 24–48 h |
| Pre-existing T1/T2 diabetes | 37+0–38+6 wk |
| GDM uncomplicated | By 40+6 wk |
| DCDA twins | ~37 wk |
| MCDA twins | ~36 wk |
| MCMA twins | 32–34 wk |
| Triplets | ~35 wk |
| Placenta praevia | 36–37 wk |
| Placenta accreta spectrum | 35–37 wk |
| Vasa praevia | ~34–36 wk |
| ICP, bile acids 19–39 | By 40 wk may be considered |
| ICP, 40–99 | 38–39 wk |
| ICP, ≥100 | 35–36 wk |
| Persistent breech | Assess/ECV around 36–37 wk |
| SGA without concerning features | 39 wk–40 wk latest |
| FGR with abnormal surveillance | Earlier, according to Doppler/CTG |

These figures are particularly useful for exams, but do not treat them as rigid rules: RCOG/NICE recommendations repeatedly emphasise maternal condition, fetal surveillance, gestation, previous obstetric history and local specialist resources when deciding the actual date and route of birth.

⭐ THE EXAM RULE FOR MODE OF DELIVERY

A very useful MRCOG framework is:

CS because the route is obstructed
→ placenta praevia, vasa praevia, persistent transverse lie.

CS because the fetus/mother cannot safely tolerate labour
→ severe fetal compromise, some severe FGR, uterine rupture, certain severe maternal conditions.

Vaginal birth preferred despite pathology
→ abruption with IUFD, chorioamnionitis, maternal sepsis, GBS, HIV with appropriate viral suppression, hepatitis B/C, ICP, obesity, anaemia.

Timing is pathology-specific
→ diabetes, pre-eclampsia, twins, ICP, FGR, placenta praevia/PAS/vasa praevia.

text:
[MASTER RCOG OBSTETRIC DRUG REGIMENS > 2. NICE]
↓
3. BNF/UK antimicrobial guidance
↓
4. ACOG for comparison where UK guidance differs

RCOG's current catalogue includes dedicated guidance covering PPH, GBS, PPROM, preterm birth, thrombosis, placenta praevia/PAS, FGR, thyroid disease, sepsis, multiple pregnancy and other obstetric conditions.

ACOG should therefore be used as the secondary comparison, not mixed into the RCOG regimen. For example, ACOG's hypertension guidance confirms the same major emergency-treatment framework, while its PPH guidance similarly includes uterotonics and TXA.

One final safety point

A truly exhaustive list of every obstetric medication would also include anaesthetic agents, blood products, antiarrhythmics, antibiotics for every organism, fetal cardiac drugs, chemotherapy/immunotherapy for maternal malignancy, psychiatric medicines, epilepsy medicines, transplant medicines and drugs for every maternal medical disorder. Those do not have one universal RCOG "drug of choice." The table above therefore focuses on the core obstetric conditions and obstetric-specific medications that are realistically tested in MRCOG/MCPS and commonly encountered clinically, while flagging specialist situations rather than inventing a universal dose.

This needs correction in your original table.

PID is primarily a clinical diagnosis.

The investigation is not simply:

“NAAT + TVUS = first-line diagnosis.”

Instead:

IOC:

Clinical assessment + pelvic examination

with:

pregnancy test
NAAT for Chlamydia
NAAT/culture for Gonorrhoea
M. genitalium testing where available/appropriate
urine/vaginal testing
inflammatory markers where useful
TVUS if TOA/pyosalpinx or another pelvic pathology is suspected.

A positive gonorrhoea/chlamydia/M. genitalium test supports PID, but a negative result does not exclude PID. BASHH explicitly emphasizes this.

PID — diagnostic hierarchy

Clinical diagnosis → STI testing → ultrasound if complication suspected → laparoscopy in selected uncertain/severe cases.

⚠️ Corrections to your original table
HMB: TVUS is not universally first-line. NICE says choose hysteroscopy or ultrasound according to history/examination.
HMB endometrial thickness ≥4.5 mm: this is not a universal NICE threshold for proceeding to hysteroscopy/biopsy. Do not memorize it as an RCOG/NICE rule.
PMB >4 mm: the exact threshold/pathway depends on the clinical pathway and whether the patient is using HRT. Do not combine different UK protocols into one universal cutoff.
Endometriosis: TVUS is now explicitly recommended for all suspected cases, even with a normal examination. Laparoscopy remains an option but is not the routine first investigation.
PCOS: ultrasound is not mandatory if the other diagnostic components establish PCOS after excluding alternative diagnoses.
POI: NICE uses FSH on two samples 4–6 weeks apart; the simplified “>30 IU/L” rule should not be presented as the current universal NICE criterion.
PID: primarily a clinical diagnosis. NAAT supports the diagnosis; negative STI testing does not exclude PID.
BV: HVS culture is not the preferred diagnostic gold standard. Microscopy/Amsel/Nugent/Hay-Ison are more appropriate diagnostic approaches.
SUI: routine multichannel urodynamics is not indicated before uncomplicated primary surgery.
Infertility: NICE 2026 recommends HSG for women without risk factors for tubal/pelvic disease; HyCoSy is an alternative where expertise exists, while laparoscopy + dye is used when comorbidity is suspected.
Cervical screening: the current UK programme uses primary HPV testing, not conventional cytology as the primary screening test.
Ovarian cancer: current NICE guidance has changed its age-specific CA-125 approach in 2026, so older “CA125 >35 for everyone” tables should not be treated as the complete current NICE algorithm.
Core source framework

POI

Current NICE diagnostic rule:

age <40
menopausal symptoms/no or infrequent periods
elevated FSH on 2 blood samples
samples 4–6 weeks apart
POI should not be diagnosed from a single FSH
AMH should not routinely be used to diagnose POI.

So:

❌ “FSH >30 IU/L twice” = older simplified exam rule
✅ Current NICE = elevated FSH ×2, 4–6 weeks apart + clinical picture.

[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 3. PCOS — DIAGNOSTIC VALUES]
Rotterdam framework

Diagnosis requires 2 of 3, after exclusion of other causes:

| Criterion | Abnormal finding |
|---|---|
| Oligo/anovulation | Irregular/infrequent cycles |
| Hyperandrogenism | Clinical and/or biochemical |
| Polycystic ovarian morphology | Increased follicle number and/or ovarian volume according to current ultrasound criteria |
Adult cycle abnormality

Common practical threshold:

<8 cycles/year or cycle interval >35 days suggests oligo-ovulation.

Current ultrasound morphology

Using modern high-resolution transvaginal ultrasound:

≥20 follicles per ovary, typically 2–9 mm, OR
ovarian volume ≥10 mL

However, the exact threshold depends on ultrasound technology and guideline used.

Important

PCOS cannot be diagnosed from ultrasound alone.

abnormal tubal contour.

There isn't a “normal number” cutoff.

NICE 2026 recommends:

Low-risk woman → HSG

Alternative → HyCoSy

PID/previous ectopic/endometriosis or other suspected pelvic disease → laparoscopy + dye.

[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 10. SEMEN ANALYSIS — IMPORTANT IN INFERTILITY]
Current NICE 2026/WHO reference values:

| Parameter | Lower reference value |

| Volume | ≥1.4 mL |
| pH | ≥7.2 |
| Sperm concentration | ≥16 million/mL |

| Total motility | ≥42% |

| Vitality | ≥54% live |

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 19. OVARIAN CANCER — CURRENT CA-125 CUT-OFFS]
This has an important 2026 NICE update.

For women ≥40 years with persistent symptoms suggesting ovarian cancer, NICE currently uses age-specific CA-125 thresholds for urgent ultrasound:

| Age | CA-125 threshold |
|---|---|
| 40–49 yr | ≥35 IU/mL |
| 50–59 yr | ≥31 IU/mL |
| 60–69 yr | ≥24 IU/mL |
| 70–79 yr | ≥25 IU/mL |
| ≥80 yr | ≥31 IU/mL |

These are NICE referral/investigation thresholds, not a statement that CA-125 above the number means “ovarian cancer.” CA-125 can be elevated in many benign conditions.

Important distinction

CA-125 ≥35 IU/mL ≠ ovarian cancer diagnosis.

Diagnosis requires imaging and ultimately histological assessment.

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 20. RMI — OVARIAN MASS]
Risk of Malignancy Index

RMI = U × M × CA125

Where:

U = ultrasound score
M = menopausal score
CA125 = IU/mL
Classical ultrasound features
multilocular cyst
solid areas
bilateral lesions
ascites
intra-abdominal metastases.
RMI
| RMI | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| <200 | Lower risk |
| ≥200 | Increased risk → specialist assessment |

⚠️ Do not confuse RMI 200 with CA-125 200.

increased vascularity.

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 1. MENSTRUAL DISORDERS & ABNORMAL UTERINE BLEEDING]
| Condition | IOC / First-line | Normal / cutoff | Abnormal / definitive |
|---|---|---|---|
| Heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) | History + examination; investigation based on suspected cause | — | CBC to assess anaemia; hysteroscopy/US according to clinical suspicion |
| HMB + suspected endometrial polyp/submucosal fibroid | Outpatient hysteroscopy | Normal cavity | Lesion identified ± biopsy/removal |
| HMB + bulky/enlarged uterus | TVUS | Normal uterine morphology | Fibroid/adenomyosis |
| HMB + suspected adenomyosis | TVUS | Normal myometrium | Adenomyosis features |
| HMB + suspected large fibroid | TVUS ± TAUS | — | Fibroid mapping |
| HMB + high risk of endometrial pathology | Hysteroscopy + biopsy | Normal histology | Hyperplasia/cancer |
| HMB + anaemia | CBC | Hb generally ≥12 g/dL | Hb <12 g/dL = anaemia in non-pregnant woman |
| Intermenstrual bleeding | Examination ± hysteroscopy | Normal cavity | Polyp/hyperplasia/cancer |
| Postcoital bleeding | Speculum + cervical assessment | Normal cervix | Cervical lesion → colposcopy/biopsy |
| Dysmenorrhoea, primary | Clinical diagnosis | — | Further investigation if atypical |
| Secondary dysmenorrhoea | TVUS | Normal pelvis | Endometriosis/adenomyosis/fibroid |
| Anovulatory bleeding | Pregnancy test + targeted endocrine tests | — | Anovulation/underlying endocrine disorder |
| Menorrhagia + bleeding disorder suspected | CBC + coagulation/haematology | Platelets ~150–400 ×10⁹/L | Thrombocytopenia/coagulopathy |
| PMS | Symptom diary | Symptoms absent/minimal | Cyclical symptoms |
| PMDD | Prospective daily symptom diary | No significant cyclical impairment | Diagnostic symptom pattern |

Important: NICE does not recommend a universal 4.5-mm endometrial thickness cutoff for HMB. Investigation is determined by symptoms, examination and suspected pathology. Hysteroscopy is preferred when endometrial pathology is suspected.

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 8. PCOS]
Rotterdam framework

Diagnosis requires 2 of 3, after exclusion of alternative causes:

1. Oligo/anovulation

Practical adult indicators:

<8 menstrual cycles/year
or cycle intervals >35 days.
2. Hyperandrogenism
Clinical: hirsutism/acne/androgenic alopecia
Biochemical: increased testosterone/free androgen index.
3. Polycystic ovarian morphology

Modern TVUS threshold:

≥20 follicles per ovary, generally 2–9 mm
OR
ovarian volume ≥10 mL
Important

Ultrasound is not mandatory if the other two diagnostic components are already present.

| Hyperprolactinaemia | Serum prolactin | Elevated above laboratory range |
| Thyroid disease | TSH ± FT4 | TSH ~0.4–4 mIU/L commonly used reference |
| Hyperandrogenism | Testosterone ± SHBG/FAI | Above assay/lab range |
| Adrenal androgen excess | DHEAS | Age-specific elevation |
| Non-classic CAH | 17-OHP | Elevated screening value |
| Pituitary disease | Prolactin ± pituitary hormones | MRI if indicated |
Prolactin

Typical non-pregnant female reference:

~4–23 ng/mL, but use the laboratory-specific reference interval.

TSH

Common reference:

~0.4–4.0 mIU/L

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 10. PREMATURE OVARIAN INSUFFICIENCY — POI]
NICE approach

Diagnosis:

age <40
amenorrhoea/irregular periods + menopausal symptoms
elevated FSH on 2 blood samples
samples 4–6 weeks apart.
Important correction

❌ Do not use “FSH >30 IU/L twice” as the universal current NICE definition.

✅ Use elevated FSH ×2, 4–6 weeks apart + clinical presentation.

AMH is not routinely used to diagnose POI.
source_file: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY.md
section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 11. OVARIAN RESERVE]
| Investigation | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| AMH | Ovarian reserve marker |
| Antral follicle count | Ovarian reserve/response prediction |
| FSH/E2 | Older/secondary reserve assessment |
Important

There is no universal AMH value that means “fertile” or “infertile.”

AMH predicts ovarian response to stimulation better than natural conception probability.
source_file: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY.md
section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 12. OVULATION ASSESSMENT]
Mid-luteal progesterone
| Result | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| >3 ng/mL | Generally supports ovulation |
| ≤3 ng/mL | Suggests anovulation if correctly timed |

The test must be appropriately timed according to cycle length.
source_file: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY.md
section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 13. INFERTILITY]
| Problem | IOC |
|---|---|
| Initial infertility assessment | History + examination + ovulation + tubal + semen assessment |
| Ovulation | Mid-luteal progesterone |
| Tubal patency, low-risk | HSG |
| Alternative | HyCoSy |
| Suspected PID/endometriosis/ectopic/adhesions | Laparoscopy + dye |
| Uterine cavity abnormality suspected | Hysteroscopy |
| Male factor | Semen analysis |
| Ovarian reserve | AMH + AFC |

NICE 2026 recommends HSG for women without comorbidities suggesting tubal/pelvic disease, with HyCoSy as an alternative. Laparoscopy with dye is used when pelvic pathology is suspected.
source_file: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY.md
section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 14. HSG — NORMAL VS ABNORMAL]
Normal
Both fallopian tubes patent
Free peritoneal spill
Normal uterine cavity
Abnormal
unilateral occlusion
bilateral occlusion
hydrosalpinx
abnormal tubal contour
intrauterine filling defect.

No numerical cutoff.
source_file: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY.md
section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 15. SEMEN ANALYSIS — CURRENT REFERENCE VALUES]
| Parameter | Lower reference |
|---|---|
| Volume | ≥1.4 mL |
| pH | ≥7.2 |
| Concentration | ≥16 million/mL |
| Total sperm number | ≥39 million/ejaculate |
| Total motility | ≥42% |
| Progressive motility | ≥30% |
| Vitality | ≥54% |
| Normal morphology | ≥4% |

These are the current reference values incorporated into NICE's 2026 fertility guideline.
source_file: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY.md
section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 16. VAGINITIS — BACTERIAL VAGINOSIS]
Amsel criteria

Diagnosis generally requires 3 of 4:

Homogeneous thin discharge
Vaginal pH >4.5
Positive whiff test
Clue cells ≥20%
Nugent score
| Score | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| 0–3 | Normal |
| 4–6 | Intermediate |
| 7–10 | BV |
Hay/Ison
| Grade | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| 0 | No bacteria |
| I | Normal lactobacilli |
| II | Intermediate |
| III | BV-type flora |
source_file: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY.md
section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 17. VULVOVAGINAL CANDIDIASIS]
IOC
Microscopy of vaginal discharge.

For recurrent/complicated/treatment-resistant disease:

Fungal culture/speciation ± susceptibility testing

| Parameter | Normal | Candidiasis |
|---|---|---|
| Vaginal pH | Usually <4.5 | Usually remains <4.5 |
| Microscopy | No yeast/hyphae | Yeast/pseudohyphae |
| Culture | Negative | Candida identified |

A positive culture can represent colonisation, so results must correlate with symptoms.
source_file: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY.md
section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 18. TRICHOMONIASIS]
IOC: NAAT
| Test | Normal | Abnormal |
|---|---|---|
| NAAT | Negative | Positive |
| Wet mount | No organisms | Motile trichomonads |
| Vaginal pH | Usually ≤4.5 | Often >4.5 |

NAAT is more sensitive than wet mount.
source_file: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY.md
section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 19. STI INVESTIGATIONS]
| Condition | IOC | Normal | Abnormal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chlamydia | NAAT | Negative | Positive |
| Gonorrhoea | NAAT + culture when required | Negative | Positive |
| M. genitalium | NAAT ± resistance testing | Negative | Positive |
| Trichomonas | NAAT | Negative | Positive |
| Genital herpes | Lesion PCR/NAAT | Negative | Positive |
| Syphilis | Serology | Non-reactive | Reactive |
| HIV | 4th-generation Ag/Ab | Non-reactive | Reactive |
| Hepatitis B | HBsAg | Negative | Positive |
| Hepatitis C | Anti-HCV → RNA | Negative | Positive |

section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 20. PID]
Most important point
PID is primarily a clinical diagnosis.
Minimum clinical criteria

Pelvic/lower abdominal pain with no better alternative diagnosis plus one or more:

cervical motion tenderness
uterine tenderness
adnexal tenderness.
Supportive investigations
Chlamydia NAAT
Gonorrhoea NAAT/culture
M. genitalium NAAT
pregnancy test
CBC
CRP/ESR
vaginal/cervical microscopy where appropriate
TVUS if TOA/pyosalpinx suspected.
TOA

TVUS is usually the key imaging test.

Important

A negative STI test does not exclude PID.
source_file: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY.md
section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 21. CERVICAL SCREENING]
UK primary screening

High-risk HPV testing

| Result | Next step |
|---|---|
| HPV negative | Routine screening |
| HPV positive + reassuring cytology | Surveillance according to programme |
| HPV positive + abnormal cytology | Colposcopy |
| High-grade abnormality | Colposcopy |
| Suspicious lesion | Biopsy |

The UK programme now uses primary HPV testing, with cytology used for HPV-positive samples.
source_file: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY.md
section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 22. CERVICAL DYSPLASIA / CIN]
IOC
Colposcopy + targeted biopsy

| Histology | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| CIN 1 | Low-grade lesion |
| CIN 2 | High-grade precursor |
| CIN 3 | High-grade precursor |
| Invasive carcinoma | Cancer |
Definitive

Histology.
source_file: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY.md
section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 23. CERVICAL CANCER]
| Stage of investigation | Test |
|---|---|
| Screening abnormality | HPV/cytology pathway |
| Suspected lesion | Colposcopy |
| Definitive diagnosis | Biopsy histology |
| Local staging | MRI pelvis |
| Advanced staging | CT ± PET-CT according to clinical stage |
source_file: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY.md
section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 24. OVARIAN/ADNEXAL MASSES]
First-line

Transvaginal ultrasound

Assess:

size
unilateral/bilateral
simple/complex
solid areas
septations
papillary projections
vascularity
ascites.
Simple cyst

Typical:

unilocular
anechoic
thin wall
no solid component
no significant internal vascularity.
Suspicious
solid areas
papillary projections
thick/irregular septations
bilateral disease
ascites
metastases
marked vascularity.
source_file: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY.md
section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 25. OVARIAN CANCER]
Initial investigation

CA-125 + ultrasound

RMI

RMI = U × M × CA-125

RMI cutoff
| RMI | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| <200 | Lower risk |
| ≥200 | Increased risk → specialist assessment |
Current NICE CA-125 age-specific thresholds

For women with persistent symptoms suggestive of ovarian cancer:

| Age | CA-125 threshold |
|---|---|
| 40–49 | ≥35 IU/mL |
| 50–59 | ≥31 IU/mL |
| 60–69 | ≥24 IU/mL |
| 70–79 | ≥25 IU/mL |
| ≥80 | ≥31 IU/mL |

CA-125 elevation does not diagnose ovarian cancer.

CT is used for staging when malignancy is suspected.
source_file: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY.md
section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 26. POSTMENOPAUSAL OVARIAN CYSTS]
RCOG
A unilateral, unilocular, simple cyst ≤3 cm generally requires no routine follow-up under current RCOG guidance.

For larger/complex cysts:

TVUS + CA-125 → risk assessment/RMI → specialist evaluation as indicated.
source_file: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY.md
section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 27. OVARIAN TORSION]
IOC
Urgent pelvic ultrasound + Doppler

Possible findings:

enlarged ovary
peripheral follicles
stromal oedema
reduced/absent flow
free fluid.
Definitive

Laparoscopy

Important

Normal Doppler flow does not reliably exclude torsion.
source_file: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY.md
section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 28. OVARIAN ENDOMETRIOMA]
IOC

TVUS
Typical:

homogeneous low-level “ground-glass” echoes
thick wall
no internal vascularity in typical endometrioma.

MRI if uncertain/complex/deep disease.
source_file: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY.md
section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 29. OTHER OVARIAN TUMOURS]
| Condition | Useful investigation |
|---|---|
| Germ-cell tumour | US + AFP/β-hCG ± LDH |
| Dysgerminoma | LDH |
| Yolk-sac tumour | AFP |
| Choriocarcinomatous component | β-hCG |
| Granulosa-cell tumour | Inhibin ± AMH/estradiol |
| Androgen-secreting tumour | Testosterone ± DHEAS |
| Dermoid | TVUS ± MRI |

Definitive diagnosis = histopathology.

section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 30. VULVAL CONDITIONS]
| Condition | IOC |
|---|---|
| Lichen sclerosus | Clinical examination |
| Atypical/uncertain lichen sclerosus | Vulval biopsy |
| Lichen planus | Clinical ± biopsy |
| VIN | Vulval biopsy |
| Vulval cancer | Punch/incisional biopsy |
| Vulval ulcer | STI testing ± biopsy |
| Vulvodynia | Clinical diagnosis/exclusion |
| Vulval dermatitis | Clinical examination |
| Bartholin cyst | Clinical examination |
| Bartholin abscess | Clinical examination |
| Suspicious Bartholin mass | Biopsy/excision |

A new Bartholin-region mass in a woman ≥40 years deserves malignancy exclusion.

[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 31. VAGINAL CONDITIONS]
| Condition | IOC |
|---|---|
| Vaginal infection | Microscopy/NAAT according to suspected organism |
| Vaginal ulcer | Examination + STI testing |
| Persistent vaginal lesion | Biopsy |
| Vaginal tumour | Biopsy |
| Vaginal cancer | Biopsy + staging imaging |
| Vaginal foreign body | Speculum examination |

section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 32. UROGYNAECOLOGY]
Stress urinary incontinence
IOC

Clinical history + pelvic examination + demonstrated stress leakage

Routine urodynamics?

No, for uncomplicated primary SUI.

Urodynamics indicated/considered when:
mixed incontinence with uncertain diagnosis
voiding dysfunction
anterior/apical prolapse
recurrent SUI
previous continence surgery.

section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 33. OVERACTIVE BLADDER]
IOC
Clinical assessment + bladder diary

Usually:

urgency
frequency
nocturia
± urgency urinary incontinence.

No single diagnostic numerical cutoff.
source_file: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY.md
section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 34. URINARY RETENTION]
IOC
Post-void residual (PVR)

There is no single universally applicable cutoff, but commonly:

| PVR | Practical interpretation |
|---|---|
| <50 mL | Generally reassuring |
| 50–100 mL | Borderline/context dependent |
| >100 mL | Increased residual |
| >200 mL | Significant retention |
| >300–400 mL | Marked retention |

Interpret according to symptoms and repeated measurements.
source_file: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY.md
section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 35. RECURRENT UTI]
IOC
Urinalysis ± urine culture

Urinalysis
| Test | Normal | Suggestive |
|---|---|---|
| Nitrite | Negative | Positive |
| Leukocyte esterase | Negative | Positive |
| WBC | Low/absent | Pyuria |
| Culture | No significant growth | Pathogen growth |

There is no single colony-count cutoff that should be applied to every symptomatic woman.

section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 36. BLADDER PAIN SYNDROME]
IOC
Clinical diagnosis + exclusion of infection/other pathology

Possible investigations:

urine culture
urinalysis
cystoscopy in selected cases.

There is no diagnostic blood/urine cutoff.

section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 37. URETHRAL DIVERTICULUM]
IOC
MRI pelvis

May show:

periurethral mass
T2 hyperintensity
circumferential/saddlebag configuration.

section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 38. GENITOURINARY FISTULA]
| Condition | IOC |
|---|---|
| Vesicovaginal fistula | Dye test + cystoscopy |
| Ureterovaginal fistula | Imaging + cystoscopy |
| Complex fistula | CT urogram/MRI |
| Bladder involvement | Cystoscopy |

section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 39. PELVIC ORGAN PROLAPSE]
IOC
Clinical pelvic examination + POP-Q

POP-Q stages
| Stage | Definition |
|---|---|
| 0 | No prolapse |
| 1 | Leading edge >1 cm above hymen |
| 2 | Leading edge within ±1 cm of hymen |
| 3 | >1 cm beyond hymen but not complete |
| 4 | Complete/near-complete vaginal eversion |
Important

Routine imaging is not required for obvious clinical prolapse.

section_path: MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 40. UTERINE ANOMALIES]
| Condition | IOC |
|---|---|
| Müllerian anomaly | 3D TVUS |
| Septate uterus | 3D TVUS |
| Bicornuate uterus | 3D TVUS/MRI |
| Complex anomaly | MRI |
| Intrauterine adhesions | Hysteroscopy |

3D ultrasound evaluates the uterine shape; hysteroscopy evaluates the cavity.

text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 49. CURRENT UK GUIDELINE PRINCIPLES TO REMEMBER]
NICE
HMB: investigation depends on suspected pathology; don't use a universal 4.5-mm biopsy threshold.
Endometriosis: TVUS for all suspected cases; normal scan does not exclude disease.
POI: FSH on two samples 4–6 weeks apart; don't diagnose from one FSH.
Infertility: HSG for low-risk tubal assessment; HyCoSy alternative; laparoscopy + dye if pelvic disease suspected.
SUI: don't routinely perform urodynamics before uncomplicated primary surgery.
POP: clinical POP-Q assessment.
Cervical screening: primary HPV testing.
Ovarian cancer: CA-125 + ultrasound with current age-specific NICE thresholds and subsequent risk assessment.
RCOG
Use RCOG Green-top guidance particularly for:
ovarian masses/cysts
endometrial hyperplasia
endometriosis
postmenopausal ovarian cysts
urogynecology/prolapse
other specialist gynaecological conditions.
BASHHUse BASHH guidance for:chlamydia
gonorrhoea
PID
M. genitalium
trichomoniasis
genital herpes
syphilis
vulvovaginal infections/STI testing.
