text:
[MASTER — INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IN GYNAECOLOGY > 1. MENSTRUAL DISORDERS & UTERINE BLEEDING]
| Condition | First-line investigation | Investigation of choice | Gold standard / definitive | Key cutoff |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Heavy menstrual bleeding | History + examination + CBC | TVUS or hysteroscopy depending on suspected pathology | Hysteroscopy + targeted biopsy when endometrial pathology suspected | Hb <12 g/dL = anaemia |
| HMB + suspected polyp | TVUS/hysteroscopy | Hysteroscopy | Hysteroscopy + histology | No universal ET cutoff |
| HMB + suspected submucosal fibroid | TVUS | Hysteroscopy ± TVUS | Histology if removed | — |
| HMB + enlarged uterus | TVUS | TVUS | Histology if surgery | — |
| HMB + suspected adenomyosis | TVUS | TVUS | Histology after hysterectomy is definitive | No universal cutoff |
| Intermenstrual bleeding | Examination + cervical assessment | Hysteroscopy if uterine source suspected | Histology if lesion present | — |
| Postcoital bleeding | Speculum examination | Colposcopy if indicated | Biopsy if lesion suspicious | — |
| Secondary dysmenorrhoea | Pelvic examination + TVUS | TVUS | Laparoscopy/histology for endometriosis where required | — |
| Primary dysmenorrhoea | Clinical diagnosis | No routine imaging | Clinical diagnosis | — |
| Anovulatory bleeding | Pregnancy test + targeted endocrine tests | Hormonal evaluation ± TVUS | Depends on cause | — |
| Suspected bleeding disorder | CBC | Haematological investigation | Specific coagulation diagnosis | Platelets <150 ×10⁹/L abnormal |
| PMS | Symptom diary | Prospective symptom diary | Clinical diagnosis | — |
| PMDD | Daily symptom diary | Prospective symptom recording | Clinical diagnosis | Symptoms must be cyclical |

NICE does not recommend a universal 4.5-mm endometrial-thickness cutoff for HMB. Investigation depends on history, examination and suspected pathology.

🚨 HIGH-YIELD EXAM CORRECTIONS1. HMB:
❌ “ET ≥4.5 mm = biopsy”
✅ No universal NICE 4.5-mm HMB cutoff.2. Endometriosis:
❌ “Laparoscopy is always first-line.”
✅ TVUS first-line; laparoscopy when appropriate.3. PCOS:
❌ “Ultrasound is mandatory.”
✅ 2/3 Rotterdam criteria; ultrasound may not be needed.4. POI:
❌ “FSH >30 twice is the NICE definition.”
✅ Elevated FSH twice, 4–6 weeks apart + clinical picture.5. PID:
❌ “NAAT diagnoses PID.”
✅ PID is primarily a clinical diagnosis; NAAT supports aetiology.

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 OSCE — EARLY PREGNANCY ATLAS > 1. UNIVERSAL EARLY-PREGNANCY OSCE APPROACH]
Any station involving pain, bleeding, vomiting or a positive pregnancy test:

Step 1 — Safety first
Introduce yourself.
Confirm identity.
Confirm gestational age/LMP.
Explain the purpose of assessment.
Gain consent.
Offer chaperone for intimate examination.
Assess ABCDE if acutely unwell.
Determine whether this is:
haemorrhagic shock
ruptured ectopic
septic miscarriage
severe hyperemesis/dehydration
molar pregnancy with complications.
Immediate observations
| Parameter | Normal adult reference | Concerning |
|---|---|---|
| HR | ~60–100 bpm | >100–120 |
| BP | approximately 90–140/60–90 | hypotension |
| RR | 12–20/min | ≥22 concerning in acute illness |
| SpO₂ | ≥95% generally | <94% |
| Temperature | ~36–37.5°C | ≥38°C infection |
| CRT | <2 sec | ≥2–3 sec |
| GCS | 15 | reduced = emergency |
| Urine output | ≥0.5 mL/kg/h | oliguria |

Do not wait for investigations in an unstable patient.

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 OSCE — EARLY PREGNANCY ATLAS > 2. ECTOPIC PREGNANCY]
5
Definition

Implantation of a pregnancy outside the endometrial cavity.

Commonest site:

Ampulla of fallopian tube.

Other sites:

isthmic
fimbrial
interstitial
cervical
ovarian
abdominal
caesarean scar
heterotopic pregnancy.

RCOG specifically recognises tubal, cervical, caesarean-scar, interstitial, ovarian, abdominal and heterotopic ectopics.

OSCE opening statement

"My immediate priority is to determine whether this woman is haemodynamically stable and whether there is evidence of a ruptured ectopic pregnancy."

Then:

ABCDE
observations
IV access
bloods
pregnancy location
ultrasound
β-hCG
management according to stability and findings.

6. β-hCG — EXAMINER FAVOURITE
Serial β-hCG

Usually measured 48 hours apart when pregnancy location is uncertain.

A normally developing intrauterine pregnancy generally demonstrates a substantial rise; RCOG patient information describes approximately 63% rise over 48 hours as typical. Ectopic pregnancy may show a slower rise, plateau or fall.

Important MRCOG warning

β-hCG alone does NOT diagnose ectopic pregnancy.

Think:

Location = ultrasound
Trend = β-hCG

Do not say:

"The β-hCG is abnormal, therefore it is ectopic."

Very early IUP

Ectopic pregnancy.
Management principle

safety-net.

13. MIScarriage
6
Definition

Pregnancy loss before fetal viability; in clinical OSCEs, early miscarriage generally refers to pregnancy loss in the first trimester.

RCOG notes that early miscarriage is common and approximately 1 in 5 women experience miscarriage.

[MRCOG Part 3 OSCE — EARLY PREGNANCY ATLAS > 17. ULTRASOUND DIAGNOSIS OF MISSED MISCARRIAGE]
Use TVUS.

Important cut-offs

A key modern principle:

Do not diagnose miscarriage from an isolated borderline scan.

For a pregnancy with:

CRL ≥7 mm

and

No visible cardiac activity

→ diagnostic of pregnancy failure when confirmed according to appropriate ultrasound criteria.

Mean gestational sac diameter ≥25 mm

with

No embryo

→ diagnostic of pregnancy failure.

But in OSCE:

If measurements are close to diagnostic thresholds or dates are uncertain, repeat TVUS rather than making a potentially irreversible diagnosis.

NICE/RCOG practice emphasises cautious ultrasound diagnosis and appropriate repeat scanning.

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 OSCE — EARLY PREGNANCY ATLAS > 60. MRCOG EXAMINER "RED FLAGS"]
If you hear:

"Pregnant + collapse + abdominal pain"

→ ruptured ectopic

"Pregnant + unilateral pain + shoulder-tip pain"

→ haemoperitoneum/ectopic

"Positive pregnancy test + no pregnancy on scan"

→ PUL — ectopic remains possible

"Bleeding + fever + offensive discharge"

→ septic miscarriage

"Very high β-hCG + snowstorm scan"

→ complete molar pregnancy

"Hyperemesis + hyperthyroidism"

→ consider hCG-mediated gestational transient thyrotoxicosis/molar pregnancy

"Vomiting + confusion + ataxia"

→ Wernicke encephalopathy

"Dextrose before thiamine"

→ major OSCE error

"Unstable ectopic + waiting for β-hCG"

→ major OSCE error

"Borderline ultrasound measurement + immediate miscarriage diagnosis"

→ major OSCE error

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 OSCE — MENOPAUSE  ADOLESCENT GYNAECOLOGY FGM > 1. MENOPAUSE]
Definition
Natural menopause
Permanent cessation of menstruation due to loss of ovarian follicular activity.
Retrospectively diagnosed after 12 consecutive months of amenorrhoea with no other cause.
Typical age:
Most commonly 45–55 years
UK average ≈ 51 years
RCOG notes the average may be lower in some Asian populations, including Pakistan/India.
Perimenopause
Transition preceding menopause.
May have:
Cycle irregularity
Hot flushes
Night sweats
Sleep disturbance
Mood symptoms
Vaginal/sexual symptoms.
Premature ovarian insufficiency — POI
Loss of ovarian function before 40 years.
Important distinction:
Early menopause: 40–44 years
POI: <40 years.

Woman ≥45 with typical symptoms

Usually:

No routine FSH needed.

Diagnosis is generally clinical.

Age 40–45 with menopausal symptoms
Age <40 with suspected POI

↑ FSH

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 OSCE — MENOPAUSE  ADOLESCENT GYNAECOLOGY FGM > 6. HRT — THE CORE MRCOG STATION]
The examiner may give:

“A 52-year-old woman with hot flushes asks whether she should start HRT.”

Your framework:

1. Confirm indication

HRT is particularly effective for:

Vasomotor symptoms
Menopausal symptoms
GSM
Prevention of bone loss in appropriate women.
2. Determine uterine status

Has she got a uterus?

| Uterus | HRT |
|---|---|
| Uterus present | Oestrogen + progestogen |
| Total hysterectomy | Usually oestrogen-only |
| Hysterectomy + significant endometriosis history | Consider combined therapy |
| LNG-IUS | Can provide endometrial protection with systemic oestrogen |

NICE recommends combined HRT for women with a uterus and oestrogen-only HRT after total hysterectomy.

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 OSCE — MENOPAUSE  ADOLESCENT GYNAECOLOGY FGM > 7. CYCLICAL VS CONTINUOUS HRT]
Sequential/cyclical HRT

Usually appropriate when:

Perimenopausal
Still having periods
Within approximately 12 months of last menstrual period.

Expected:

Withdrawal bleed.

Continuous combined HRT

Usually for:

Postmenopausal woman
≥12 months since last period.

Goal:

Amenorrhoea/no scheduled bleeding.

RCOG describes cyclical treatment for women who start combined HRT before menopause or within 12 months of the last period, and continuous combined HRT when started >12 months after the last period.

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 OSCE — MENOPAUSE  ADOLESCENT GYNAECOLOGY FGM > 8. HRT — ROUTE]
Oral oestrogen

Advantages:

Convenient
Cheap
Effective.

Disadvantages:

Increased VTE risk compared with transdermal route.
First-pass hepatic effect.
Transdermal

Patch/gel/spray.

Advantages:

Avoids first-pass hepatic metabolism.
Preferred when VTE risk is increased.

Important OSCE point:

Obesity is a VTE risk factor; consider transdermal rather than oral oestrogen.

RCOG specifically notes that women with VTE risk factors such as BMI ≥30 should generally be offered transdermal oestrogen.

[MRCOG Part 3 OSCE — MENOPAUSE  ADOLESCENT GYNAECOLOGY FGM > 10. HRT RISKS — EXAM TABLE]
| Issue | Important point |
|---|---|
| Breast cancer | Risk varies with regimen/duration |
| VTE | Greater with oral than transdermal oestrogen |
| Stroke | Small increased risk particularly with oral therapy |
| Endometrium | Unopposed systemic oestrogen increases hyperplasia/cancer risk |
| Gallbladder | Risk may increase |
| Cardiovascular | Benefit-risk depends strongly on age/timing/baseline risk |

RCOG notes that combined HRT can increase breast cancer risk, while oestrogen-only therapy has little or no increased breast cancer risk in the evidence summarised in its patient guidance.

1. Introduce yourself

[MRCOG Part 3 OSCE — MENOPAUSE  ADOLESCENT GYNAECOLOGY FGM > 27. ADOLESCENT MENSTRUAL NUMBERS]
Typical adolescent cycle:

21–45 days
Bleeding usually 2–7 days.

Bleeding needing product changes every 1–2 hours, especially >7 days, suggests heavy menstrual bleeding.

An adolescent should be assessed for amenorrhoea if:

≥15 years and no menarche, OR
≥3 years after breast development without menarche.

Also:

>90 days between periods is not considered normal even in adolescence and warrants evaluation.

12 months amenorrhoea = menopause retrospectively.

Typical menopause

45–55 years

POI

<40 years

Early menopause

40–44 years

Adolescent menstrual cycle

21–45 days

Adolescent bleeding

Usually 2–7 days

Adolescent concerning amenorrhoea

>90 days

Primary amenorrhoea

15 years without menarche

OR

3 years after thelarche without menarche.

DXA

T-score ≥ −1 = normal

−1 to −2.5 = osteopenia

≤ −2.5 = osteoporosis.

PMB

Think ~4 mm endometrial thickness as the important ultrasound threshold in a symptomatic postmenopausal woman, while recognising that exact pathways depend on the clinical setting/guideline.

MRKH

≈ 1:4,500–5,000

MRKH associated anomalies

Up to 53%.

MRKH vaginal dilation success

Approximately 90–96% in appropriately selected patients.

[MRCOG Part 3 — Gynaecological Oncology OSCE Atlas > 25. ENDOMETRIAL CANCER INVESTIGATIONS]

Endometrial thickness

A commonly used threshold in PMB pathways is:

≤4 mm

→ very low probability of endometrial cancer when the endometrium is appropriately visualised and there are no concerning additional findings.

>4 mm

→ requires further assessment, commonly endometrial sampling/hysteroscopy depending on pathway.

Important OSCE point

Do not say:

“4 mm excludes cancer.”

Instead:

“A thin endometrium substantially lowers the likelihood, but persistent/recurrent bleeding requires further assessment even if the endometrium is thin.”

[MRCOG Part 3 — Gynaecological Oncology OSCE Atlas > 38. RMI — RISK OF MALIGNANCY INDEX]
High-yield numerical OSCE formula:

RMI = U × M × CA-125

Where:

U = ultrasound score

Common scoring:

0 = no abnormal ultrasound features
1 = one abnormal feature
3 = ≥2 abnormal features.

Features include:

multilocular cyst
solid areas
metastases
ascites
bilateral lesions.
M = menopausal score
premenopausal = 1
postmenopausal = 3.
CA-125

Measured in U/mL.

RMI ≥200

Traditionally considered a high-risk threshold in many UK pathways and warrants specialist gynaecological oncology referral.

OSCE caution: local guidelines may use updated referral algorithms, so state that you would follow the current local pathway.

[MRCOG Part 3 — Gynaecological Oncology OSCE Atlas > 77. BREAKING BAD NEWS — MRCOG PART 3]
Use SPIKES.

S — Setting
private
quiet
sit down
no interruptions.
P — Perception

“What is your understanding of what has been happening?”

I — Invitation

“Would you like me to explain the results in detail?”

K — Knowledge

Give warning shot:

“Unfortunately, the biopsy has shown that this is a cancer.”

Then pause.

E — Emotion

Acknowledge:

“I can see this is a lot to take in.”

S — Strategy

Explain:

what happens next
MDT
staging
treatment
support.
78. “I'M WORRIED I WILL DIE” — MODEL RESPONSE

“I understand why you are frightened. A diagnosis of cancer is understandably overwhelming. At this stage, I would not want to give you an inaccurate prognosis before we know the exact type and stage. We will arrange the appropriate staging investigations and discuss your case at the specialist MDT, and then I can give you a much clearer picture of the treatment options and outlook.”

Excellent MRCOG communication point:

Do not give false reassurance.

79. “WHY DO I NEED A BIOPSY?”

Say:

“Imaging can show us that an area is suspicious, but tissue diagnosis tells us exactly what type of tumour this is. That information is essential for selecting the appropriate treatment.”

80. “CAN YOU TELL ME THE STAGE FROM THE SCAN?”

Say:

“The scan provides important information about the extent of disease, but the final stage may depend on clinical examination, pathology and sometimes surgical findings. I would integrate all of this information before confirming the final stage.”

🔴 MRCOG EXAMINER “GOLDEN POINTS”

If you remember only a few things, remember these:

Postmenopausal bleeding → exclude endometrial cancer.
Postcoital bleeding → consider cervical cancer.
Persistent bloating/early satiety → consider ovarian cancer.
Persistent vulval itch/ulcer → biopsy suspicious lesion.
A suspicious cervical lesion requires tissue diagnosis.
CA-125 is not a stand-alone diagnostic test.
RMI = U × M × CA-125.
RMI ≥200 is a traditional UK high-risk threshold.
Cervical cancer staging is heavily dependent on local extension and nodes.
Endometrial cancer now uses the 2023 FIGO system.
Endometrial molecular classification matters: POLE, MMRd, NSMP, p53abn.
GTD → follow β-hCG trends, not just a single value.
GTN FIGO score 0–6 = low risk; ≥7 = high risk.
Always ask about fertility before treatment in reproductive-age patients.
Always ask about sexual function and menopause after gynaecological cancer treatment.
Always mention MDT.
Do not give prognosis before stage/histology are known.
Cancer examination must be systematic and documented in centimetres.
Think about lymph nodes and distant metastases, not just the primary tumour.
In MRCOG Part 3, communication and patient-centred care are examined just as much as factual oncology knowledge.

37. Pelvic organ prolapse measurements

Important numerical framework:

POP-Q

Know:

Aa
Ba
C
D
Ap

perineal body
total vaginal length.
POP-Q staging
| Stage | Definition |
|---|---|
| 0 | No prolapse |
| I | Leading edge >1 cm above hymen |
| II | Leading edge within 1 cm above/below hymen |
| III | >1 cm beyond hymen but < TVL −2 cm |
| IV | Essentially complete vaginal eversion |

Hymen = 0 cm reference point.

38. Cervical screening — OSCE awareness

Do not confuse:

screening with

diagnostic assessment of a symptomatic cervix.

If cervix is:

friable
ulcerated
irregular
bleeding on contact
suspicious

→ clinical assessment/referral is required rather than simply reassuring the patient because screening is up to date.

PART XV — DIFFERENTIAL TABLE FOR EXAMINATION FINDINGS
| Finding | Most important causes |
|---|---|
| Firm irregular uterus | Fibroids |
| Globular tender uterus | Adenomyosis |
| Fixed retroverted uterus | Endometriosis/adhesions |
| Cervical excitation | PID, ectopic, endometriosis |
| Adnexal tenderness | PID, ectopic, torsion, endometriosis |
| Mobile cystic adnexal mass | Benign ovarian cyst |
| Fixed irregular adnexal mass | Malignancy/endometriosis |
| Bilateral adnexal masses | Endometriosis, malignancy, PID |
| Posterior fornix nodularity | Deep endometriosis |
| Ascites + pelvic mass | Ovarian malignancy until assessed |
| Acute unilateral pain + vomiting | Ovarian torsion |
| Acute pain + positive pregnancy test | Ectopic until excluded |
| Vulval white plaques | Lichen sclerosus |
| Vulval ulcer | HSV/trauma/malignancy |
| Vulval irregular pigmented lesion | Melanoma/malignancy |
PART XVI — INVESTIGATION FRAMEWORK FOR ANY GYNAE MASS
Always think:
1. Pregnancy
urine pregnancy test
serum β-hCG when indicated.
2. Blood tests

Depending on presentation:

FBC
CRP
U&E
LFT
coagulation
group and save/crossmatch
STI testing where indicated.
3. Imaging

First-line pelvic imaging commonly:

→ transvaginal ultrasound

Consider:

transabdominal ultrasound
MRI for selected deep endometriosis/complex pelvic pathology
CT when malignancy/staging or non-gynaecological pathology requires it.

For suspected endometriosis, NICE recommends TVUS even when examination is normal.

PART XVII — MRCOG "EXAMINER THINKING"

When given a pelvic examination finding, don't stop at:

"This is a fibroid."

Say:

FINDING → INTERPRETATION → DIFFERENTIAL → INVESTIGATION → MANAGEMENT

Example:

"The uterus is approximately 14-week size, firm, irregular and mobile. This is most consistent with uterine fibroids. I would assess the severity of symptoms, particularly heavy menstrual bleeding, pressure symptoms and fertility wishes. I would arrange pelvic ultrasound to define number, size and location of fibroids and assess the endometrial cavity where relevant. Management would then be individualised according to symptoms, fibroid characteristics, age, fertility wishes and patient preference."

That demonstrates applied clinical knowledge, rather than simple examination recall.

PART XVIII — HIGH-YIELD MRCOG PART 3 SAFETY POINTS
Never forget:
Pregnancy test in reproductive-age woman with acute pelvic pain.
ABCDE before detailed examination if unstable.
Consent and chaperone for intimate examination.
Stop if the patient asks you to stop.
Normal examination does not exclude endometriosis.
Normal ultrasound does not exclude endometriosis.
CA-125 is not a diagnostic test for endometriosis.
TVUS is recommended for suspected endometriosis.
Acute unilateral pain + vomiting → consider torsion.
Pain + positive pregnancy test → ectopic until excluded.
Ascites + adnexal/pelvic mass → malignancy must be considered.
Fixed pelvic mass → think malignancy, endometriosis or adhesions.
Irregular firm uterus → fibroid.
Globular tender/boggy uterus → adenomyosis.
Posterior fornix/uterosacral nodularity → deep endometriosis.
Do not over-reassure based on a normal cervical screening history when the cervix looks suspicious.
Always establish fertility wishes before recommending definitive gynaecological treatment.

The RCOG specifically expects candidates to demonstrate effective communication, logical information gathering, interpretation of findings, justification of investigations and discussion of management options—not merely perform a physical examination.

The golden MRCOG structure

CONSENT → SAFETY → EXAMINE → DESCRIBE → INTERPRET → DIFFERENTIAL → INVESTIGATE → MANAGE → SAFETY-NET

RCOG notes that episiotomy may be used when the baby needs rapid birth, including instrumental birth, or when serious perineal tearing is a concern.

Mediolateral episiotomy

High-yield number:

Start at the posterior fourchette and direct approximately 60° away from the midline at the time of incision.

Why?

Because an incision made at approximately 60° is associated with a lower risk of extension toward the anal sphincter than a midline episiotomy.

Shock index = heart rate / systolic BP

0.5–0.7

A rising shock index in obstetric haemorrhage is concerning.

HR 120 / SBP 90 =

[MRCOG Part 3 — OPERATIVE  TOACS OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 83. DRAIN — TOACS]

“I will put a drain routinely.”

Instead:

“I would use a drain selectively if there is a specific indication, such as concern about ongoing bleeding or contamination.”

Monopolar

between two jaws of the instrument.

Complications

87. OPERATIVE OSCE — “5 THINGS TO SAY” FOR EVERY PROCEDURE

If you become stuck, use:

1. Indication

“The indication for this procedure is…”

2. Preparation

“I would confirm consent, allergies, blood results, imaging, anaesthetic assessment, VTE risk and appropriate prophylaxis.”

3. Anatomy

“I would identify and protect the relevant anatomical structures, particularly the ureter, bladder and bowel where applicable.”

4. Complications

“I would anticipate haemorrhage, infection and injury to adjacent organs and have a plan to manage them.”

5. Completion

“Before closure I would confirm haemostasis, perform swab/needle/instrument counts, check specimens and document the procedure.”

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — OPERATIVE  TOACS OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 89. MOST COMMON MRCOG PART 3 OPERATIVE EXAMINER TRAPS]
Trap 1

“Perform a vacuum delivery.”

Don't immediately put on the cup.

First say:

“I would confirm full dilatation, ruptured membranes, engagement, position, station, absence of contraindications, adequate analgesia, empty bladder and informed consent.”

Trap 2

“Repair this perineal tear.”

Don't start suturing.

First:

“I would inspect the entire perineum, vagina and cervix and perform a rectal examination to exclude OASI.”

Trap 3

“This is a 3rd-degree tear.”

Don't simply say “repair it.”

Classify:

3a / 3b / 3c / 4th degree.

Trap 4

“There is PPH despite uterotonics.”

Don't jump straight to hysterectomy.

Say:

“I would simultaneously assess the 4 Ts and escalate through uterine tamponade and surgical measures while activating the major haemorrhage protocol.”

Trap 5

“Perform hysterectomy.”

Examiner wants anatomy.

Say:

“My key structures to identify and protect are the ureters, uterine vessels, bladder and bowel.”

Trap 6

“Perform ovarian cystectomy.”

Mention:

“I will aim to preserve maximal healthy ovarian tissue and minimise thermal damage because ovarian reserve is important.”

Trap 7

“Perform laparoscopy.”

Mention:

“I would assess previous abdominal surgery and entry risk before choosing the safest entry technique.”

89. MOST COMMON MRCOG PART 3 OPERATIVE EXAMINER TRAPS

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — OPERATIVE  TOACS OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 90. GOLDEN MRCOG OPERATIVE PHRASES]
Memorise these.

Before cutting

“I have confirmed the indication, consent, patient identity, allergies and relevant investigations.”

Before instrument application

“I have confirmed the anatomy and prerequisites and will use the instrument in a controlled manner.”

During surgery

“I will maintain good exposure, identify anatomy, minimise tissue trauma and maintain haemostasis.”

Before closure

“I will confirm haemostasis, inspect for organ injury, complete swab/needle/instrument counts and ensure correct specimen handling.”

If complication occurs

“I would recognise the complication, stop the procedure where appropriate, call for senior assistance, stabilise the patient and manage the injury definitively.”

If you don't know

Never invent.

Say:

“I would refer to the relevant local guideline/device instructions and seek senior assistance before proceeding.”

That is much safer than giving a falsely precise number.

⭐ THE OPERATIVE STATION MASTER ALGORITHM

For virtually every MRCOG Part 3 operative station, mentally run:

INDICATION → CONSENT → CONTRAINDICATIONS → PREPARATION → ANAESTHESIA → POSITION → ANTIBIOTICS/VTE → ANATOMY → INSTRUMENT → TECHNIQUE → NUMBERS → COMPLICATIONS → HAEMOSTASIS → COUNTS → SPECIMEN → POST-OP → FOLLOW-UP

And for obstetric procedures:

MOTHER + BABY + SPEED + SAFETY + BLOOD LOSS + FUTURE FERTILITY

The RCOG specifically emphasises prompt recognition and repair of OASI because delayed diagnosis can worsen long-term outcomes.

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 1. THE FIVE DOMAINS — YOUR MASTER CHECKLIST]
Every answer should subconsciously cover these five areas:

① Patient safety

Ask yourself:

Is this patient stable?
Is there an immediate life-threatening problem?
What must happen now?
Who needs to know?
What could go wrong?
What monitoring is required?
What is my escalation plan?
What is my safety-net?
② Communication with patient/family

Demonstrate:

Introduction
Rapport
Open questions
Active listening
Empathy
Responding to cues
Plain English
Checking understanding
Shared decision-making
Consent
Autonomy
Safety-netting
③ Communication with colleagues

Demonstrate:

Respect
Clear delegation
Appropriate escalation
Closed-loop communication
Structured handover
SBAR
Appropriate consultant involvement
④ Information gathering

Don't take an exhaustive history.

Take a focused history relevant to the task.

Think:

What information would change my management?

⑤ Applied clinical knowledge

Don't merely list facts.

Explain:

Finding → interpretation → significance → action.

This distinction is extremely important.

The RCOG specifically describes the assessment as testing application of knowledge rather than isolated knowledge recall.

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 2. THE 12-MINUTE STATION STRATEGY]
Current timing
| Time | What you do |
|---|---|
| 0–2 min | Read/preparation |
| 2–3 min | Introduction + agenda |
| 3–6 min | Information gathering / patient's concerns |
| 6–9 min | Explain/assess/options |
| 9–11 min | Shared decision / management / safety |
| 11–12 min | Summary + safety-net + final question |

The exact division will vary depending on the station.

Do not rigidly force every station into these timings.

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 3. THE 2-MINUTE READING STRATEGY]
As soon as you receive the scenario, identify:

A. Who am I?
SHO?
Registrar?
ST5?
O&G consultant?
On-call registrar?
B. Who is the other person?
Patient?
Partner?
Relative?
Midwife?
Junior doctor?
Consultant?
MDT?
C. What is my task?

Underline mentally:

Discuss
Explain
Counsel
Consent
Prioritise
Manage
Escalate
Break bad news
Communicate with colleague
D. What is the hidden danger?

Ask:

What could kill/harm this patient if I miss it?

E. What information is already provided?

Don't waste time asking for information already given.

F. What is the likely emotional agenda?

Patient may be:

frightened
angry
guilty
grieving
confused
disappointed
anxious about fertility
worried about cancer
concerned about baby
worried about surgery

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 4. YOUR FIRST 30 SECONDS]
A strong opening:

"Hello, I'm Dr ___, one of the doctors looking after you. I'd like to understand what has been happening, discuss the options with you and make sure we agree on a safe plan. Is that okay?"

Then:

"Before we start, is there anything in particular you're most worried about?"

This immediately demonstrates:

introduction
role
purpose
patient-centred approach
agenda
concern identification

The RCOG's communication framework specifically emphasises introduction, rapport, focused questioning, empathy, active listening, manageable information, shared decision-making, consent and dignity.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 5. SIMULATED PATIENT — THE GOLDEN STRUCTURE]
Use:

ICE → INFO → OPTIONS → DECISION → SAFETY
ICE

I — Ideas

"What is your understanding of what is happening?"

C — Concerns

"What is worrying you most?"

E — Expectations

"What were you hoping we could achieve today?"

6. SIMULATED PATIENT: OPEN → FOCUSED → CLOSED

Start:

"Can you tell me what has been happening?"

Then focus:

"When did the pain start?"

Then close:

"Is the pain constant?"

Avoid interrogating the patient with:

"Pain? Fever? Bleeding? Vomiting? Urine?"

That sounds robotic.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 7. ACTIVE LISTENING]
Use:

Verbal
"I see."
"Tell me more about that."
"That sounds difficult."
"What happened next?"
Non-verbal
Appropriate eye contact
Don't interrupt
Open posture
Nod appropriately
Calm tone
Reflecting

Patient:

"I'm terrified this means I'll never have another baby."

You:

"It sounds as though your biggest concern is what this might mean for your future fertility."

Excellent communication.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 8. EMPATHY — DON'T JUST SAY "I'M SORRY"]
Weak:

"I'm sorry."

Better:

"I can see that this has been very frightening for you."

Then pause.

Then:

"Would you like to tell me a little more about what worries you?"

Empathy formula

Acknowledge → validate → support

"I can see this is very upsetting. Anyone in this situation could feel overwhelmed. We'll go through this together and I'll explain what we know and what we still need to find out."
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 9. RESPONDING TO EMOTIONAL CUES]
Patient:

"Is this because I did something wrong?"

Don't immediately explain pathology.

Say:

"It sounds like you're blaming yourself."

Then:

"There is nothing you've told me that suggests you caused this."

Then explain.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 10. SIMULATED COLLEAGUE]
Treat the colleague as a professional—not as a patient.

Structure:

1. Establish the situation

"Can you tell me what's happening?"

2. Assess urgency

"What are the patient's observations and current clinical status?"

3. Clarify
diagnosis
investigations
treatment already given
response
concerns
4. Decide

"My immediate concern is..."

5. Delegate

"Please repeat the observations and establish IV access."

6. Escalate

"I would like you to contact the consultant while I review the patient."

7. Confirm

"Can you repeat back what you're going to do?"
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 11. CLOSED-LOOP COMMUNICATION]
Extremely important in emergencies.

Instead of:

"Someone get blood."

Say:

"Sarah, please activate the major haemorrhage protocol and tell me when blood products are available."

Then:

"Can you confirm that has been activated?"

This demonstrates safe teamworking.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 12. STRUCTURED DISCUSSION]
This is essentially a consultant-style discussion.

The examiner may ask:

"What would you do?"

Don't give a random list.

Use:

ASSESS → DIAGNOSE → STABILISE → INVESTIGATE → MANAGE → ESCALATE → REVIEW

Example:

"First I would assess ABCDE and determine whether she is clinically stable. I would then establish the likely diagnosis and differential diagnoses. I would initiate appropriate investigations while treating immediately reversible problems. I would involve the senior team early if there are concerns about deterioration and reassess her response to treatment."

Then give specifics.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 13. HOW TO ANSWER EXAMINER VIVA QUESTIONS]
If asked: "What are your differentials?"

Don't list 15.

Give:

Common
Dangerous
Relevant

Example:

"My leading diagnosis is X. Important alternatives would be Y and Z, particularly because I need to exclude the life-threatening diagnosis A."

14. IF ASKED "WHAT WOULD YOU DO?"

Use:

Immediate → Further → Definitive → Follow-up

Immediate
ABCDE
observations
monitoring
IV access
bloods
resuscitation
analgesia
senior help
Further
investigations
imaging
specialist review
Definitive
medical
surgical
obstetric
interventional
Follow-up
reassessment
documentation
safety-net
communication
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE
13. HOW TO ANSWER EXAMINER VIVA QUESTIONS

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 15. NUMERICAL VALUES — HOW TO USE THEM]
MRCOG Part 3 is not a "numbers dumping" exam.

Use numbers when they influence a decision.

For example:

"Her blood pressure is 170/110 mmHg, which is severe hypertension and requires urgent assessment and treatment."

Better than:

"Normal BP is 120/80."

Useful emergency thresholds to know
| Parameter | Important value |
|---|---|
| Severe hypertension | ≥160 systolic or ≥110 diastolic mmHg |
| Maternal tachycardia | Usually >100–120/min, interpret clinically |
| Maternal hypoxia | SpO₂ <94% generally concerning |
| Fever | ≥38°C |
| Oliguria | <0.5 mL/kg/hour |
| Significant PPH | ≥1000 mL with ongoing bleeding |
| Major PPH | ≥2500 mL |
| Hypoglycaemia | <4.0 mmol/L often triggers treatment in pregnancy |
| Severe thrombocytopenia | <50 ×10⁹/L particularly important around procedures/bleeding |
| Platelets in pre-eclampsia | <100 ×10⁹/L is a severe-feature laboratory abnormality |
| Proteinuria | PCR ≥30 mg/mmol or ACR ≥8 mg/mmol |
| Normal adult HR | approximately 60–100/min |
| Normal adult respiratory rate | approximately 12–20/min |

Important: Always use the clinical context and local guideline/laboratory reference ranges rather than treating a number in isolation.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE
15. NUMERICAL VALUES — HOW TO USE THEM

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 16. BREAKING BAD NEWS — MASTER FRAMEWORK]
Use:

SPIKES
S — Setting
private room
sit down
adequate time
no interruptions
offer support person
P — Perception

"Can you tell me what you understand so far?"

I — Invitation

"Would you like me to explain what we've found?"

K — Knowledge

Give information in small chunks.

"Unfortunately, the scan has shown something very concerning."

Pause.

"The findings are consistent with..."

Pause.

E — Emotions

"I can see this is a lot to take in."

Allow silence.

S — Strategy/Summary

Explain:

what happens next
treatment
prognosis where appropriate
support
follow-up
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 17. BREAKING BAD NEWS — NEVER DO THESE]
❌ "I have some bad news."

Then immediately unload 10 facts.

❌ "Unfortunately your baby is dead."

Better:

"I'm afraid the scan has confirmed that your baby has died."

Then STOP.

Allow silence.

Don't immediately fill the silence.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE
17. BREAKING BAD NEWS — NEVER DO THESE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 18. IF THE PATIENT CRIES]
Don't rush.

Say:

"Take your time."

Then:

"Would you like someone with you?"

Then assess:

support
understanding
immediate needs
safety
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 19. IF THE PATIENT BECOMES ANGRY]
Don't become defensive.

Use:

Acknowledge

"I can see that you're extremely upset."

Explore

"Can you tell me what has made you feel this way?"

Validate

"I understand why that would be frustrating."

Explain

"Let me explain what happened."

Solution

"Let's see what we can do now."
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 20. CONSENT — MRCOG GOLD STANDARD]
Consent isn't:

"Do you agree to surgery?"

It is a process.

Consent framework
1. Confirm identity
2. Explain procedure

"I'd like to explain what the procedure involves."

3. Purpose

"The reason for recommending it is..."

4. Benefits
5. Material risks
6. Alternatives
7. Consequences of no treatment
8. Patient-specific risks
9. Questions
10. Voluntary decision
11. Check understanding
12. Consent
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 21. MATERIAL RISKS]
Don't just recite generic risks.

Ask:

"Are there any particular concerns you have about the procedure?"

And tailor risks.

For example, before hysterectomy:

bleeding
transfusion
infection
injury to bladder
ureteric injury
bowel injury
thromboembolism
anaesthetic complications
conversion of surgical approach
ovarian consequences depending on procedure
impact on fertility
psychological implications
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 22. NUMERICAL RISK COMMUNICATION]
When a specific numerical risk is known, communicate it naturally.

Example:

"The risk of ureteric injury is approximately X%, although your individual risk may be higher because of..."

Then:

"Would you like me to explain what that means in practical terms?"

Avoid:

"There is a 0.2% chance."

Then moving on.

The patient may not understand what that means.

Instead:

"That is approximately 2 people in 1000."

Golden rule

Absolute risk > relative risk

Instead of:

"This doubles the risk."

Say:

"The risk increases from approximately 1 in 1000 to 2 in 1000."
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 23. SHARED DECISION-MAKING]
Use:

CHOICE + OPTIONS + PREFERENCES + DECISION

Say:

"There are a few reasonable options."

Then:

Option 1
advantages
disadvantages
Option 2
advantages
disadvantages
Option 3
advantages
disadvantages

Then:

"Which aspects are most important to you?"
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 24. DON'T PUSH YOUR PREFERRED OPTION]
Weak:

"I think you should have surgery."

Better:

"Medically, I think surgery is a reasonable option because... However, the choice depends on your priorities, and I'd like to discuss the alternatives with you."
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 25. PATIENT REFUSES TREATMENT]
Never say:

"You must have it."

Assess:

Capacity

Can the patient:

Understand?
Retain?
Weigh?
Communicate the decision?

If capacity is present:

"I respect your decision, even though I believe there is a significant risk in declining treatment."

Then:

explain consequences
offer alternatives
safety-net
document
involve senior team when appropriate
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 26. RISK COMMUNICATION — THE 7-STEP MODEL]
1. Establish baseline

"The overall risk is low."

2. Give absolute risk

"Approximately 1 in 1000."

3. Explain meaning

"So approximately one person in every thousand undergoing this procedure."

4. Individualise

"Your risk may be different because..."

5. Balance

"The procedure also has important benefits..."

6. Compare alternatives
7. Check understanding

"Does that make sense?"

27. WHEN THE PATIENT ASKS "WHAT WOULD YOU DO?"

Don't say:

"I'd have surgery."

Instead:

"If I were in your position, I would want to understand the benefits, risks and alternatives. Based on the information you've given me, medically I would lean towards X because..."

This preserves professional boundaries and autonomy.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 28. MDT — MULTIDISCIPLINARY TEAM]
Know who needs to be involved and why.

Potential O&G MDT:

consultant obstetrician/gynaecologist
anaesthetist
midwife
neonatologist
radiologist
pathologist
oncologist
urologist
colorectal surgeon
specialist nurse
physiotherapist
dietitian
safeguarding team
psychologist
haematologist
geneticist
fertility specialist

Don't simply say:

"I will discuss with MDT."

Say:

"I would involve the gynaecological oncology MDT because the diagnosis may require coordinated surgical, pathological and oncological planning."
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 29. MDT COMMUNICATION]
Use:

Problem → Evidence → Question → Recommendation

Example:

"This is a 42-year-old with an adnexal mass and concerning imaging features. The CA-125 is elevated and imaging suggests possible malignancy. I would like the MDT to review the imaging and agree whether she requires primary surgery or further diagnostic assessment."
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 30. SBAR — MUST KNOW]
S — Situation

"I'm Dr X, the O&G registrar. I'm calling about a 34-week pregnant woman with severe hypertension and neurological symptoms."

B — Background

"She has chronic hypertension and is currently admitted with suspected pre-eclampsia."

A — Assessment

"Her BP is 170/112, she has severe headache and brisk reflexes. CTG is currently reassuring."

R — Recommendation

"I would like you to review her urgently. I am starting immediate management for severe hypertension and magnesium sulfate is being considered according to the clinical picture."
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 31. SBAR — NEVER FORGET THE "R"]
Many candidates give:

Situation
Background
Assessment

Then stop.

The consultant needs:

"What do you want me to do?"

Always end with a clear recommendation.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 32. PRIORITISATION STATION]
Imagine:

You are the registrar with 5 simultaneous problems.

Don't simply say:

"I'll deal with them one by one."

Use:

ABCDE + TIME + RISK + RESOURCES

Prioritise:

1. Immediately life-threatening
maternal collapse
major PPH
eclampsia
severe sepsis
ruptured ectopic
uterine rupture
massive PE
2. Time-critical fetal emergencies
cord prolapse
pathological CTG
placental abruption with compromise
uterine rupture
3. Potential deterioration
severe pre-eclampsia
suspected sepsis
significant APH
4. Stable patients
routine review
discharge
non-urgent counselling
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 33. THE PRIORITISATION PHRASE]
Use:

"I would prioritise according to immediate threat to life, time-criticality, likelihood of deterioration and whether another appropriately trained member of the team can safely manage the other tasks."

Excellent MRCOG language.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 34. DELEGATION]
Don't delegate your responsibility.

Bad:

"You deal with the PPH."

Better:

"Please assess the stable patient in bed 4 and update me within 10 minutes, while I personally attend the woman with the major PPH."

Then specify:

who
what
timeframe
expected feedback
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 35. EMERGENCY ESCALATION]
Use:

RECOGNISE → RESUSCITATE → CALL → DELEGATE → DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT → REASSESS
Recognise

"This patient is deteriorating."

Resuscitate

ABCDE.

Call
senior registrar
consultant
anaesthetics
relevant specialty
theatre
blood bank
neonatal team
Delegate

Clear tasks.

Definitive management

Treat the underlying cause.

Reassess

"I will reassess her response after intervention and escalate further if she remains unstable."
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 36. WHEN TO CALL THE CONSULTANT]
Don't wait until you've completed your entire differential.

Escalate early for:

maternal instability
severe haemorrhage
eclampsia
suspected uterine rupture
major sepsis
difficult operative decision
major operative complication
unexpected deterioration
uncertainty involving patient safety
conflict with patient/relative
safeguarding concern
significant ethical/legal issue

Excellent phrase:

"I would rather escalate early than delay senior input when there is a potential threat to maternal or fetal safety."

37. "I DON'T KNOW" — HOW TO SURVIVE A VIVA

Never invent.

Say:

"I don't recall the exact figure, but the clinically important threshold is..."

Or:

"I'm not certain of the exact numerical value, so I would check the current local guideline. My immediate management would be..."

This is much safer than giving an incorrect number confidently.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 38. EXAMINER VIVA — WHEN YOU GET STUCK]
Use:

"Let me structure my answer."

Then:

"I would consider this under immediate management, investigation, definitive treatment and follow-up."

This buys you thinking time without appearing lost.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE
38. EXAMINER VIVA — WHEN YOU GET STUCK

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 39. IF THE EXAMINER INTERRUPTS]
STOP.

Listen.

Answer exactly what was asked.

Don't continue your rehearsed speech.

The examiner may be deliberately moving you to another domain.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 40. IF EXAMINER GIVES NEW INFORMATION]
Treat it as clinically important.

Example:

Examiner:

"Her BP is now 180/120."

Don't continue your previous answer.

Say:

"That changes my immediate priority. This is severe hypertension and requires urgent treatment and senior review."

41. "WHAT IF SHE REFUSES?"

Use:

Explore why

"Can I ask what is making you reluctant?"

Check understanding
Capacity
Explain risks
Alternatives
Respect autonomy
Safety-net
Document
Senior involvement if appropriate
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 42. SAFETY-NETTING]
Every patient station should finish with some form of safety-net.

Include:

What to look for

"If you develop worsening pain, heavy bleeding, fever, breathlessness or feel faint..."

What to do

"...please seek urgent medical attention."

Who to contact

"You can contact the maternity assessment unit / emergency service depending on the situation."

Follow-up

"We will arrange follow-up in..."
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 43. DOCUMENTATION]
Mention when relevant:

assessment
examination
investigations
discussions
consent
patient's decision
risks explained
alternatives
senior discussion
MDT discussion
safety-netting
escalation
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 44. CONFIDENTIALITY]
If asked about relatives:

"I would normally maintain confidentiality and would only share information with the patient's consent, unless there is a specific legal or safeguarding reason requiring disclosure."
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 45. SAFEGUARDING]
Think:

Adult/child safety
domestic abuse
sexual violence
trafficking
FGM
coercive control
exploitation
child safeguarding

Never confront a suspected perpetrator in front of the patient.

Ensure:

private conversation
immediate safety
appropriate safeguarding referral
documentation
senior input
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 46. CAPACITY / CONSENT — QUICK NUMBERS]
Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific.

The patient must be able to:

Understand
Retain
Use/weigh
Communicate

Do not equate:

disagreement
unwise decision
psychiatric diagnosis

with lack of capacity.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 47. SHARED DECISION-MAKING — EXAMINER PHRASES]
Useful phrases:

"There isn't necessarily one correct option."

"There are benefits and disadvantages to each approach."

"I'd like to understand what matters most to you."

"Would you like some time to consider this?"

"Would you like your partner/family member involved?"

"What questions do you have?"
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 48. THE "PATIENT-FRIENDLY LANGUAGE" RULE]
Avoid:

❌ "PPROM"

Say:

"Your waters have broken earlier than expected."

Avoid:

❌ "IUFD"

Say:

"Sadly, the baby has died."

Avoid:

❌ "Malignant"

Say:

"Cancerous."

Avoid:

❌ "EUA"

Say:

"An examination under anaesthetic."

Avoid:

❌ "MUA"

Say:

"A procedure to remove remaining pregnancy tissue from the womb."

The RCOG specifically expects information to be delivered in manageable amounts using patient-friendly language and avoiding unexplained jargon.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 49. THE "CHUNK AND CHECK" TECHNIQUE]
Don't give a 3-minute monologue.

Chunk 1

"The scan has shown a pregnancy outside the womb."

Pause.

Check

"Is that clear so far?"

Chunk 2

"This is called an ectopic pregnancy."

Pause.

Check

"Would you like me to explain how we normally treat this?"

This demonstrates communication rather than information dumping.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 50. HOW TO EXPLAIN A COMPLEX MEDICAL ISSUE]
Use:

WHAT → WHY → OPTIONS → RISKS → PLAN

Example:

"The problem is X."

"This is important because Y."

"We have three possible approaches."

"Each has benefits and risks."

"Considering your circumstances, I would recommend X."

"However, the final decision is yours."

51. "WHY?" QUESTIONS FROM EXAMINER

Examiner:

"Why would you do that?"

Don't repeat the management.

Explain the reasoning.

"Because the immediate priority is to prevent maternal deterioration."

"Because this result changes the risk-benefit balance."

"Because delaying treatment could result in significant morbidity."

52. "WHAT ARE THE RISKS?"

Use:

Common
Serious
Procedure-specific
Patient-specific

Example:

"Common risks include pain and infection. Serious risks include haemorrhage and injury to surrounding organs. In this patient, the risk may be increased because of previous surgery."

53. "WHAT ARE THE BENEFITS?"

Don't say:

"It will cure her."

Instead:

symptom improvement
disease control
prevention of complications
diagnostic information
improved quality of life
survival benefit where relevant
54. "WHAT ARE THE ALTERNATIVES?"

Always consider:

A — Active treatment
B — Alternative treatment
C — Conservative/expectant management
D — No treatment

Then explain consequences.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE
50. HOW TO EXPLAIN A COMPLEX MEDICAL ISSUE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 55. CLINICAL REASONING — HIGH-SCORING FORMAT]
When presenting a diagnosis:

"My leading diagnosis is X because of A, B and C."

"The important differential is Y because of D."

"The diagnosis I particularly need to exclude is Z because it is potentially life-threatening."

This is much stronger than:

"Differentials are A, B, C, D, E, F..."
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 56. WHEN YOU HAVE LIMITED INFORMATION]
Say:

"I would first establish whether she is clinically stable."

Then:

"My immediate management would not wait for all investigations if she is unstable."

Excellent patient-safety thinking.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 57. WHEN THERE IS A CONFLICT BETWEEN PATIENT AND DOCTOR]
Use:

Explore → Understand → Explain → Negotiate → Respect → Safety-net

Never become authoritarian.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE
57. WHEN THERE IS A CONFLICT BETWEEN PATIENT AND DOCTOR

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 58. WHEN PATIENT WANTS AN UNNECESSARY TEST]
Don't say:

"No, you don't need it."

Say:

"I understand why you'd like the test. Let me explain what information it would and wouldn't give us, and whether it would change what we do."

Then discuss:

benefits
harms
false positives
false reassurance
alternatives
cost/resources where relevant
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE
58. WHEN PATIENT WANTS AN UNNECESSARY TEST

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 59. WHEN PATIENT WANTS AN UNAVAILABLE TREATMENT]
Acknowledge:

"I understand why that option is attractive."

Then:

"Unfortunately, I don't think it would be safe/appropriate in your circumstances because..."

Offer alternative.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE
59. WHEN PATIENT WANTS AN UNAVAILABLE TREATMENT

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 60. DEALING WITH COMPLAINTS]
Use:

Listen

Don't interrupt.

Acknowledge

"I can see why you're unhappy."

Apologise when appropriate

"I'm sorry that you experienced this."

An apology does not necessarily mean accepting blame.

Explain

Only after listening.

Action

"I'll make sure this is discussed with the senior team."

Follow-up

Provide appropriate complaint pathway.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 61. TEAM CONFLICT]
If a colleague disagrees:

"I appreciate your concern."

"Can you explain your reasoning?"

Then:

"My concern is patient safety because..."

If unresolved:

"I think we should involve the senior clinician."

Never humiliate a colleague.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 62. JUNIOR DOCTOR MAKES A MISTAKE]
Priorities:

Patient safety
Stabilise patient
Escalate
Honest communication
Documentation
Learning/support

Don't start by blaming the junior.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 63. DISCLOSING AN ERROR]
Say:

"I would be open and honest with the patient about what happened."

Explain:

what happened
current consequences
what has been done
what will happen next
appropriate apology
support
investigation/governance

Avoid:

❌ blaming colleagues
❌ speculation
❌ hiding information
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 64. ETHICAL SCENARIOS — FOUR PRINCIPLES]
Remember:

Autonomy

Patient's right to choose.

Beneficence

Act in patient's best interests.

Non-maleficence

Avoid harm.

Justice

Fair allocation and treatment.

But don't just name them.

Apply them:

"Although I believe treatment would be beneficial, she has capacity and is entitled to refuse it."
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 65. PRIORITISATION — A QUICK MATRIX]
| Situation | Priority |
|---|---|
| Maternal collapse | 🔴 Immediate |
| Major PPH | 🔴 Immediate |
| Eclampsia | 🔴 Immediate |
| Suspected uterine rupture | 🔴 Immediate |
| Cord prolapse | 🔴 Immediate |
| Severe sepsis | 🔴 Immediate |
| Pathological CTG | 🔴 Very urgent |
| Severe pre-eclampsia | 🟠 Urgent |
| Suspected ectopic, unstable | 🔴 Immediate |
| Stable ectopic | 🟠 Urgent |
| Stable gynae problem | 🟢 Routine |
| Administrative request | 🟢 Lower priority |
66. "WHAT WOULD YOU DO FIRST?"

Your default:

"First, I would assess ABCDE and establish whether the patient is clinically stable."

Then:

"If unstable, I would initiate immediate resuscitation and call for senior help."

Then:

"I would investigate and treat the underlying cause simultaneously."
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 67. EMERGENCY NUMERICAL VALUES WORTH KNOWING]
Shock

Don't wait for hypotension.

Important signs:

tachycardia
tachypnoea
altered mental state
prolonged capillary refill
oliguria
cool peripheries
rising lactate
Urine

Target commonly:

≥0.5 mL/kg/hour

Capillary refill

Usually:

≤2 seconds

Prolonged refill suggests poor peripheral perfusion but must be interpreted clinically.

Oxygen

In an acutely unwell adult, commonly aim around:

94–98%

unless a specific condition requires a different target.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 68. THE "RED FLAGS" HABIT]
At every station ask:

"Is there anything here that could deteriorate rapidly?"

Obstetric red flags:

bleeding
severe hypertension
seizure
reduced consciousness
chest pain
dyspnoea
hypoxia
severe abdominal pain
fever
fetal compromise
reduced fetal movements
abnormal CTG
oliguria
sepsis
shock
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 69. THE FINAL 60 SECONDS]
Never suddenly stop.

Use:

Summarise

"So, to summarise..."

Decision

"We've agreed that..."

Safety

"The important symptoms that should prompt urgent review are..."

Follow-up

"We'll arrange..."

Check

"Before we finish, is there anything else you're worried about?"
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 70. THE UNIVERSAL 10-MINUTE PERFORMANCE TEMPLATE]
For almost any patient station:

0:00–0:30

Introduce

0:30–1:00

Agenda + patient's main concern

1:00–3:00

Focused information gathering

3:00–4:00

ICE

4:00–6:00

Explain diagnosis/problem

6:00–8:00

Options + risks + benefits

8:00–9:00

Shared decision

9:00–10:00

Safety-net + summary
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 71. UNIVERSAL STRUCTURED-DISCUSSION TEMPLATE]
When examiner asks a clinical question:

1. Stability

"Is the patient stable?"

2. Immediate management

"I would start with ABCDE..."

3. Diagnosis

"My leading diagnosis is..."

4. Differential

"Important differentials include..."

5. Investigations

"I would perform..."

6. Interpretation

"The result would influence management because..."

7. Definitive treatment

"I would..."

8. Escalation

"I would involve..."

9. Reassessment

"I would reassess..."

10. Safety-net

"If she deteriorates..."
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 72. COMMON MRCOG PART 3 FAILING BEHAVIOURS]
❌ Knowledge dumping

You know the answer but don't answer the question.

❌ No empathy

Technically perfect but patient feels ignored.

❌ No patient agenda

You immediately start lecturing.

❌ Excessive jargon

Patient doesn't understand.

❌ No safety-net

You finish after giving the diagnosis.

❌ No escalation

You attempt to manage everything yourself.

❌ Delayed consultant involvement

Dangerous.

❌ Poor prioritisation

Treating routine issues before life-threatening ones.

❌ Giving false certainty

"Definitely."

Instead:

"The most likely diagnosis is..."

❌ Ignoring patient autonomy

"You need to have this."

❌ Inventing numerical values

If unsure, don't guess.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE.md
section_path: MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 73. THE "SAFE DOCTOR" TEST]
Before leaving every station, ask yourself:

Patient
Did I understand their concern?
Did I explain clearly?
Did I give choices?
Did I check understanding?
Safety
Did I identify red flags?
Did I escalate?
Did I give safety-netting?
Clinical
Did I justify my decisions?
Did I give appropriate investigations?
Did I discuss alternatives?
Team
Did I delegate appropriately?
Did I communicate clearly?
Did I close the loop?

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — PERFORMANCE & COMMUNICATION OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 74. THE MRCOG "EXAMINER WANTS TO WORK WITH YOU" TEST]
Imagine the examiner is your consultant and asks:

"Would I trust this registrar with my labour ward?"

You should appear:

Calm + safe + organised + kind + decisive + appropriately humble.

Not:

Panicked + authoritarian + encyclopaedic + indecisive.

The RCOG's own description makes clear that the assessment integrates clinical knowledge with communication and patient safety rather than testing knowledge in isolation.

Patient
"What is worrying you most?"
"What is your understanding of what is happening?"
"Would it be okay if I explain what we have found?"
"I can see that this is very difficult for you."
"I'll explain this in small steps."
"There are several reasonable options."
"I'd like to understand what matters most to you."
"Does that explanation make sense?"
"Would you like someone with you?"
"Before we finish, is there anything else you're worried about?"
Clinical
"My immediate priority is patient safety."
"First I would assess ABCDE."
"I would not delay treatment while waiting for investigations if she is unstable."
"My leading diagnosis is..."
"The important diagnosis I need to exclude is..."
"I would involve the senior team early."
Colleague
"Can you please repeat that back to me so I know the plan is clear?"
"I'd like you to escalate this to the consultant now."
"I appreciate your concern; let's work through the options."
"Let's make sure we have a clear plan and contingency plan."

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — SEXUAL HEALTH OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 1. UNIVERSAL SEXUAL-HEALTH OSCE APPROACH]
A. Opening the consultation
Introduction
Wash hands.
Introduce yourself.
Confirm patient identity.
Confirm age.
Explain confidentiality.
Establish whether they are comfortable discussing sexual health.
Offer a chaperone for examination.
Obtain consent before examination/swabs.
Useful opening

“I understand you have some concerns regarding your sexual or genital health. I ask these questions routinely because they help me provide the correct care. Everything you tell me is confidential, subject to the usual safeguarding exceptions. Is it okay if I ask you some personal questions?”

Confidentiality caveat

Explain:

Information is confidential.
Exceptions include:
serious risk of harm to patient/another person
safeguarding concerns
certain legal/public-health requirements.
2. SEXUAL HISTORY — 6 Ps

A very useful MRCOG structure:

1. Partners

Ask:

Current partner?
Number of partners recently?
New partner?
Male/female/both?
Partner's STI history?
Partner symptoms?
Partner treated?

Avoid assumptions about heterosexuality or monogamy.

2. Practices

Ask sensitively:

Vaginal intercourse?
Oral sex?
Anal sex?
Genital-to-genital contact?
Sex toys?
Condom use?
Shared sex toys?
Frequency of intercourse?

This determines which anatomical sites require testing.

3. Protection

Ask:

Condoms?
Consistency of use?
Contraception?
HPV vaccination?
HIV PrEP/PEP where appropriate?
Previous STI screening?
4. Past STIs

Ask:

Previous chlamydia?
Gonorrhoea?
Syphilis?
HIV?
Hepatitis B/C?
Herpes?
HPV/genital warts?
PID?

Also:

Previous treatment?
Partner treated?
Recurrence?
5. Pregnancy prevention/plans

Ask:

LMP.
Pregnancy possibility.
Current contraception.
Future fertility plans.
Desire for pregnancy.

Always perform a pregnancy test when clinically appropriate before certain investigations/treatments.

6. Protection from coercion/abuse

Ask:

“Do you feel safe in your relationship?”

“Has anyone ever pressured or forced you to have sex?”

“Are you free to say no?”

“Has anyone ever controlled your contraception?”

“Are you worried about anyone finding out that you have attended today?”

[MRCOG Part 3 — SEXUAL HEALTH OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 4. CANDIDAL VULVOVAGINITIS]
Cause

Usually:

Candida albicans

Risk factors:

Diabetes.
Pregnancy.
Recent antibiotics.
Immunosuppression.
Oestrogen exposure.
Poorly controlled glycaemia.

Not necessarily sexually transmitted.

Symptoms
Intense vulval itching.
Burning.
Vulval soreness.
Dyspareunia.
Dysuria due to external irritation.
Thick white discharge.
Examination
Vulval erythema.
Excoriations.
Fissuring.
Oedema.
Thick white discharge.
Important OSCE distinction

Candida → itch predominates.

Vaginal pH

Usually:

<4.5

A pH >4.5 should make you consider BV or trichomoniasis rather than uncomplicated Candida.

Diagnosis
Vaginal microscopy.
KOH preparation.
Culture if:
recurrent
complicated
persistent
non-albicans suspected.
Microscopy

Look for:

budding yeast
pseudohyphae.

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — SEXUAL HEALTH OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 5. BACTERIAL VAGINOSIS]
Cause

Disruption of normal Lactobacillus-dominant flora with increased anaerobic organisms.

Common organisms include:

Gardnerella vaginalis
anaerobes
Atopobium and others.
Symptoms

Often asymptomatic.

Typical:

Thin homogeneous discharge.
Grey/white discharge.
Fishy odour.
Odour particularly noticeable after intercourse/menstruation.

Usually minimal inflammation.

pH

>4.5

Amsel criteria

Four criteria:

Homogeneous thin discharge.
Vaginal pH >4.5.
Positive whiff test.
Clue cells on microscopy.
Diagnosis

≥3 of 4 = BV by Amsel criteria.

Clue cells

Vaginal epithelial cells coated with bacteria.

Microscopically:

stippled appearance
poorly defined cell borders.
Whiff test

Add KOH to vaginal discharge.

Positive:

fishy/amines odour

Nugent score

Gram-stain scoring:

0–3: normal flora
4–6: intermediate
7–10: BV

This is a very useful numerical value for MRCOG.

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — SEXUAL HEALTH OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 6. TRICHOMONIASIS]
Organism

Trichomonas vaginalis

Sexually transmitted protozoan.

Symptoms
Frothy discharge.
Yellow-green discharge.
Offensive odour.
Vulval irritation.
Dysuria.
Dyspareunia.

Can be asymptomatic.

Examination

Classic:

“Strawberry cervix”
punctate cervical haemorrhages.
erythematous cervix.
pH

Usually:

>4.5

Microscopy

Wet mount:

motile flagellated organisms.

However, wet microscopy has limited sensitivity.

Preferred test

NAAT is much more sensitive.

Important OSCE point

Treat:

Patient + sexual partner(s)

because reinfection is common.

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — SEXUAL HEALTH OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 8. CERVICITIS]
Definition

Inflammation of the cervix.

Common causes
Infectious
Chlamydia trachomatis.
Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
Mycoplasma genitalium.
Trichomonas vaginalis.

HSV can occasionally be associated.

Non-infectious
Chemical irritation.
Foreign body.
Cervical ectropion.
Trauma.
Instrumentation.
Clinical features
Abnormal vaginal discharge.
Mucopurulent discharge.
Postcoital bleeding.
Intermenstrual bleeding.
Dyspareunia.
Dysuria.
Pelvic pain may indicate ascending infection/PID.
Examination
Speculum

Look for:

mucopurulent discharge from cervical os.
cervical erythema.
friability.
contact bleeding.
ectropion.
ulcers.
masses.
Key finding

Cervical motion/contact may cause bleeding.

Investigations
NAAT

Test for:

Chlamydia.
Gonorrhoea.

Depending on circumstances:

Trichomonas.
M. genitalium.

Also consider:

HIV.
Syphilis.
Hepatitis B/C depending on risk.
Treatment principle

Treat according to:

organism.
local resistance.
pregnancy status.
allergy.
STI risk.
current BASHH/local guideline.

For example, CDC guidance lists doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days as a cervicitis regimen, with gonorrhoea treatment added when indicated; local/BASHH guidance should be followed in UK-style MRCOG answers.

Pregnancy

Do not automatically use doxycycline.

Choose a pregnancy-appropriate regimen according to current guideline.

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — SEXUAL HEALTH OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 12. GENITAL HERPES]
Cause

HSV-1 or HSV-2.

HSV-2 traditionally causes more recurrent genital disease, although genital HSV-1 is increasingly recognised.

Primary episode

May cause:

painful grouped vesicles.
painful ulcers.
dysuria.
vaginal discharge.
tender inguinal lymph nodes.
fever.
malaise.
headache.

Severe primary disease can cause urinary retention or neurological complications.

Examination

Look for:

vesicles.
shallow ulcers.
crusting.
erythema.
tender inguinal nodes.
Diagnosis
Preferred

Lesion swab for:

HSV PCR/NAAT

Type HSV-1 versus HSV-2 when possible.

Important counselling

HSV:

establishes lifelong latency.
can recur.
can be transmitted during asymptomatic shedding.
may be transmitted by people without obvious lesions.

CDC specifically emphasises asymptomatic shedding and transmission counselling.

First episode treatment

Example CDC regimen:

Acyclovir 400 mg PO three times daily for 7–10 days

or

Valaciclovir 1 g PO twice daily for 7–10 days

Treatment may be extended if lesions have not healed by 10 days.

For MRCOG:

“I would follow the current BASHH regimen.”

Do not rely on an old memorised regimen if the station asks for current UK guidance.

Recurrent herpes

Options:

episodic treatment.
suppressive therapy for frequent/severe recurrences.
suppressive treatment can also be considered when psychological distress is substantial.
Pregnancy

This is an important MRCOG crossover.

Ask:

first episode or recurrent?
gestation?
lesions/prodrome at labour?
previous history?
treatment.

Management is obstetric-led and depends on timing, recurrence, lesions/prodrome and delivery circumstances.

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — SEXUAL HEALTH OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 13. SYPHILIS]
Organism

Treponema pallidum

Primary syphilis
Classic lesion

Chancre

usually single.
painless.
clean-based.
indurated.
regional lymphadenopathy.
Secondary syphilis

Features:

widespread rash.
palms and soles.
mucous patches.
condyloma lata.
lymphadenopathy.
systemic symptoms.
Important differential

Condyloma lata ≠ genital wart.

Condyloma lata occurs in secondary syphilis.

Tertiary syphilis

May cause:

cardiovascular disease.
neurological disease.
gummatous disease.
Investigations

Serology:

treponemal tests.
non-treponemal tests such as RPR/VDRL.
Important numerical concept

RPR/VDRL titres are useful for:

baseline.
monitoring treatment response.
detecting reinfection.

A clinically significant change is generally a fourfold change in titre, equivalent to a two-dilution change.

text:
[MRCOG Part 3 — SEXUAL HEALTH OSCE MASTER GUIDE > 14. GENITAL WARTS]
Cause

HPV.

Approximately 90% of anogenital warts are associated with HPV 6 and 11, which are low-oncogenic-risk types.

Appearance
papular.
flat.
pedunculated.
cauliflower-like.
flesh-coloured.

Sites:

vulva.
vagina.
cervix.
perineum.
perianal region.
anus.
Diagnosis

Usually:

Clinical examination.

HPV testing is not recommended simply to diagnose genital warts.

When to biopsy

Biopsy if:

pigmented.
indurated.
fixed.
ulcerated.
bleeding.
atypical.
diagnosis uncertain.
immunocompromised patient.
failure to respond to treatment.
lesion worsens.

Treatment options
Patient-applied
Imiquimod.
Podophyllotoxin/podofilox where appropriate.
Clinician-applied
Cryotherapy.
TCA/BCA.
Surgical excision.
Electrosurgery.
Laser in selected cases.

Treatment depends on:

number.
size.
location.
pregnancy.
patient preference.
cost.
clinician expertise.

Pregnancy

Very important:

Avoid podophyllin/podophyllotoxin and sinecatechins during pregnancy.

Imiquimod is generally avoided until better pregnancy safety data are available.

Cryotherapy or appropriate surgical treatment may be considered if required.

HPV COUNSELLING

Explain:

HPV is extremely common.
Infection may be asymptomatic.
Warts can appear months or years after acquisition.
Therefore, appearance of warts does not establish when HPV was acquired or prove recent infidelity.
Treatment removes visible warts but does not necessarily eradicate HPV.
Recurrence can occur.
HPV vaccination prevents infection with vaccine-covered types but does not treat existing infection/warts.

[MRCOG Part 3 — UROGYNAECOLOGY OSCE ATLAS > 2. IMPORTANT NORMAL NUMBERS]
| Parameter | Important value |
|---|---|
| Normal bladder capacity | ~300–500 mL |
| Normal voided volume | commonly ~200–400 mL |
| Normal frequency | approximately 6–8/day |
| Nocturia | ideally 0–1/night |
| Post-void residual | ideally <50 mL; <100 mL often acceptable depending on context |
| Significant retention | commonly >300 mL |
| Recurrent UTI | ≥2/6 months OR ≥3/12 months |
| POP-Q reference | Hymen = 0 cm |
| POP-Q above hymen | negative |
| POP-Q below hymen | positive |
| PFM training for SUI | ≥8 contractions × 3/day |
| SUI PFMT duration | ≥3 months |
| POP stage I/II PFMT | ≥16 weeks |
| OAB bladder training | ≥6 weeks |

The recurrent-UTI definition of ≥2 UTIs in 6 months or ≥3 in 12 months is specifically used by NICE.

NICE recommends a minimum 3-day bladder diary, routine urine dipstick testing in women presenting with urinary incontinence, and supervised pelvic-floor training for at least 3 months for stress/mixed incontinence.
