[MRCOG Part 3 — UROGYNAECOLOGY OSCE ATLAS > 57. POST-VOID RESIDUAL — INTERPRETATION]
There is no single universally applicable “abnormal” PVR cutoff.

Practical interpretation:

<50 mL

Generally reassuring.

50–100 mL

Usually acceptable depending on symptoms/context.

>100–200 mL

Potentially abnormal → interpret clinically.

>300 mL

Significant retention is likely.

Very large PVR

Consider:

acute/chronic retention
obstruction
detrusor underactivity

OSCE principle: trend + symptoms + bladder volume matter more than one isolated number.
source_file: MRCOG Part 3 — UROGYNAECOLOGY OSCE ATLAS.md

Methods:

Important

Do not simply say:

“PVR is abnormal.”

Say:

“I would interpret the PVR alongside voided volume, symptoms, renal function and the clinical context.”

| Topic | Number to remember |
|---|---|
| POP-Q hymen | 0 cm |
| Above hymen | negative |
| Below hymen | positive |
| Stage I | >1 cm above hymen |
| Stage II | −1 to +1 cm |
| Stage III | >+1 cm but not complete eversion |
| Stage IV | within ~2 cm of TVL / complete eversion |
| Bladder capacity | ~300–500 mL |
| Normal frequency | ~6–8/day |
| Nocturia | 0–1/night |
| PVR reassuring | <50 mL |
| Significant PVR | >100–200 mL, context dependent |
| Major retention | ~>300 mL |
| Recurrent UTI | ≥2/6 months or ≥3/12 months |
| Bladder diary | ≥3 days |
| OAB bladder training | ≥6 weeks |
| SUI PFMT | ≥3 months |
| PFMT dose | ≥8 contractions × 3/day |
| POP stage I/II PFMT | ≥16 weeks |
| Qmax reassuring | >15 mL/s |
| Low Qmax | <10 mL/s |

Important in:

Vulval cancer
Endometrial cancer
Selected breast cancer pathways

RCOG's gynaecological oncology curriculum specifically includes sentinel lymph-node dissection for vulval cancer and sentinel-node biopsy for endometrial cancer.

Principle

The sentinel node is the first draining lymph node from the primary tumour.

Technique concept
Identify primary tumour.
Inject tracer according to protocol.
Identify lymphatic drainage.
Locate sentinel node.
Remove node.
Send for histopathology/ultrastaging according to tumour protocol.

|---|---|

| Endometrial polyp | Hysteroscopic polypectomy |
| Vulval skin lesion | Punch/incisional biopsy |
| Small vulval lesion | Excisional biopsy |
| Suspected vulval cancer | Representative incisional biopsy |
| Vaginal lesion | Vaginal biopsy |
| Breast mass | Core biopsy usually provides tissue architecture |
| Breast cyst | FNA/aspiration in selected circumstances |
| Enlarged lymph node | Core/FNA/excision depending on diagnosis |

This is another major MRCOG/MCPS OSCE procedure.7RCOG's current Green-top Guideline recommends outpatient hysteroscopy as an important diagnostic/therapeutic service, particularly for abnormal uterine bleeding, and emphasises informed consent and pain management.Indications
Postmenopausal bleeding
Abnormal uterine bleeding
Heavy/prolonged bleeding
Intermenstrual bleeding
Suspected endometrial polyp
Submucous fibroid
Endometrial pathology
Fertility assessment in selected circumstances
Retained/missing IUCD
Following miscarriage in selected casesRCOG specifically lists abnormal bleeding, postmenopausal bleeding, intracavitary pathology, fertility concerns and missing coil threads among indications.Types
Diagnostic hysteroscopyVisualisation only ± biopsy.Operative hysteroscopy
Polypectomy
Small fibroid removal
Removal of retained IUCD
Endometrial biopsy
Other minor intrauterine procedures
ApproachVaginoscopic/no-touch approachOften preferred for outpatient diagnostic hysteroscopy.Instruments
Hysteroscope
Camera
Light source
Monitor
Saline distension system
Speculum if required
Cervical instruments if required
Biopsy forceps
Tissue removal system
Polyp forceps
Formalin potRCOG recommends miniature hysteroscopes for diagnostic outpatient hysteroscopy; current guidance also recommends using the smallest suitable diameter for operative procedures.BASIC HYSTEROSCOPY TECHNIQUE
Explain procedure.
Confirm indication.
Exclude pregnancy.
Consent.
Chaperone.
Discuss pain-control options.
Position patient.
Vaginoscopic entry where appropriate.
Identify cervix.
Pass hysteroscope gently.
Use normal saline for distension.
Enter uterine cavity.
Inspect systematically:Cervix → anterior wall → posterior wall → fundus → right tubal ostium → left tubal ostium.Identify:
polyp
fibroid
hyperplastic/irregular endometrium
adhesions
septum
retained products
Take biopsy if indicated.
Perform minor operative procedure if appropriate.
Remove hysteroscope.
Document findings.
Send tissue for histology.RCOG notes that outpatient hysteroscopy commonly takes approximately 5–10 minutes for the actual procedure, although additional procedures take longer.

If persistent significant symptoms or abnormal specialist investigations → discuss planned caesarean.

This should be shared decision-making, not an automatic caesarean for everyone.

If pregnancy is continuing, discharge requires:

Maternal stability
No ongoing significant bleeding
Fetal wellbeing reassuring
Clear return precautions
Appropriate antenatal follow-up
Delivery plan
Blood group/Rh status
Anaemia management
Steroid/other treatment if indicated

text:
[Obstetric discharge & follow-up — RCOG-style comprehensive checklist > 15. PPROM / PRETERM PROM — ANTENATAL DISCHARGE]
This is an important distinction:

Discharge may be considered only in selected stable patients.

Before discharge:

No infection
No labour
No significant bleeding
Reassuring fetal wellbeing
Appropriate gestational age
Clear plan
Reliable access to hospital
Patient understands warning signs

RCOG patient guidance states that some women with PPROM may be offered discharge after a period of inpatient observation if they are well and not considered at high risk of early birth.

Return immediately for
Fever
Chills/flu-like symptoms
Vaginal bleeding
Green/smelly fluid
Contractions
Abdominal pain
Back pain
Reduced fetal movements

RCOG notes that women discharged with PPROM should have regular follow-up, commonly once or twice weekly depending on the clinical situation.

Delusions

text:
[Obstetric discharge & follow-up — RCOG-style comprehensive checklist > 40. MASTER FOLLOW-UP TABLE]
| Obstetric patient | Key follow-up |
|---|---|
| Normal vaginal delivery | Routine postnatal care |
| Episiotomy/1st–2nd degree tear | Perineum, pain, infection, continence |
| 3rd/4th degree tear/OASI | Specialist perineal/continence follow-up |
| Caesarean section | Wound, pain, bleeding, VTE, BP, mental health |
| PPH | Hb/anaemia, recovery, psychological wellbeing |
| Major PPH/transfusion | Anaemia + debrief + future pregnancy counselling |
| Gestational hypertension | BP + medication review |
| Pre-eclampsia | BP + symptoms + renal/LFT/FBC as indicated |
| Eclampsia | Specialist medical/obstetric follow-up |
| GDM | Postpartum diabetes testing + long-term screening |
| Anaemia | Iron treatment + Hb response |
| VTE/high risk | LMWH + duration + safety-net |
| Sepsis | Clinical recovery + antibiotics/cultures |
| PPROM | Antenatal surveillance if pregnancy ongoing |
| FGR/SGA | Growth/Doppler/CTG + delivery plan |
| Placenta praevia | Bleeding surveillance + delivery plan |
| Multiple pregnancy | Growth + maternal surveillance + delivery planning |
| Rh-negative | Anti-D assessment/documentation |
| Alloimmunisation | Specialist fetal/haematology plan |
| ICP | Symptom/LFT/bile-acid resolution |
| Cardiac disease | Cardiology/MDT plan |
| Renal disease | Renal/BP/proteinuria follow-up |
| Epilepsy | Medication + neurology |
| Thyroid disease | TFT + medication adjustment |
| NICU baby | Maternal + neonatal coordinated plan |
| Stillbirth/neonatal death | Bereavement + physical + psychological + future pregnancy care |
| Birth trauma | Debrief + mental-health assessment |
| Obesity | VTE, wound, weight and future pregnancy counselling |

52. COMPLICATION → FINDING → INVESTIGATION
| Complication | Typical findings | First investigations |
|---|---|---|
| Haemorrhage | Tachycardia, hypotension, bleeding, pallor | FBC, group/crossmatch, coagulation ± imaging |
| Infection/sepsis | Fever, tachycardia, pain, discharge | FBC, CRP, lactate, cultures, imaging/source assessment |
| Wound infection | Redness, warmth, discharge | Clinical ± wound culture |
| Pelvic collection | Fever, pelvic pain, discharge | US ± CT |
| Ileus | Distension, vomiting, no flatus | U&E ± abdominal imaging |
| Bowel injury | Peritonism, sepsis, distension | FBC/CRP/lactate + CT ± surgical assessment |
| Urinary retention | Unable to void, suprapubic pain | Bladder scan |
| Bladder injury | Haematuria, leakage, oliguria | Urinalysis, renal function, imaging/cystoscopy as appropriate |
| Ureteric injury | Flank pain, oliguria, urinary leakage | Creatinine, imaging ± CT urogram |
| DVT | Unilateral leg swelling/pain | Compression ultrasound |
| PE | Dyspnoea, chest pain, tachycardia/hypoxia | ECG, CXR ± CTPA according to pathway |
| Electrolyte disturbance | Weakness, confusion, arrhythmia | U&E |
| Anaemia | Fatigue, tachycardia, dizziness | FBC |
| Wound dehiscence | Wound separation, discharge | Clinical assessment ± urgent surgical review |
| Vault/cuff dehiscence | Pelvic pain, bleeding, discharge, tissue prolapse | Urgent pelvic assessment + surgical review |

text:
[Postoperative assessment monitoring investigations examination Gynaecology > 53. THE MRCOG POST-OP OSCE ANSWER]
If the examiner says:

"Please assess this postoperative gynaecology patient."

A strong opening is:

"I would first review the operation, anaesthetic record, intraoperative findings, blood loss, complications, drains, catheter and postoperative instructions. I would assess the patient using an ABCDE approach, review observations and fluid balance, assess pain and bleeding, examine the abdomen and wound, assess urinary and bowel function, assess for infection and thromboembolism, and investigate selectively according to my clinical findings. I would then formulate a postoperative plan including analgesia, thromboprophylaxis, mobilisation, nutrition, catheter/drain management, histology and discharge/follow-up."

That structure directly addresses the RCOG expectation of immediate, short- and long-term postoperative assessment, prevention/recognition of complications, investigation, management and follow-up.

THE “10-POINT MRCOG PRE-OP” ANSWERIf the examiner asks:“How would you prepare this patient for the procedure?”Give this structure:1. Indication“First, I would confirm the indication and urgency.”2. Maternal assessment“I would perform ABCDE assessment and assess comorbidities and haemodynamic stability.”3. Fetal assessment“I would assess fetal wellbeing, presentation, position, gestation and estimated weight as appropriate.”4. Investigations“I would obtain appropriate blood tests including FBC and group-and-save/crossmatch depending on haemorrhage risk.”5. Anaesthesia“I would involve the anaesthetist and assess airway, aspiration risk, coagulation and suitability for regional versus general anaesthesia.”6. Consent“I would explain the procedure, benefits, alternatives, material risks and consequences of refusing or delaying it.”7. Blood“I would assess haemorrhage risk and ensure appropriate blood and blood products are available.”8. Team“I would involve the appropriate senior obstetric, anaesthetic, midwifery and neonatal teams.”9. Theatre safety“I would complete the WHO surgical safety checks, antibiotics where indicated, VTE prophylaxis and equipment preparation.”10. Post-procedure plan“I would have a clear plan for maternal observations, analgesia, antibiotics where indicated, thromboprophylaxis, catheter/urine output, neonatal care, complications and follow-up.”

text:
[rcog master table > 1. NORMAL / GENERAL PREGNANCY]
| Condition | Ideal timing of birth |
|---|---|
| Uncomplicated singleton pregnancy | 40+0 weeks; spontaneous labour acceptable |
| Uncomplicated pregnancy approaching 41 weeks | Offer induction by 41+0 weeks under NICE |
| Previous uncomplicated LSCS — planned ERCS | ≥39+0 weeks |
| Previous CS + planned VBAC | Await spontaneous labour unless another indication |
| Maternal request for elective CS without medical indication | ≥39+0 weeks |
| Obesity alone | No routine early delivery solely for obesity |
| Well-controlled hypothyroidism | No alteration in timing |
| Well-controlled hyperthyroidism | No routine early birth solely for thyroid disease |
| Well-controlled epilepsy | No routine early birth solely because of epilepsy |

RCOG specifically states that well-controlled thyroid disease should not alter when/how birth occurs, and epilepsy alone is not an indication for early birth or planned CS.
source_file: rcog master table.md

text:
[rcog master table > 2. HYPERTENSIVE DISORDERS]
Chronic hypertension
| Situation | Timing |
|---|---|
| Chronic HTN, BP <160/110, no complications | Do not routinely deliver <37 weeks |
| ≥37 weeks | Timing individualized with senior obstetrician |
| BP ≥160/110 despite treatment / complications | Earlier birth may be required |
| Superimposed pre-eclampsia | Follow pre-eclampsia timing |

NICE states that planned early birth should not routinely be offered before 37 weeks when BP is below 160/110 mmHg.

Gestational hypertension
| Situation | Timing |
|---|---|
| BP <160/110 and uncomplicated | No planned birth <37 weeks |
| ≥37 weeks | Plan birth according to maternal/fetal circumstances |
| Severe hypertension / maternal or fetal compromise | Earlier delivery |
source_file: rcog master table.md

text:
[rcog master table > 3. PRE-ECLAMPSIA]
| Pre-eclampsia | Timing |
|---|---|
| <34 weeks, stable mother + fetus | Expectant management if safe |
| 34–36+6 weeks | Individualized; consider planned birth |
| ≥37+0 weeks | Initiate birth within 24–48 h |
| Severe pre-eclampsia + maternal/fetal deterioration | Deliver irrespective of gestation |

Important exam point:

Pre-eclampsia itself is not automatically “deliver at 34 weeks.”

Stable disease can be managed expectantly before 37 weeks.

Immediate/urgent delivery indications include
Uncontrolled severe hypertension
Eclampsia
Pulmonary oedema
Progressive renal dysfunction
Significant liver dysfunction
HELLP
Placental abruption
Persistent neurological symptoms
Non-reassuring fetal status
Severe FGR with fetal compromise
source_file: rcog master table.md

text:
[rcog master table > 4. DIABETES]
Pre-existing type 1 / type 2 diabetes
| Condition | Timing |
|---|---|
| Uncomplicated type 1/type 2 diabetes | 37+0–38+6 weeks |
| Poor glycaemic control | Consider earlier |
| Maternal vascular disease | Earlier according to severity |
| Fetal compromise/FGR | Earlier |
| Severe complications | Individualized urgent delivery |

NICE recommends elective birth between 37+0 and 38+6 weeks for type 1 or type 2 diabetes without other complications.

Gestational diabetes
| GDM | Timing |
|---|---|
| Diet-controlled / uncomplicated | By 40+6 weeks |
| Medication/insulin-treated | Individualize; do not automatically apply pre-existing diabetes timing |
| Poor control / macrosomia / complications | Consider earlier |
| Maternal/fetal complication | Earlier according to indication |

RCOG states women with GDM should have their baby no later than 40+6 weeks, unless complications justify earlier birth.

Exam distinction

Pre-existing DM → 37–38+6

Uncomplicated GDM → ≤40+6
source_file: rcog master table.md

text:
[rcog master table > 5. INTRAHEPATIC CHOLESTASIS OF PREGNANCY — VERY HIGH YIELD]
Based on peak bile acids:

| Bile acids | Severity | Planned birth |
|---|---|---|
| 19–39 µmol/L | Mild | By 40 weeks may be considered; expectant management also reasonable if no other risk factors |
| 40–99 µmol/L | Moderate | 38–39 weeks |
| ≥100 µmol/L | Severe | 35–36 weeks |

These are specifically RCOG ICP categories.

Memory

ICP: 19 → 40 → 100

19–39 → 40 weeks

40–99 → 38–39 weeks

≥100 → 35–36 weeks

Earlier delivery may be appropriate if there is:

pre-eclampsia
GDM
multiple pregnancy
fetal compromise
other maternal/fetal risk
source_file: rcog master table.md
section_path: 5. INTRAHEPATIC CHOLESTASIS OF PREGNANCY — VERY HIGH YIELD

text:
[rcog master table > 6. FETAL GROWTH RESTRICTION / SGA]
This is one of the most important RCOG timing questions.

First distinguish:

SGA

EFW or AC <10th centile

FGR

Pathological failure to reach genetic growth potential, particularly when accompanied by abnormal Doppler/other evidence of compromise.

Timing depends on Doppler.
| Fetal condition | Typical timing |
|---|---|
| SGA, normal UA Doppler, no other concern | Around 39 weeks / by 40 weeks |
| FGR with abnormal UA Doppler | Earlier, commonly 37 weeks range depending on severity |
| Absent/reversed end-diastolic flow | Much earlier delivery according to Doppler/CTG/DV and gestation |
| Abnormal DV / severe fetal compromise | Urgent delivery depending on gestation |
| Non-reassuring CTG | Immediate delivery |

RCOG emphasizes that delivery timing in FGR must integrate umbilical artery, MCA and ductus venosus Doppler, fetal surveillance and gestational age, rather than applying one universal week.

RCOG's updated 2026 guidance also confirms that SGA and FGR should not simply be treated as synonymous.
source_file: rcog master table.md

text:
[rcog master table > 7. PRETERM PRELABOUR RUPTURE OF MEMBRANES — PPROM]
| PPROM situation | Timing |
|---|---|
| PPROM + stable mother/fetus + no infection | Expectant management to 37 weeks |
| PPROM + chorioamnionitis | Deliver immediately after maternal stabilization |
| PPROM + fetal compromise | Deliver |
| PPROM + significant abruption | Deliver |
| PPROM + established labour | Manage labour |
| PPROM + GBS carriage | RCOG patient guidance indicates birth may be advised from 34 weeks |

RCOG's current patient guidance says that if mother and baby remain well without infection, pregnancy may be continued until 37 weeks; known GBS carriage may alter this to birth from 34 weeks.
source_file: rcog master table.md
section_path: 7. PRETERM PRELABOUR RUPTURE OF MEMBRANES — PPROM

text:
[rcog master table > 8. PLACENTA PRAEVIA]
Confirmed placenta praevia
| Situation | Timing |
|---|---|
| Uncomplicated placenta praevia | Usually 36–37 weeks |
| Heavy/recurrent bleeding | Earlier |
| Active major APH / maternal instability | Immediate delivery |
| Labour with placenta praevia | Usually CS |

RCOG's current patient information states that uncomplicated placenta praevia usually results in CS between 36 and 37 weeks, with earlier birth if significant bleeding occurs.

Placental edge at 36 weeks
<20 mm from internal os → CS generally safest
>20 mm → vaginal birth may be possible
source_file: rcog master table.md

text:
[rcog master table > 9. PLACENTA ACCRETA SPECTRUM — PAS]
| PAS | Timing |
|---|---|
| Suspected placenta accreta | Planned birth around 35–37 weeks, individualized |
| Significant bleeding / instability | Earlier |
| Uncontrolled haemorrhage | Emergency delivery |

RCOG's updated 2026 guidance has replaced the older 2018 framework and emphasizes delivery planning in specialist centres. Current RCOG patient information gives 35–37 weeks as the usual planned window depending on circumstances.

Exam memory

Accreta → 35–37

Praevia → 36–37
source_file: rcog master table.md

text:
[rcog master table > 10. VASA PRAEVIA]
| Condition | Timing |
|---|---|
| Antenatally diagnosed vasa praevia | Planned CS around 34–36 weeks |
| Labour / ROM with vasa praevia | Emergency CS |
| Fetal vessel rupture | Immediate emergency CS |

RCOG patient information recommends planned CS around 34–36 weeks.

The updated 2026 RCOG guideline draft describes a broader 34–37-week range depending on clinical circumstances.

Memory

Vasa praevia → 34–36 weeks
source_file: rcog master table.md

text:
[rcog master table > 11. MULTIPLE PREGNANCY]
Twins
| Pregnancy | Planned birth |
|---|---|
| DCDA twins | 37 weeks |
| MCDA twins | 36 weeks |
| MCMA twins | 32–34 weeks |
| Triplets | 35 weeks |

These are RCOG's usual recommended timings for uncomplicated multiple pregnancy.

Memory

DCDA 37

MCDA 36

MCMA 32–34

Triplets 35
source_file: rcog master table.md

text:
[rcog master table > 12. BREECH]
| Situation | Timing |
|---|---|
| Uncomplicated term breech | No indication for early delivery solely because breech |
| Planned CS | Usually ≥39 weeks |
| Labour with breech | Individualized |
| Fetal/maternal indication | Earlier |

RCOG focuses on mode of birth and ECV rather than recommending routine preterm delivery for breech.
source_file: rcog master table.md

text:
[rcog master table > 13. PREVIOUS CAESAREAN]
| Situation | Timing |
|---|---|
| Planned repeat CS | ≥39+0 weeks |
| VBAC | Await spontaneous labour |
| Previous classical CS | Planned earlier according to scar type/individual circumstances |
| Previous uterine rupture | Earlier planned CS, individualized |
| Placenta praevia/accreta + previous CS | Follow PAS/placenta timing |

RCOG emphasizes the neonatal respiratory disadvantage of elective CS before 39 weeks.
source_file: rcog master table.md

text:
[rcog master table > 14. RED-CELL ALLOIMMUNISATION / FETAL ANAEMIA]
Timing depends on:

antibody
titre/history
MCA-PSV
fetal anaemia
intrauterine transfusion
hydrops
fetal condition
General principle
| Situation | Timing |
|---|---|
| Stable alloimmunised pregnancy | Continue surveillance |
| Significant fetal anaemia | IUT and/or delivery according to gestation |
| Repeated IUT | Continue until appropriate gestation |
| Severe fetal compromise/hydrops | Earlier delivery |

Do not memorize a single universal week.

The decision is based on fetal anaemia and specialist fetal-medicine assessment.
source_file: rcog master table.md

text:
[rcog master table > 15. THROMBOCYTOPENIA / ITP]
| Situation | Timing |
|---|---|
| Maternal ITP alone | No indication for early delivery |
| Stable platelet count | Term birth |
| Severe maternal bleeding / complications | Individualized |
| Fetal concerns | Individualized |

Important:

ITP does not automatically mean early delivery or CS.

Mode of birth is usually based on obstetric indications rather than fetal platelet count alone.
source_file: rcog master table.md

text:
[rcog master table > 16. EPILEPSY]

Below is the single consolidated version, combining the previous tables and correcting the areas where a fixed gestational age would be misleading. RCOG is used as the primary framework and NICE where it provides the relevant UK timing recommendation. Exact timing must always be individualized when maternal/fetal deterioration, abnormal Dopplers, infection, bleeding or other complications are present.

🧠 ONE-LINE MRCOG MEMORY

MCMA 32–34 → Vasa 34–36 → Triplets 35 → Severe ICP 35–36 → PAS 35–37 → MCDA 36 → Praevia 36–37+6 → DCDA 37 → PPROM 37 → Pre-eclampsia 37 → Pre-existing DM 37–38+6 → ICP 38–39 → ERCS 39 → GDM ≤40+6 → Postdates IOL 41.

The major exceptions

FGR, hypertension, PPROM, cardiac disease, alloimmunisation, polyhydramnios/oligohydramnios and complicated multiple pregnancy are NOT safely reduced to one gestational-age number.

And:

Maternal or fetal compromise overrides the planned gestational age.

Examples: eclampsia, uncontrolled severe hypertension, HELLP, pulmonary oedema, major abruption, pathological CTG, severe fetal hypoxia, vasa praevia rupture, cord prolapse, uterine rupture, severe infection/sepsis or maternal collapse → urgent delivery when indicated.

Definition
Primary infertility

No previous pregnancy despite regular unprotected intercourse.

Secondary infertility

Difficulty conceiving after a previous pregnancy, regardless of outcome.

Important OSCE definition

Traditionally:

12 months of regular unprotected intercourse without conception.

But investigate earlier when there are risk factors such as:

age ≥36 years
irregular/absent periods
previous pelvic infection
previous ectopic pregnancy
previous pelvic surgery
known endometriosis

suspected male-factor infertility
sexual dysfunction.
Frequency of intercourse

How often?

Any dyspareunia?
Erectile/ejaculatory problems?
Use of lubricants?
Previous contraception?

A practical recommendation:

intercourse every 2–3 days throughout the cycle optimises chance of conception.

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 4. OVULATION ASSESSMENT]
History

Evidence suggesting ovulation:

regular cycles
premenstrual symptoms
mittelschmerz
cyclical breast tenderness
cervical mucus changes.

But symptoms alone do not prove ovulation.

Mid-luteal progesterone

Classic OSCE point:

Day 21 progesterone

Only appropriate for:

28-day cycle.

For other cycles:

Measure approximately 7 days before the expected next period.

Examples:

| Cycle | Approximate progesterone timing |
|---|---|
| 28 days | Day 21 |
| 30 days | Day 23 |
| 35 days | Day 28 |

NICE specifically recommends timing progesterone according to cycle length rather than blindly using day 21 in women with prolonged/irregular cycles.

Interpretation

A clearly elevated mid-luteal progesterone supports ovulation.

Common exam teaching:

>30 nmol/L → strong evidence of ovulation.
Lower values do not necessarily mean anovulation if sampling was mistimed.

Important MRCOG point: do not interpret one low progesterone as definitive anovulation.

AMH
Anti-Müllerian hormone reflects:

ovarian response to stimulation.
Low AMH

Suggests:

reduced ovarian reserve.

Possible causes:

increasing age
POI
previous ovarian surgery
chemotherapy
radiotherapy.

Crucial OSCE distinction

AMH does NOT reliably predict natural fertility.

It is primarily useful for:

Do not tell a patient:

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 12. MALE INFERTILITY]
Semen analysis

First-line male investigation.

Important parameters:

Current WHO reference limits vary with edition/laboratory; for MRCOG, know the commonly used WHO 2021 lower reference limits:

| Parameter | Lower reference value |
|---|---|
| Volume | ≥1.4 mL |
| Sperm concentration | ≥16 million/mL |
| Total sperm number | ≥39 million/ejaculate |
| Total motility | ≥42% |
| Progressive motility | ≥30% |
| Normal morphology | ≥4% |
| Vitality | ≥54% |
| pH | ≥7.2 |
OSCE warning

These are reference limits, not a fertility/infertility cut-off.

A man below a reference value can still father a child, and a man above all values can still be infertile.

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 13. SEMEN SAMPLE TECHNIQUE]
Tell the patient:

abstinence approximately 2–7 days
collect entire ejaculate
preferably by masturbation
sterile container
avoid lubricants unless fertility-safe
deliver promptly according to laboratory instructions
keep sample near body temperature.

If abnormal:

Repeat semen analysis, generally after approximately 3 months, because spermatogenesis takes about 74 days.

If severe abnormality:

repeat sooner according to fertility-service protocol
examine testes
hormonal testing
consider genetic testing.

medications
idiopathic hirsutism.
21. VIRILISATION = RED FLAG

Features:

deep voice
clitoromegaly
rapid severe hirsutism
increased muscle mass
male-pattern alopecia
rapid onset.

Think:

Androgen-secreting ovarian/adrenal tumour until proven otherwise.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 22. PCOS LABS]
Possible tests:

total testosterone
free testosterone/free androgen index
SHBG
DHEAS when adrenal source suspected
17-hydroxyprogesterone
TSH
prolactin when indicated
pregnancy test.
Exclude mimics
pregnancy
thyroid disease
hyperprolactinaemia
hypothalamic amenorrhoea
POI
Cushing syndrome
androgen-secreting tumour
non-classical CAH.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 23. PCOS ULTRASOUND]
Polycystic ovarian morphology is not synonymous with PCOS.

Modern ultrasound criteria depend on:

transducer frequency
ovarian morphology
follicle count
ovarian volume.

Classic teaching:

increased follicle number and/or
ovarian volume ≥10 mL.

The exact follicle-number threshold has changed with improved ultrasound technology, so in an MRCOG station state:

“I would apply the current ultrasound threshold appropriate to the equipment and guideline rather than relying on an outdated fixed follicle count.”
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 24. PCOS METABOLIC SCREENING]
Assess:

BP
BMI/waist
glucose status
lipid profile.
OGTT

Particularly important where diabetes risk is high.

PCOS is associated with:

insulin resistance
impaired glucose tolerance
type 2 diabetes
dyslipidaemia
hypertension
obstructive sleep apnoea.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 25. PCOS INFERTILITY MANAGEMENT]
Stepwise

1. Lifestyle

nutrition
physical activity
weight management
sleep
psychological support.

2. Ovulation induction

Current international guidance generally favours:

Letrozole as first-line pharmacological ovulation induction for anovulatory infertility in PCOS when there are no other infertility factors.

Older MRCOG material may mention clomifene as first-line, so know the distinction between older NICE evidence and current international practice. NICE's older fertility evidence describes clomifene/metformin strategies, whereas contemporary PCOS guidance has moved toward letrozole.

Letrozole

Common regimen:

2.5–5 mg daily
usually for 5 days early in cycle
dose adjusted according to response.
Clomifene

Traditional regimen:

50 mg daily × 5 days
increase to 100–150 mg if necessary.

Clomifene can cause:

multiple pregnancy
ovarian enlargement
anti-oestrogenic endometrial/cervical effects.

Older NICE evidence notes approximately 10% multiple pregnancy risk with clomifene and recommends ultrasound monitoring particularly in the first cycle.

Metformin

Useful particularly when:

insulin resistance/metabolic features
glucose intolerance
PCOS.

But it is not the most effective ovulation-induction drug compared with letrozole.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 26. SECOND-LINE PCOS OVULATION INDUCTION]
If oral ovulation induction fails:

gonadotrophins
laparoscopic ovarian drilling in selected patients
IVF where appropriate.
Gonadotrophins

Risks:

multiple pregnancy
OHSS.

Need:

ultrasound monitoring
follicular tracking
careful dose adjustment.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 27. AMENORRHOEA — OSCE]
First question

“Could you be pregnant?”

Always exclude pregnancy first.

Causes

Think:

Pregnancy

↓

Hypothalamus

weight loss
excessive exercise
stress
chronic illness

↓

Pituitary

hyperprolactinaemia
pituitary tumour
Sheehan syndrome

↓

Ovary

PCOS
POI

↓

Uterus/outflow

Asherman syndrome
cervical stenosis
Müllerian anomalies.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 28. AMENORRHOEA INVESTIGATIONS]
First-line
urine/serum β-hCG
TSH
prolactin when indicated
FSH/LH
estradiol
pelvic ultrasound.

Further tests according to findings:

testosterone
DHEAS
17-OHP
pituitary MRI
karyotype
AMH
progesterone withdrawal testing in selected situations.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 29. FSH INTERPRETATION]
High FSH + low estradiol

→ ovarian failure/POI.

Low/normal FSH + low estradiol

→ hypothalamic/pituitary hypogonadism.

Normal/low FSH + normal/high androgen

→ consider PCOS.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 30. HYPERPROLACTINAEMIA]
Symptoms
amenorrhoea
oligomenorrhoea
infertility
galactorrhoea
reduced libido
vaginal dryness.

Mass effect:

headache
visual field defect.

NICE notes that hyperprolactinaemia can produce galactorrhoea, menstrual disturbance and infertility and that prolactin testing should be targeted to women with symptoms of ovulatory disorder, galactorrhoea or suspected pituitary tumour.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 31. PROLACTIN — CAUSES]
Physiological
pregnancy
breastfeeding
sleep
stress
nipple stimulation.
Pathological
prolactinoma
hypothyroidism
renal failure
liver disease
chest-wall stimulation/pathology.
Drugs

Classic causes:

antipsychotics
metoclopramide
domperidone
some antidepressants
opioids.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 32. PROLACTIN — OSCE TECHNIQUE]
If mildly raised:

Repeat prolactin.
Avoid excessive stress.
Consider timing.
Review medication.
Check pregnancy.
Check TSH.
Consider macroprolactin.
If persistent/significant → endocrinology assessment ± MRI.
Macroprolactin

Important cause of apparent biochemical hyperprolactinaemia.

Often:

high laboratory prolactin
relatively few clinical symptoms.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 33. PROLACTINOMA]
Microadenoma
<10 mm.
Macroadenoma
≥10 mm.

Possible macroadenoma symptoms:

headache
visual field defect
cranial nerve symptoms.
Treatment

First-line:

Dopamine agonist

Usually:

cabergoline.

Alternative:

bromocriptine.

NICE identifies dopamine agonists as treatment for hyperprolactinaemia.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 34. VISUAL FIELD DEFECT]
Pituitary macroadenoma can compress:

optic chiasm

producing:

bitemporal hemianopia.

OSCE:

ask about visual symptoms
formal visual fields if indicated
urgent imaging if neurological/visual symptoms.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 35. PREMATURE OVARIAN INSUFFICIENCY — POI]
Definition

Loss of ovarian activity before age 40.

Presentation:

amenorrhoea
oligomenorrhoea
infertility
hot flushes
night sweats
vaginal dryness
reduced libido.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 36. POI CAUSES]
Genetic
Turner syndrome
mosaic Turner
FMR1 premutation.
Autoimmune
autoimmune thyroid disease
Addison disease
other autoimmune disorders.
Iatrogenic
chemotherapy
radiotherapy
ovarian surgery.
Infectious/metabolic

Less common.

Idiopathic

Common.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 37. POI INVESTIGATION]
Typical:

repeatedly raised FSH
low estradiol.

Current diagnostic approaches generally require two elevated FSH measurements, separated by at least 4–6 weeks, in the appropriate clinical setting.

Do not diagnose POI from:

one random FSH alone.

Investigate:

pregnancy
TSH
prolactin when indicated
karyotype
FMR1 premutation
autoimmune testing according to clinical context.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 38. POI COUNSELLING]
Major consequences:

Fertility

Spontaneous intermittent ovarian activity can occur.

Therefore:

POI ≠ absolute sterility.

But natural conception is significantly reduced.

Long-term consequences
osteoporosis
cardiovascular disease
urogenital atrophy
psychological impact.
Management

Unless contraindicated:

Hormone replacement until approximately the natural age of menopause.

Also:

calcium/vitamin D adequacy
weight-bearing exercise
smoking cessation
cardiovascular risk assessment
bone health
fertility counselling.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 39. POI AND FERTILITY]
Most effective established fertility option when ovarian reserve is severely compromised:

oocyte donation IVF.

Discuss:

donor eggs
embryo donation where appropriate
adoption
fertility preservation before gonadotoxic treatment where possible.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 40. ENDOMETRIOSIS AND INFERTILITY]
Endometriosis may cause infertility through:

inflammation
altered pelvic anatomy
adhesions
tubal dysfunction
impaired ovarian reserve
endometrioma
altered sperm–oocyte interaction
implantation effects.

RCOG notes that endometriosis is associated with infertility and may present with dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, bowel/bladder pain and difficulty conceiving.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 41. ENDOMETRIOSIS HISTORY]
Ask:

Pain
dysmenorrhoea
chronic pelvic pain
deep dyspareunia
dyschezia
cyclical rectal pain
cyclical haematuria
cyclical urinary symptoms.
Fertility
duration trying
previous infertility
previous surgery
previous IVF.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 42. ENDOMETRIOSIS EXAMINATION]
Look for:

uterosacral nodularity
fixed retroverted uterus
reduced uterine mobility
adnexal mass
posterior fornix tenderness.

But:

Normal examination does NOT exclude endometriosis.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 43. ENDOMETRIOMA]
Ultrasound typically:

homogeneous low-level internal echoes
“ground-glass” appearance
ovarian cyst.

Important fertility issue:

Both endometriosis itself and ovarian surgery can reduce ovarian reserve.

RCOG specifically highlights the fertility implications of surgery for endometriomas.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 44. ENDOMETRIOSIS — INVESTIGATION]
First-line imaging
transvaginal ultrasound.

MRI:

useful for deep infiltrating disease
surgical planning
complex anatomy.
Laparoscopy

Historically diagnostic gold standard.

However, modern management increasingly uses:

symptoms
clinical examination
ultrasound
MRI where indicated

rather than requiring diagnostic laparoscopy for every patient.

45. ENDOMETRIOSIS + INFERTILITY

Management depends on:

age
ovarian reserve
severity
symptoms
duration infertility
tubal status
semen analysis
previous surgery
endometrioma size
previous treatment.
Important OSCE principle

If the primary goal is conception:

Do not automatically suppress ovulation with hormonal treatment.

Hormonal suppression:

improves pain
prevents ovulation
therefore does not treat infertility itself.

NICE/RCOG evidence notes that medical treatment without pelvic pain is not an appropriate fertility strategy.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 46. ENDOMETRIOSIS SURGERY]
Possible:

ablation/excision
adhesiolysis
endometrioma surgery.

But counselling must include:

reduced ovarian reserve
ovarian damage
adhesions
recurrence
surgical complications.

Therefore:

fertility-preservation implications must be discussed before ovarian surgery.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 47. IVF IN ENDOMETRIOSIS]
Consider IVF when:

tubal damage
significant male factor
advanced age
prolonged infertility
reduced ovarian reserve
previous unsuccessful treatment
severe disease.

The decision should be individualised.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 48. UNEXPLAINED INFERTILITY]
Diagnosis only after:

ovulation established
tubes patent
semen reasonably satisfactory
no obvious pelvic pathology.
Do not say:

“Everything is normal.”

Instead:

“Standard investigations have not identified a cause.”

This is more accurate.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 49. IMPORTANT FERTILITY NUMBERS — RAPID REVISION]
| Parameter | High-yield number |
|---|---|
| Infertility definition | 12 months |
| Normal menstrual cycle | ~21–35 days |
| Mid-luteal progesterone | ~7 days before expected period |
| Strong evidence of ovulation | commonly >30 nmol/L |
| PCOS diagnostic features | 2 of 3 |
| PCOS classic ovarian volume | ≥10 mL |
| Hirsutism mFG | traditionally ≥8 |
| POI age | <40 years |
| Prolactinoma microadenoma | <10 mm |
| Prolactinoma macroadenoma | ≥10 mm |
| Semen volume | ≥1.4 mL |
| Sperm concentration | ≥16 million/mL |
| Total sperm number | ≥39 million |
| Total motility | ≥42% |
| Progressive motility | ≥30% |
| Normal morphology | ≥4% |
| Vitality | ≥54% |
| Adult testicular volume | ~15–25 mL |
50. MRCOG PART 3 — “ABNORMAL RESULT → CAUSE”
FSH HIGH + E2 LOW

Think:

POI
ovarian failure.
FSH LOW/NORMAL + E2 LOW

Think:

hypothalamic amenorrhoea
pituitary disease.
PROLACTIN HIGH

Think:

pregnancy
drugs
hypothyroidism
prolactinoma
renal disease
macroprolactin
physiological stress.
TESTOSTERONE HIGH

Think:

PCOS
androgen-secreting tumour
CAH
exogenous androgen.

Rapid virilisation:

tumour until proven otherwise.

DHEAS HIGH

Think:

adrenal androgen excess.

Very high levels:

adrenal tumour must be considered.

HIGH AMH

Think:

PCOS
large follicular pool
increased response to stimulation.
LOW AMH

Think:

diminished ovarian reserve
increasing age
POI
ovarian surgery
chemotherapy.

But:

low AMH ≠ no natural pregnancy.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 51. INFERTILITY OSCE — COMPLETE STATION ALGORITHM]
If examiner says:

“A 32-year-old woman has been trying to conceive for 18 months. Assess her.”

Say:

Step 1 — Establish the problem
duration
primary/secondary
intercourse frequency
contraception
age of both partners.
Step 2 — Menstrual history
cycle length
regularity
LMP
dysmenorrhoea
amenorrhoea
ovulatory symptoms.
Step 3 — Look for specific causes
PCOS
endometriosis
tubal disease
POI
hyperprolactinaemia
uterine pathology.
Step 4 — Sexual history
frequency
timing
erectile dysfunction
ejaculation
dyspareunia
libido.
Step 5 — Previous history
PID
STI
ectopic
surgery
chemotherapy
radiotherapy
endometriosis.
Step 6 — Examination
BMI
BP
hirsutism/acne
thyroid
galactorrhoea
abdominal examination
pelvic examination.
Step 7 — Investigations

Woman:

ovulation
ultrasound
targeted hormones
tubal assessment.

Man:

semen analysis.
Step 8 — Management

Treat the identified cause:

PCOS → ovulation induction
tubal disease → surgery/IVF depending on severity
severe male factor → ICSI
endometriosis → individualised surgery/ART
POI → donor-oocyte IVF
hyperprolactinaemia → dopamine agonist
unexplained infertility → fertility-service management according to age/duration.
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 52. HIGH-YIELD MRCOG COUNSELLING PHRASES]
When AMH is low

“AMH is primarily a marker of ovarian reserve and expected response to ovarian stimulation. It does not by itself diagnose infertility or predict whether you can conceive naturally.”

When PCOS is diagnosed

“PCOS is a diagnosis of exclusion. I would ensure alternative causes of menstrual irregularity and androgen excess have been considered.”

When prolactin is raised

“I would first confirm the abnormality and exclude physiological, drug-related and secondary causes before assuming a prolactinoma.”

When semen analysis is abnormal

“A single abnormal semen analysis does not establish permanent male infertility; I would repeat the test and assess the man clinically.”

With endometriosis

“I would balance symptom control with reproductive goals and avoid unnecessary ovarian surgery where it could compromise ovarian reserve.”

With POI

“POI significantly reduces fertility but does not mean spontaneous conception is impossible because intermittent ovarian activity can occur.”
source_file: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS.md
section_path: REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS

text:
[REPRODUCTIVE MEDICINE — MRCOG PART 3 OSCE ATLAS > 53. MRCOG PART 3 — COMMON EXAMINER TRAPS]
Trap 1

“AMH 0.8 = infertile.”

❌ Wrong.

Trap 2

“Day 21 progesterone for everyone.”

❌ Wrong.

Use approximately 7 days before the expected next period.

Trap 3

“Polycystic ovaries = PCOS.”

❌ Wrong.

Need the appropriate diagnostic criteria and exclusion of other causes.

Trap 4

“High prolactin = prolactinoma.”

❌ Wrong.

Check pregnancy, medications, hypothyroidism, macroprolactin and other causes.

Trap 5

“Normal semen analysis excludes male infertility.”

❌ Wrong.

Male fertility is multifactorial.

Trap 6

“Endometriosis → laparoscopy immediately.”

❌ Not necessarily.

Use appropriate imaging and individualised management.

Trap 7

“POI means no chance of pregnancy.”

❌ Wrong.

Intermittent ovarian activity can occur, although fertility is markedly reduced.

Trap 8

“Infertility is the woman's problem.”

❌ Major MRCOG communication error.

Always assess both partners.
